title: Ravens to acquire QB Jacoby Brissett from Cardinals
summary: The Baltimore Ravens are acquiring Jacoby Brissett from the Arizona Cardinals amid their injury crisis at quarterback. The two teams are expected to finalize the deal this weekend ahead of next Tuesday’s trade deadline, per ESPN’s Adam Schefter. The Ravens already need to make roster adjustments ahead of their Thursday night matchup with the Jacksonville […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 01: Jacoby Brissett #7 of the Arizona Cardinals drops back to pass during a game against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium on November 01, 2026 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens are acquiring Jacoby Brissett from the Arizona Cardinals amid their injury crisis at quarterback. The two teams are expected to finalize the deal this weekend ahead of next Tuesday’s trade deadline, per ESPN’s Adam Schefter . The Ravens already need to make roster adjustments ahead of their Thursday night matchup with the Jacksonville Jaguars, so it would be easier to add Brissett after the game. He could be in Baltimore as soon as Friday and start in Week 10 against the Los Angeles Chargers, according to Sports Illustrated’s Albert Breer . The Ravens are already down their top two passers. Lamar Jackson is set to undergo surgery on his right thumb, while Tyler Huntley is dealing with a case of turf toe. Both will be placed on injured reserve and could miss the rest of the season. Undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano, who closed out Sunday’s loss to the Buffalo Bills, will start on Thursday night with Austin Reed and Kedon Slovis, who were signed this week, as depth. Brissett, 33, profiles as an instant upgrade over Fagnano who can run Baltimore’s offense until (and unless) Jackson returns. Elevating the unit to keep the team’s playoff hopes alive, though, seems like a long shot unless the Ravens’ defense makes significant improvements. Brissett is a capable passer, but executing a new offense at a high level is a tall task even for a 10-year veteran. He does not have much, if any, experience in a scheme similar to Declan Doyle’s. This year, Brissett started the Cardinals’ first seven games with underwhelming numbers relative to his career-best 2025 campaign. He was benched for Gardner Minshew in Week 8, making him surplus to requirements in Arizona and available for the quarterback-needy Ravens. There are a few moving parts holding up the deal beyond Thursday night’s game. Brissett is owed $4.85 million over the rest of the season, a number Baltimore cannot currently accommodate under the salary cap. Asking the Cardinals to eat some of his salary would raise the price of the deal, something the Ravens will prefer to avoid. Once they get out of Thursday’s game, they can restructure a contract or two to complete the trade. General manager Eric DeCosta could also be shopping one or two of his own players to backfill draft capital and clear cap space. This is part of a careful balancing act as the Ravens try to remain optimistic but realistic about their chances this season. Originally a Patriots third-round pick in 2016, Brissett backed up Tom Brady as a rookie and started two games. He was traded to the Colts the following year after an injury to Andrew Luck and started 15 games. Luck’s return in 2018 returned Brissett to a backup role, but he was once again thrust into the starting job following Luck’s sudden retirement during the 2019 preseason. He started 15 games that year but did not play well enough to earn the Colts’ trust heading into 2020. Brissett served as Philip Rivers’ backup during his final year in Indianapolis before a series of one-year stints in Miami, Cleveland, Washington, and New England (again). He won the Browns’ starting job in 2022 but otherwise occupied a backup/bridge role, including five starts ahead of a rookie Drake Maye in 2024. Brissett signed with the Cardinals in 2025 to back up Kyler Murray and emerged as a starter after the former No. 1 pick went down. He finished the season with 240.4 passing yards per game, the seventh-most in the league, though that was also a result of negative game scripts. Arizona opted to keep Brissett as their starter after hiring Mike LaFleur this offseason, allowing him to negotiate a raise that ultimately makes him more expensive for the Ravens. He is currently slated to hit free agency after the season. What should the Ravens do at the trade deadline? | Baltimore Beatdown
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: NFL trade deadline: Buffalo Bills trade candidate – Budda Baker
summary: Time to highlight another safety for the Buffalo Bills ahead of this year’s NFL trade deadline Taking center stage today is Cardinals safety Budda Baker, a 10th-year, smaller, do-everything safety with 8,999 career snaps entering Week 9 who resides on an 3-5 Arizona team that has surprising wins thus far on its 2026 resume but […]
full_text: Time to highlight another safety for the Buffalo Bills ahead of this year’s NFL trade deadline Taking center stage today is Cardinals safety Budda Baker, a 10th-year, smaller, do-everything safety with 8,999 career snaps entering Week 9 who resides on an 3-5 Arizona team that has surprising wins thus far on its 2026 resume but doesn’t feel like a true NFC contender. This article is the tenth in the trade-candidate series I’ll continue to sprinkle onto the site until the actual trade deadline until November 10. Past installments in this series: Derwin James , Brian Thomas Jr. Jessie Bates , Tariq Woolen , Amani Hooker , Antoine Winfield Jr. , Cam Bynum , Zack Baun , Josh Downs Age: 30 A second-round pick in 2017 after an awesome career at the University of Washington, Baker quickly became a key piece on the Cardinals defense, logging 515 snaps as a rookie before 939 in his second season. He’s played over 1,000 in five seasons since. Baker’s first interception came in his fourth professional since, and since the start of 2020, he has nine picks. In his 10 seasons to date, Baker also has 48 pass breakups, and averages 125 tackles and six tackles for loss per year. 2026 snap splits Box: 45.6% Free safety: 38.8% Slot corner: 10.5% Defensive line: 4.7% Baker is listed at 5’10” and 190 pounds. He’s long lived in the box and been plenty productive there. He plays like a small extra linebacker on the field with coverage ability. His career missed tackle rate is 12.3%, which isn’t ridiculously good but given how often he’s near the football, it’s respectable. That rate in 2026 is currently 13.7%, the lowest rate he’s managed since a very low 7.6% in 2023. As he’s gotten older, Arizona has transitioned Baker’s role closer to the line of scrimmage. The 2024 campaign was the last in which he played the most snaps at free safety. Last season marked this move into the box, and he’s stayed there more than any other pre-snap alignment in the first eight games of 2026. How he’d fit with Bills Baker is a good, versatile football player. I’ve always thought he was a touch overrated because he’s never been a true star in coverage. He’s a magnet to the football, plays with insane energy and reckless abandon. Do the Bills need a box safety who can play a little free safety in a pinch? Not really. Cole Bishop has proven to be best in that role, and he’s the one constant in Buffalo’s safety room right now. If anything, they could use a rangy, center-field type. Baker did play that role earlier in his career. At nearly 31, that’s simply not his specialty anymore. Financial obligation for Bills to trade for him 2026 salary: $14.415M If the Bills trade for Baker after Week 9, they’d be on the hook for $7.2M in prorated 2026 base salary. Buffalo has roughly $4M in 2026 space currently, so they’d most likely ask Arizona to eat some of Baker’s remaining salary to facilitate this trade. In 2027, his base salary is $16M. Projected cost to acquire Using Syndicate32.com’s trade machine , the projected cost to trade for Baker is a late third-round pick in 2027 . That feels a bit rich given his age, but his reputation as a tackling machine could keep the compensation in that range. Should the Bills trade for Budda Baker? This is the one deal I’m essentially all the way out on for the Bills. And I’ll be brief with my rationale. Baker is good. He’d help the Bills defense. No doubt. Stability across the board. But he turns 31 in January, is pretty costly, and Buffalo would get the most out of his current-day talents by placing him in the box, where Bishop is clearly at his best. Plus, you’re likely sending a third or fourth-round pick to Arizona for him, not a late Day 3 selection. Baker would simply cause too much disruption in the Bills defensive scheme and on the books for me to view this trade as tenable. But if the Bills really do want to add a veteran safety with a high floor, he might be the only option available.

title: Buffalo Bills record book Week 9: Josh Allen, James Cook, Greg Rousseau chase history
summary: Last week was a busy one for the Buffalo Bills’ Record Book. Josh Allen, Greg Rousseau, and Tyler Bass all gave us reasons to put down our pencils and pick up the permanent markers. A few records that were on our watch list are now officially in the books, and we can put the erasers […]
full_text: Last week was a busy one for the Buffalo Bills’ Record Book. Josh Allen, Greg Rousseau, and Tyler Bass all gave us reasons to put down our pencils and pick up the permanent markers. A few records that were on our watch list are now officially in the books, and we can put the erasers away for those. Allen moved past Jim Kelly on the franchise touchdown list, Rousseau climbed past Darryl Talley in career sacks, and Bass continued rewriting Buffalo’s kicking records. That’s three fewer things to keep track of, but don’t worry, we’ve still got plenty to watch. _____________________________________________________________________________ Chapter 1: Sure Things Dawson Knox — One Yard Away Dawson Knox doesn’t need much to move up Buffalo’s all-time receiving list. In fact, one yard will do it. Knox enters Week 9 with 2,736 career receiving yards, tied with James Lofton for 16th in franchise history. His next receiving yard would put him ahead of the Hall of Fame wide receiver. But Knox might want to keep an eye on Khalil Shakir. The Bills’ receiver has 2,666 career receiving yards, just 70 behind Knox. With the season only half over, this is going to be a teammate race through Week 18. _____________________________________________________________________________ Chapter 2: A Good Bet Josh Allen — The 5,000-Yard Club Josh Allen needs just nine rushing yards to reach 5,000 for his career. After picking up 30 against Baltimore, the Buffalo quarterback sits at 4,991. Nine yards doesn’t sound like much for Allen, but remember, he managed just one rushing yard against Las Vegas three weeks ago. So, we’re keeping the pencil handy for this one. Josh Allen — Passing Peyton Manning Peyton Manning holds the NFL record for the most combined touchdowns through a player’s first 10 seasons with 322. Allen is sitting at 321, and he still has plenty of football left to play in his ninth year. One more touchdown, whether it’s through the air or on the ground, would tie Manning. Two would give Allen the record outright. James Cook — Catching His Quarterback James Cook has been keeping our pencil and eraser busy. His pursuit of Josh Allen on Buffalo’s all-time rushing list started in the Superhuman chapter, moved up to Not Impossible, slipped back to Superhuman, and now he’s made it all the way to A Good Bet. Cook has 4,966 career rushing yards, just 25 behind Allen’s 4,991. He’ll need to outgain his quarterback by 26 yards to take over fourth place on the franchise leaderboard. Like Knox and Shakir, this is one that could prove to be a race – although we will likely have a winner before Week 18 here. _____________________________________________________________________________ Chapter 3: Not Impossible Josh Allen — Chasing Two Hall of Famers Allen has 88 career rushing touchdowns, putting him two away from tying Eric Dickerson and Curtis Martin at 90. Two rushing touchdowns in one game certainly isn’t out of the question for Buffalo’s quarterback. He’s done it before. But with James Cook carrying the ball and Allen also looking to do damage through the air, we’re not ready to call this one a sure thing. Greg Rousseau — A New Personal Best Greg Rousseau already has seven sacks this season, just one shy of his career high of eight, which he reached in both 2022 and 2024. One sack against the Minnesota Vikings would tie that mark. Two would give him nine on the season and a new career best, with plenty of games still on the calendar this year. _____________________________________________________________________________ Chapter 4: Superhuman Greg Rousseau — Chasing Mario Williams Rousseau has already passed Darryl Talley on Buffalo’s career sack list, but the next name is a little farther away. Mario Williams recorded 43 sacks during his time with the Bills. Rousseau has 39, meaning he needs four to tie Williams and 4.5 to move past him. That’s a pretty tall order for one game. But this is the Superhuman chapter, after all. We wouldn’t be doing our job if we didn’t leave room for something a little ridiculous. _____________________________________________________________________________ We’ll keep the pencils sharpened, the erasers handy, and the permanent markers ready. With the way these records have been moving around lately, there’s a good chance we’ll need all three before the final whistle blows Monday night.
author: Rachel Auberger

title: Buffalo Bills Week 9 rooting interests: Who Bills Mafia Should Cheer For
summary: That was an interesting weekend of football. The Buffalo Bills won, although I’m still trying to figure out how. Seems like that’s happened a lot this season, but, hey, no one ever claimed being a member of Bills Mafia was easy.  Anyway, the Bills won. The Chiefs lost. And, as tough as being a Bills […]
full_text: That was an interesting weekend of football. The Buffalo Bills won, although I’m still trying to figure out how. Seems like that’s happened a lot this season, but, hey, no one ever claimed being a member of Bills Mafia was easy. Anyway, the Bills won. The Chiefs lost. And, as tough as being a Bills fan can be, there may have been a little sweetness in seeing Patrick Mahomes holding the ball when the clock hit zero, unable to get the job done. Really, the only thing that could have made Week 8 any better would have been a Patriots loss. But they say beggars can’t be choosers, and when it comes to New England, the only team to have bested the Bills up to this point, we have to be beggars. At least until Week 13, when Allen and Co. get a chance to even the score. When the dust settled and the lights went out in stadiums across the league Sunday night, the Buffalo Bills were sitting alone atop the AFC. And that sure looked nice. So, let’s take a look at who we, as members of Bills Mafia, need to be rooting for this weekend. After all, there’s a lot of football to be played before the Bills take the field Monday night, and we need something to do while we wait. _____________________________________________________________________________ AFC Standings — Through Week 8 1. Buffalo Bills (6-1) 2. Denver Broncos (6-2) 3. Pittsburgh Steelers (6-2) 4. Jacksonville Jaguars (5-2) 5. Kansas City Chiefs (5-2) 6. Cincinnati Bengals (5-2) 7. New England Patriots (5-3) 8. Cleveland Browns (5-3) 9. Las Vegas Raiders (4-4) 10. Baltimore Ravens (4-4) 11. Houston Texans (2-5) 12. New York Jets (2-6) 13. Indianapolis Colts (2-6) 14. Miami Dolphins (1-6) 15. Tennessee Titans (1-7) 16. Los Angeles Chargers (0-7) _____________________________________________________________________________ AFC East Buffalo Bills at Minnesota Vikings Root for: Bills The Bills have worked their way to the top of the AFC, and now the job is to stay there. A win in Minnesota would keep Buffalo in control of its own path toward the No. 1 seed, regardless of what happens around the league on Sunday. Go Bills! Green Bay Packers at New England Patriots Root for: Packers The Patriots are the only team to have beaten Buffalo this season, and they’re still the biggest threat to the Bills in the AFC East. New England also holds the head-to-head tiebreaker, at least until the two meet again in Week 13. A Packers win would give Buffalo a little more breathing room at the top of the division. Go Pack Go! Detroit Lions at Miami Dolphins Root for: Lions Miami is sitting at the bottom of the AFC East with just one win, and there’s no reason to help the Dolphins climb out of that hole. A Detroit win keeps another division rival further behind Buffalo, and that’s good enough for us. New York Jets at Kansas City Chiefs Root for: Jets Yes, we’re rooting for the Jets. Kansas City is still a threat to Buffalo’s hold on the top spot in the AFC, and another Chiefs loss would go a long way toward keeping the Bills there. The Jets, meanwhile, are far enough behind Buffalo that we can afford to let them have this one. Just this once. J-E-T-S! JETS! JETS! JETS! _____________________________________________________________________________ Rest of the AFC Jacksonville Jaguars at Baltimore Ravens Root for: Ravens Jacksonville is a little too close to Buffalo in the AFC standings for comfort, so we’d like to see the Jaguars pick up another loss. And since the Bills just beat Baltimore, a Ravens win gives Buffalo a little boost in strength of victory. Two birds, one stone. And we don’t even have to like the Ravens — or whoever they have under center. Cincinnati Bengals at Atlanta Falcons Root for: Falcons The Bengals are sitting at 5-2, and that’s a little closer to the top of the AFC than we’d like. Atlanta can do us a favor here by handing Cincinnati its third loss. Nothing complicated about this one. Denver Broncos at Carolina Panthers Root for: Panthers Denver is sitting right behind Buffalo in the AFC standings, and we’d really like to put another game between the two. Yes, a Broncos loss hurts the Bills’ strength of schedule, but with Buffalo and Denver set for a Christmas Day showdown, we’d be happy to see the Panthers play the part of the Grinch in November. Dallas Cowboys at Indianapolis Colts Root for: Colts The Colts aren’t going anywhere in the AFC standings right now, but that doesn’t mean they can’t do us a favor. Indianapolis traded its 2027 first-round pick to the Jets, and the more games the Colts win, the worse that pick gets. The last thing we need is New York getting its hands on a franchise-changing player with the first pick in the draft. Cleveland Browns at New Orleans Saints Root for: Saints The Browns are sitting at 5-3, and that’s close enough to the top of the AFC for us to want them to stay right where they are. Or, better yet, take another step backward. New Orleans hasn’t exactly been setting the world on fire, but we’re not asking the Saints to win the Super Bowl. Just one game on Sunday will do. Houston Texans at Los Angeles Chargers Root for: Chargers The Chargers are 0-7, and the last thing we need is for them to turn that miserable season into the first overall pick in next year’s draft. So, we’re rooting for Los Angeles to finally get a win. Come on, Chargers. Surely you can manage just one. Las Vegas Raiders at San Francisco 49ers Root for: Raiders Buffalo already has a win over Las Vegas in the books, so another Raiders win would give the Bills a little help with strength of victory. Strange how quickly a team can go from an opponent to a temporary friend. _____________________________________________________________________________ NFC Rooting Interests Los Angeles Rams over Washington Commanders — Strength of Victory Chicago Bears over Tampa Bay Buccaneers — Strength of schedule. Games that don’t move the needle for Buffalo: New York Giants at Philadelphia Eagles Arizona Cardinals at Seattle Seahawks _____________________________________________________________________________ Teams on Bye Pittsburgh Steelers, Tennessee Titans _____________________________________________________________________________ Being at the top of the AFC is a pretty good place to be. The problem is, now we’re going to spend the rest of the season looking over our shoulders to see who’s coming for that No. 1 seed. This weekend, we’ll be keeping one eye on the Patriots, another on the Chiefs, and somehow finding a way to root for the Jets without feeling too dirty about it. Being a Bills fan sometimes requires sacrifices. And if Sunday goes our way, a Buffalo win on Monday night would just be the icing on the cake. Go Bills!

full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 1: Cole Bishop #24 of the Buffalo Bills hits Tyler Huntley #5 of the Baltimore Ravens as he's throwing the ball during the first half at Highmark Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. As great as the Bills defense fared vs. Baltimore, the level of competition does have to be considered, as Buffalo did much of its damage against second-stringer Tyler Huntley (injured after only 10 snaps), and emergency QB Joe Fagnano, an undrafted rookie making his NFL debut with little preparation. Today’s edition of Buffalo Rumblinks leads off with thoughts on whether the positives shown vs. Baltimore are sustainable for the rest of the season, or whether the results are fool’s gold. Greg Rousseau and Ed Oliver were constantly in Baltimore’s backfield and finished with three quarterback hits apiece, while Cole Bishop came up with a strip-sack, Rousseau, Landon Jackson and T.J. Parker each added sacks, and Davison Igbinosun came away with his first career interception after Geno Stone batted away a pass. First-year defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard tried a few new wrinkles on Sunday, calling plays from the booth instead of on the field while guiding a defense that set season-best marks in man coverage rate (54.8%), blitz rate (61.3%), and middle-of-field closed coverages (67.7%). “We talked about it all week, just being aggressive after coming off the bye, and we looked at things we could work on,” Rousseau said . “And I feel like we did a good job of going out there and starting fast. And most importantly, finishing, because we’ve had good games as a defense. Despite the positives, there are still warts on defense: the play of Buffalo’s linebackers has been less than stellar; the pass rush—outside of Rousseau and Deone Walker—has been inconsistent; the secondary has battled through injuries and erratic play; and penalties continue to be an issue. “I think our defense should look at today and understand that that’s what the expectation is,” Brady said. “And I’m not talking about the production. title: The Buffalo Bills should be considering value of trading for player on expiring contract
summary: Of course I’ve been thinking plenty about what the Buffalo Bills might do before the NFL trade deadline. And I’ve decided to transfer my stream of consciousness on this topic to my keyboard for this piece. I’m a firm believer that in the NFL, in-season trade value is set, or at least calibrated against, the […]
full_text: Of course I’ve been thinking plenty about what the Buffalo Bills might do before the NFL trade deadline. And I’ve decided to transfer my stream of consciousness on this topic to my keyboard for this piece. I’m a firm believer that in the NFL, in-season trade value is set, or at least calibrated against, the compensatory pick a player most likely would be able to fetch his original team in the future. Of course, those compensatory picks don’t arrive until the year after a player signs a new deal in following March, so the waiting game must be considered. But for example, I’d essentially make no sense for a team to accept a fifth-round pick in a deadline deal for a veteran if said veteran could net the club a third-rounder a year down the road. Let’s use Josh Downs for example, the most recent feature in the Bills trade candidate series here at Rumblings. Spotrac’s current market value for Downs is $16.9 million per year. It projects him to sign a four-year, $67M contract in free agency next March, if he makes it there. With Downs on an expiring contract, the team he’s on the end of 2026 NFL season would likely receive a fourth-round compensatory pick (and a third-rounder isn’t out of the question) in 2028 for his departure, if, of course, that club signs fewer unrestricted free agents than it loses in the 2027 free-agent cycle. (Given the Bills are set to be $37.8M OVER the 2027 cap and currently have eight players set to be qualifying unrestricted free agents, it’s a reasonably safe bet they will lose more UFAs than they sign. In 2026’s free-agent cycle, Buffalo lost three qualifying UFAs and signed two.) For the sake of the argument here, let’s assume a deal for Downs in the $16M – $17M APY range would net that fourth-round compensatory selection in the 2028 NFL Draft. That likely sets the floor regarding what the Colts would like to get in return for Downs in a trade before the deadline on November 10. Assuming there are a few suitors for Downs, the Colts could be in search of a third-round pick for the veteran receiver. The Bills are expected to have two fourths in the 2027 NFL Draft — their own pick and the projected compensatory pick they got for David Edwards signing a sizable deal with the Saints. In continuing this hypothetical, the Bills would, of course, prefer to send a fourth-round pick for Downs and initially reluctant to trade away a 2027 third-round selection for him. (again, I do not know anything in the previous sentence to be true… we are living in hypothetical land right now) Here’s why I think it’d make perfect sense for the Bills to ultimately decide to use that third-round selection for Downs (or any other trade candidate on an expiring deal): If they did make that trade, these are the possible outcomes, within reason. And let’s start by assuming Downs almost assuredly makes the Bills a better team for the second half of the 2026 regular season, and presumably, the playoffs: After major productivity, he prices himself out of what the Bills want to pay him on a second contract, a nd he signs a lucrative, multi-year deal elsewhere in free agency. In this scenario, Buffalo nets a 2028 third-round (or fourth-round) compensatory pick for their “rental.” The draft-pick cost to acquire him would, at worst, would be Buffalo moving down from one round to the next, and waiting a year. At best, the compensatory pick would negate the draft-pick cost to trade for him. After major productivity, the Bills decide he’s a core piece of the receiving corps who will be 26 years old before the start of the 2027 campaign and sign him to a multi-year extension. Said extension features a reasonable cap hit in the first year, a slightly higher one in the next, then finally a cap hit above his contract’s APY in 2029, when he’ll be 28 and D.J. Moore will be 32. After solid-but-unspectacular productivity, the Bills let Downs walk in free agency, and net a fifth or sixth-round compensatory pick in the process. Of course, this is the least desirable outcome for the Bills and Downs. A two or three-round “drop” in the draft for the Downs rental (going from third-round pick to acquire him to, potentially, a sixth-round pick from the compensatory system). After solid-but-unspectacular productivity, the Bills and Downs agree to a more team-friendly deal in the $10M – $14M APY range. For context, the contract Khalil Shakir signed before the 2025 campaign features $13.6M in APY. Buffalo gets a solid-but-unspectacular possession wideout entering his prime at somewhat of a bargain price. Of course, there are other possible outcomes, including Downs playing horribly and/or getting hurt. It’s impossible to predict whether or not the latter would occur, so it’s not worth mentioning here. As far as the former, given his steadiness in the NFL, fine start to 2026, and the offense he’d be entering, it’s reasonably safe to project Downs making a solid impact at the very least in Buffalo. Therefore, the worst possible outcome (within reason) for the Bills would be sending a third-round pick to the Colts and only getting a sixth-round pick in 2028 for his March 2027 departure from Buffalo. But wouldn’t amplifying the offense this season be worth, in the worst-case scenario, a possible three-round drop in the draft? I think it would.

title: How did Tylan Grable play vs. Ravens in place of Spencer Brown?
summary: While Buffalo Bills swing tackle Tylan Grabe has started a pair meaningless regular season finales the past, his first real start in the NFL came in Week 8 at home against the Ravens. The third-year pro from University of Central Florida was thrust into the lineup with star right tackle Spencer Brown nursing a back […]
full_text: While Buffalo Bills swing tackle Tylan Grabe has started a pair meaningless regular season finales the past, his first real start in the NFL came in Week 8 at home against the Ravens. The third-year pro from University of Central Florida was thrust into the lineup with star right tackle Spencer Brown nursing a back injury. And we know back ailments have plagued the towering, uber-athletic tackle for much of his professional career. And Grable made relief appearances for Brown in Week 5 against the Rams and in the Week 6 victory over the Raiders. Unsurprisingly, the 82 snaps — yes, 82 snaps — against the Ravens were the most in a single game in Grable’s young NFL tenure. Heck, he’d been on the field for fewer than 80 total snaps in each of the 2024 and 2025 campaigns. And the recently turned 27 year old played some steady right tackle protecting Josh Allen and paving lanes for James Cook in the Week 8 victory. The charting-based metrics were kind to Grable, as he was hit with allowing just two pressures on 42 pass-blocking snaps against Baltimore. Both of the pressures he allowed came in “true” pass-set situations — meaning, no play-action, screen, or chip help — and he had 12 of those against Baltimore. On runs between Grable and the tight end and the tight end and outside the tackle box, Cook toted the rock nine times for 46 yards (5.11 yards per). Grable did receive the highest negatively graded run-block play percentage from PFF among Buffalo’s starting offensive linemen in this game, at 13.2%. For context, Buffalo’s bookend tackle to Grable in Week 8 was of course Dion Dawkins, and his negatively graded run-block play rate was just 5.3%. Undeniably there’s room for improvement for Grable. But the upside — while not All-Pro caliber — is there. And in what was a respectable albeit not otherworldly performance against the Ravens, the Bills swing tackle got valuable starting experience.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Bills vs Ravens game balls: Wasn’t perfect but several players stepped up for Buffalo
summary: The Buffalo Bills came out of their bye with plenty to celebrate. A rookie cornerback collected his first career interception. Josh Allen passed a franchise legend. And a defense that had spent too many afternoons trying to hang on finally gave its head coach a reason to celebrate the finish. Buffalo’s 36–10 win over the […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills came out of their bye with plenty to celebrate. A rookie cornerback collected his first career interception. Josh Allen passed a franchise legend. And a defense that had spent too many afternoons trying to hang on finally gave its head coach a reason to celebrate the finish. Buffalo’s 36–10 win over the Baltimore Ravens moved the Bills to 6–1, with Joe Brady’s postgame game balls recognizing individual milestones and a collective response. Baltimore’s quarterback injuries are part of the story. Lamar Jackson left after the Ravens’ first offensive play, and Tyler Huntley later exited as well. But Buffalo still had to capitalize, and this time the defense did more than make an occasional play. Official game-ball recipients Davison Igbinosun Igbinosun’s first career interception came with a little help and plenty of awareness. Late in the second quarter, a pass bounced off Geno Stone’s hands and helmet, leaving the football hanging in the air. Igbinosun tracked it, secured the interception and returned it 17 yards, giving Buffalo another scoring opportunity before halftime. The rookie played 41 defensive snaps and made his opportunity count. In the locker room, Igbinosun thanked God and his teammates for pushing him to become “the best version of myself,” closing with a simple, “Go Bills.” A first interception is a milestone on its own. Bass turning it into 3 points before halftime made it even better. Josh Allen Allen’s game ball recognized a milestone that deserves a moment of its own. His 11-yard touchdown pass to DJ Moore in the fourth quarter was the 259th of his Bills career, including postseason games, moving him past Jim Kelly’s 258 for the franchise record. Allen added another touchdown pass to Dalton Kincaid later in the quarter. Allen finished 21-of-34 passing for 289 yards, two touchdowns and an interception. He also rushed for 30 yards and the game’s opening touchdown. Kelly has been the standard against which generations of Buffalo quarterbacks have been measured. But Allen continues to rewrite the record book and has become the new standard. It wasn’t a flawless afternoon, but it was another reminder of the legacy Allen has built and continues building in Buffalo. The Defense Brady’s third game ball went to the defense, with Bradley Chubb called forward to accept it on behalf of the group. “145 total yards, 3 takeaways, 4 sacks…and we finished,” Brady said. “Defense the way you respond. How we practiced. You earned it. Bradley Chubb. Here we go baby.” Cole Bishop’s strip-sack led to a fumble recovery by Kaleb Elarms-Orr. Igbinosun added the interception, and Dorian Williams recovered Baltimore’s other lost fumble. Buffalo finished with four sacks, 12 quarterback hits and three takeaways, holding the Ravens to 3-of-13 on third down. The Bills also limited Derrick Henry to 53 rushing yards and held Zay Flowers without a reception on five targets. Yes, Baltimore’s injuries changed the matchup. But Buffalo took advantage instead of allowing an undermanned opponent to hang around. After several games where the defense struggled to close the door, the finish was worth recognizing. Honorable mentions Tyler Bass Bass made all three field goals, connecting from 56, 22 and 51 yards, and converted all three extra-point attempts. Dalton Kincaid Kincaid led Buffalo with 86 receiving yards on four catches, averaging 21.5 yards per reception. His afternoon included a 40-yard gain and the 23-yard fourth-quarter touchdown that pushed Buffalo’s lead to 36–10. Damar Hamlin With C.J. Gardner-Johnson suspended, Hamlin played all 51 defensive snaps, finishing with five combined tackles and a pass defensed. He was the only Bills defender who never came off the field. A full workload alone doesn’t earn an honorable mention. But handling that responsibility in a secondary that held Baltimore to 91 gross passing yards deserves recognition. DJ Moore In his return to the lineup, Moore caught four passes for 82 yards and a touchdown, including a 49-yard reception that helped spark Buffalo’s second-half offense. Khalil Shakir Shakir hauled in five receptions for 64 yards, providing a reliable target for Josh Allen and helping move the chains. Te’Cory Couch With Buffalo’s secondary shorthanded, Couch stepped up for 36 defensive snaps (71%), recording four combined tackles and helping the Bills limit Baltimore’s passing attack. The game balls celebrated a first, a franchise record and a collective response. Next comes Minnesota, where Buffalo will need to prove that finishing was more than a one-week improvement.
author: Sara Larson

title: Bills snap counts: Offensive-line depth steps up as defense gets a breather
summary: The Buffalo Bills came out of their bye with something that had been missing through much of the season: a little breathing room. Buffalo’s 36–10 win over the Baltimore Ravens featured a substantial difference in workloads. The Bills logged 82 offensive snaps and just 51 defensive snaps on the gamebook’s unofficial playtime sheet, controlling time […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills came out of their bye with something that had been missing through much of the season: a little breathing room. Buffalo’s 36–10 win over the Baltimore Ravens featured a substantial difference in workloads. The Bills logged 82 offensive snaps and just 51 defensive snaps on the gamebook’s unofficial playtime sheet, controlling time of possession for 37:36. Baltimore losing Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley to injuries is important context. Still, Buffalo capitalized, created turnovers and finally finished a game without needing its offense to rescue the result late. Offense With Spencer Brown inactive, Tylan Grable played all 82 offensive snaps. O’Cyrus Torrence was the only other Bills offensive player to handle the full workload. Dion Dawkins and Connor McGovern each played 78 snaps (95%), while Alec Anderson finished with 76 (93%). Austin Corbett contributed eight snaps (10%), with Lloyd Cushenberry and Jude Bowry each playing four (5%). The line helped Buffalo produce 426 total yards while allowing just one sack. Grable’s full afternoon was particularly encouraging with Brown unavailable, providing some reassurance about Buffalo’s offensive-line depth. Josh Allen played 78 snaps (95%), with Kyle Allen getting the final four (5%). Those are the kind of backup-quarterback snaps Buffalo would happily see more often. Coleman leads in playing time, Moore and Shakir lead in production Keon Coleman led the receivers with 63 snaps (77%), followed by Khalil Shakir with 55 (67%) and DJ Moore with 54 (66%). The production told a different story. Moore returned with four catches for 82 yards and a touchdown. Shakir caught five passes for 64 yards, while Coleman finished with one catch for four yards on three targets. Snap counts tell us who was on the field, but not necessarily who made the biggest impact. Joshua Palmer played just seven snaps (9%) before a hamstring injury ended his afternoon. Greg Dortch added four offensive snaps (5%), with his larger role coming on special teams. Kincaid makes his opportunities count Dawson Knox led the tight ends with 57 snaps (70%), followed by Dalton Kincaid with 47 (57%), Jackson Hawes with 32 (39%) and Keleki Latu with eight (10%). Kincaid led Buffalo with 86 receiving yards on four catches, including a 23-yard touchdown. Knox caught one pass for six yards, while Hawes added one for seven yards. Once again, the tight-end workload and receiving production looked different. Kincaid didn’t need the most snaps to deliver the biggest plays. Cook leads a three-back rotation James Cook played 44 offensive snaps (54%), Ty Johnson handled 20 (24%) and Ray Davis played 17 (21%). Cook finished with 80 rushing yards and a touchdown on 21 carries, adding two catches for 21 yards. Davis contributed 30 rushing yards on six attempts, while Johnson caught all three of his targets for 19 yards. With Buffalo pulling away, the Bills had room to spread the workload rather than leaning heavily on Cook or Allen late in the game. Defense With C.J. Gardner-Johnson suspended and Dee Alford inactive, Buffalo needed contributions from its defensive-back depth. Bishop delivered a strip-sack, while Igbinosun recorded his first career interception. Both made the most of their opportunities. Damar Hamlin was Buffalo’s only defender to play all 51 snaps. Cole Bishop and Christian Benford each played 45 (88%), while Davison Igbinosun handled 41 (80%). Te’Cory Couch played 36 (71%), Geno Stone contributed 19 (37%) and Maxwell Hairston finished with 16 (31%). Deone Walker led Buffalo’s defensive front with 33 snaps (65%). Greg Rousseau and Bradley Chubb each played 31 (61%). TJ Parker and Landon Jackson each handled 25 snaps (49%), followed by DeWayne Carter and TJ Sanders with 21 apiece (41%). Ed Oliver played 20 (39%) in his return. Michael Hoecht added 12 snaps (24%), with Javon Solomon playing seven (14%). At linebacker, Terrel Bernard played 39 snaps (76%), Dorian Williams handled 29 (57%) and Kaleb Elarms-Orr contributed 14 (27%). Special Teams Joe Andreessen and Sam Franklin led Buffalo with 21 special-teams snaps apiece (78%). Neither played a defensive snap. Hoecht, Solomon and Latu each played 18 (67%). Stone, Hairston and Elarms-Orr followed with 16 apiece (59%). Tyler Bass played 14 snaps (52%) and made all three field-goal attempts. Dortch handled 10 special-teams snaps (37%), returning three punts for 40 yards and one kickoff for 22 yards. Buffalo’s depth contributed across all three phases. More importantly, the Bills finally had a fourth quarter focused on maintaining control rather than trying to survive.

title: Buffalo Bills No. 1 offense facing No. 1 ranked Vikings defense: what history says about this rare matchup
summary: The Buffalo Bills and Minnesota Vikings will provide the football world a rather unique matchup in Week 9 on Monday Night Football. It will mark just the seventh time since 2017 that the No. 1 offense in EPA per play will meet the No. 1 defense in EPA allowed per play. Even if you’re not […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills and Minnesota Vikings will provide the football world a rather unique matchup in Week 9 on Monday Night Football . It will mark just the seventh time since 2017 that the No. 1 offense in EPA per play will meet the No. 1 defense in EPA allowed per play. Even if you’re not a big analytics enthusiast, you can be assured that EPA per play is a truer measure of a unit’s quality than yards per game or points per game metrics traditionally used in offensive and defensive rankings. Here are the previous six contests that pitted No. 1 offense vs. No. 1 defense and their results: Season + Week No. 1 Offense No. 1 Defense Result 2019, Week 9 Ravens Patriots Ravens 37, Patriots 20 2020, Week 6 Packers Buccaneers Buccaneers 38, Packers 10 2021, Week 5 Chiefs Bills Bills 38, Chiefs 20 2021, Week 14 Buccaneers Bills Buccaneers 33, Bills 27 (OT) 2022, Week 7 Chiefs 49ers Chiefs 44, 49ers 23 2025, Week 13 Colts Texans Texans 20, Colts 16 Overall that equates to an even 3-3 record. So recent history suggests there’s no clear advantage for the top-ranked offense or defense. If we check all the way back to 2001 — which then includes nine additional of these specific games — the team with the No. 1 offense is 10-6 in these matchups. A slight advantage over the past 25 years, but nothing drastic. The average points scored for the No. 1 offense was 25.6. The average EPA per play for the No. 1 offense entering the game was, naturally, a very high +0.217. The average EPA per play in the game against the No. 1 defense was just +0.059, which for context, would place between the No. 9-ranked Patriots and No. 8-ranked Bears (in offensive EPA per play) right now. However, seven of those 16 matchups featured the No. 1 offense managing a negative EPA per play against the No. 1 defense. As expected, this unique matchup has been, for the most part, evenly matched… with a reasonably minor edge to the club with the No. 1 offense. We are in for a treat in Bills – Vikings on MNF.

title: Carolina Panthers 2027 NFL Draft Prospect Profile: Cayden Green
summary: The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the […]
full_text: COLUMBIA, MISSOURI - OCTOBER 03: Cayden Green #70 of the Missouri Tigers blocks Jeramiah McCloud #91 of the Florida Gators at Faurot Field at Memorial Stadium on October 03, 2026 in Columbia, Missouri. (Photo by Jay Biggerstaff/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the Draft. In this series, we’ll only be looking at prospects the Panthers could seriously consider. Today our profile will focus on Missouri Tigers offensive lineman Cayden Green. Bio Green (6’5”, 325 lbs.) was a four star recruit and ranked as the state of Missouri’s second best prospect coming out of high school in 2022. Originally signing with Oklahoma, he started five games for the Sooners at left guard before transferring back to his home state. Green continued to hold down the left guard spot until 2025, when the Tigers moved him to left tackle. In his first year at the position, he allowed only seven pressures across over 350 pass blocking snaps, earning him First Team All-SEC recognition. After missing the first game due to injury, Green has been a stalwart at left tackle for the Tigers, allowing five pressures and zero sacks through five games this year. Strengths/Weaknesses One of Green’s biggest strengths is how naturally he took to the change of position. Usually linemen make the transition outside in, but in his first season moving from guard to tackle he earned All-SEC honors. On top of that, the switch to left tackle happened just two weeks before the 2025 season, showing just how coachable and adaptable he is. Green uses his heavy frame to anchor well and has the athleticism to not get beat around the edge on speed rushes. He is a coach’s dream: finishing blocks and playing through the whistle with a true versatility that will total over 1,500 snaps at guard and tackle in his career. While performing well, Green is still new to the left tackle position. His performance this year has really solidified his ranking among the Draft’s top tackles, but there are still some raw moments. He has also battled injuries the last couple of seasons. Nothing major, but still something that some teams might want to look further into. Projection Green is the epitome of a player that every coaching staff wants. He has the coachability and versatility to immediately start at a minimum of three positions on the offensive line, he is consistent in his performance against SEC competition, and he does not commit penalties (flagged just twice so far this season). As he continues to grow into the position, expect his stock to continue rising through the middle of the first round, potentially higher after teams get to interview him at the Combine. The Panthers have had a rash of injuries and poor performance on the offensive line, and Green would be a better version of Brady Christensen. He could start at left tackle (depending on Icky Ekwonu’s status and position moving forward) or right guard (if the Panthers move on from Robert Hunt). I wouldn’t even put it past him to learn the center position and be just as dominant there. Depending on where the Panthers pick in the first round, Green might be available to shore up several spots on their starting offensive line and give them some mix-and-match options in 2027 and beyond. What do you think, Panthers fans? If Cayden Green is available when the Panthers select in the 2027 NFL Draft, should they take him? Sound off in the comments!

title: Taking stock of the Panthers cornerback room following the firing of Ejiro Evero
summary: Hello CSR! We’re coming off a wild week following the most recent Panthers loss to the Packers, one that saw them decide to jettison defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero and defensive passing game coordinator Jonathan Cooley. It was quite a jarring move to make in the middle of a season where despite a myriad of injuries […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 18: DeVonta Smith #6 of the Philadelphia Eagles catches a touchdown pass against Will Lee III #24 of the Carolina Panthers in the fourth quarter at Lincoln Financial Field on October 18, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The Panthers defeated the Eagles 25-14. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hello CSR! We’re coming off a wild week following the most recent Panthers loss to the Packers, one that saw them decide to jettison defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero and defensive passing game coordinator Jonathan Cooley. It was quite a jarring move to make in the middle of a season where despite a myriad of injuries along the defense, the Panthers still have a shot at the playoffs. As far as the Evero firing goes, I still haven’t quite settled on how I feel about it. I think I am currently leaning towards that it makes sense, but probably should have happened following the 2025 season rather than spending the 2026 off-season building around the scheme Evero would use. There were many questionable personnel decisions like not playing 2025 standout UDFA Corey Thornton or 3rd year CB Chau Smith-Wade, along with subbing out some of the younger guys with upside like Princely Umanmielen when the pass rush has struggled. All in all, I think the decision ultimately makes logical sense and I am looking forward to seeing what kind of changes the Panthers make post-Evero to try and right the ship, or at the very least keep it floating with duct tape until they get back Jaycee Horn, Mike Jackson, and Jaelan Phillips. The biggest question mark moving forward is going to be what the team does with their depleted CB room. Recently brought back coach and former cornerback DeAngelo Hall will have his work cut out for him. Let’s take a look at the current room as it stands. Will Lee III The 2026 4th round pick became the de facto CB1 following the injuries to Horn and Jackson. He’s logged 7 pass deflections in 7 games played and continues to progress after being thrown right into the fire. The Panthers planned on him being heavily involved early, as he manned one of the boundary spots in nickel formations when the cornerback room was fully healthy. Unfortunately, he is day to day right now with a hamstring injury, which means they may miss him for at least a game, possibly more depending on how his recovery goes. Not great, but the experience he’s getting this season as a 4th round rookie should prove very valuable from a long term perspective. Chau Smith-Wade The former 5th round pick played quite a bit since his rookie season in 2024. He’s played in 36 career games with 11 starts, though curiously his defensive snap counts went down this season following a career high 63% of snaps played on defense in 2025. This season, he’s only accounted for 21% of the defensive snaps, playing almost as many snaps on special teams (86) as he has on defense (88). This is a very curious decision considering all of the injuries surrounding this position group. However, that could change this week, especially if Will Lee can’t go. The Panthers primarily used Chau as a nickel corner, so prior to Evero’s firing, they were playing with additional safeties rather than with as much traditional nickel sets. I think if you’re looking to change the fortunes of the secondary, this is the week to throw him out there and see what happens. And that’s if they even have a choice pending Will Lee’s status. Malcolm DeWalt IV DeWalt, the final member of the active roster on this list, was brought in on the practice squad on October 24th, and promoted to the active roster ahead of the Packers game last week. He was an undrafted free agent this season, made the 53 man roster for the Atlanta Falcons, but was ultimately waived in October after being a healthy scratch for six games. He made one special teams tackle last week and played no defensive snaps. He played for 3 different colleges prior to entering the NFL, so I don’t really know what to expect from him should they be forced to play him this week. Practice Squad options The Panthers (as of this writing, per their team site) have 5 corners on their practice squad. They released Robert Rochell on Tuesday. Most likely, they will be calling up 2 or 3 of them for Sundays game depending on what happens with Will Lee. The first one I have to highlight is Marco Wilson. He’s a former 4th round pick from 2021 who has bounced around the league before landing on the Panthers practice squad on October 6th. He was called on to start against the Packers, being credited with 2 pass deflections and 8 total tackles. Of course, the Panthers defense was still not great in that game as the Packers tore them apart in the passing game, but it was an impressive showing for Wilson and I’d expect him to get called up again and possibly start this week. Next, we have 2025 UDFA Corey Thornton. Thornton was an impressive preseason story and played in 12 games for the Panthers in 2025, and managed to break in to the corner rotation before a broken fibula ended his season. Curiously, he hasn’t been called up at all during the Panthers injury woes from the practice squad. That might change this week depending on what kind of changes the Panthers are making and what options they have for significant playing time. Rounding out the last of the names is DeVonta Smith, Zion Childress, and Caelen Carson. Smith spent the entire off-season on the roster before being waived during final roster cuts and being added to the practice squad, so he has about as much familiarity as you could ask for from an undrafted rookie. Childress had stints with the Cowboys and Texans since entering as a UDFA in 2025. Carson was drafted in the 5th round pick by the Cowboys in 2024, and has 8 starts in his career. He could very well see some time depending on what decisions the Panthers make during the near future of the post-Evero defense. In closing, the Panthers have some… interesting decisions to make going into their next few games. It doesn’t appear they will be looking for cornerback help outside of the usual roster churning of the NFL season, which makes sense for a team that hasn’t made a ton of trades during the season under Dave Canales. I could see a low risk/low price move potentially being made, but dealing a high pick or even mid round pick for a corner doesn’t seem to be something they will consider. Personally, I’d really like to see them give Chau Smith-Wade and Corey Thornton some opportunities, and I was impressed with Marco Wilson despite getting thrown out there with less than a month under his belt in this scheme. Caelen Carson could also see some time. But either way, they’ll have do a lot of things schematically to mask this weakness currently. They may look to play more man coverage and press to change things up, or they may sit back in the same soft cushion zones we have grown accustomed to. Maybe some calculated aggression in coverage will help? What are your thoughts, Panthers fans?

title: How the Chicago Bears Are Controlling the Clock This Season
summary: One of the more notable aspects of the Chicago Bears‘ performance this season has been their ability to control the clock. The Bears are averaging 35:26 in time of possession, putting together extended drives, consistently moving the chains, and giving opposing offenses fewer opportunities with the football. On Monday night, the Bears put together a […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - NOVEMBER 02: Kalif Raymond #14 of the Chicago Bears stiff-arms Nehemiah Pritchett #28 of the Seattle Seahawks during the fourth quarter of the game at Lumen Field on November 02, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images One of the more notable aspects of the Chicago Bears ‘ performance this season has been their ability to control the clock. The Bears are averaging 35:26 in time of possession, putting together extended drives, consistently moving the chains, and giving opposing offenses fewer opportunities with the football. On Monday night, the Bears put together a 17-play, 80-yard opening drive against the Seattle Seahawks that took 8:32 off the clock. Caleb Williams noted that sustaining drives was something the offense spent time working on during training camp and OTAs. “We do these long-drive drills in training camp and OTAs that you hate, that you dread at the end of practice,” he said. “They show up in big moments for us.” And while the Bears’ offense is well-prepared to execute those extended drives, Johnson’s priority remains making the most of each possession rather than focusing on how long a drive lasts. “It’s not something we stress,” Johnson said. “We really talk more about getting explosive plays. I would rather have a one-play drive for a touchdown than a 10-play drive for a touchdown. But the ability to stay efficient, stay on schedule, I think that’s something that good offenses show that they can do.” Johnson also pointed out that long drives leave little room for mistakes, since one misstep can bring an otherwise promising possession to an end. “I prefer some more explosive plays be mixed in there, just so it takes the onus off just a little bit,” Johnson explained. “It feels like you’ve got to be perfect throughout those long drives, and one mistake could derail you.” One factor contributing to the Bears’ success in controlling possession has been their performance on third down on both sides of the ball. The Bears convert 44.3% of their third downs, the fifth-best mark in the NFL, while their defense ranks No. 1 in the league, allowing conversions on just 23.8% of third downs. Key behind the Bears' success this season has been third downs for both sides of the football. Chicago converts on 44.3% of third downs, ranked 5th in the NFL, while boasting the No. 1 defense in that category at just 23.8%. — Chris Emma (@ChrisEmma1) November 3, 2026 What’s made Chicago particularly dangerous on third down is that the offense hasn’t just been converting in those situations. Some of the Bears’ most explosive plays this season have come when they’ve needed to move the chains. A game changer for the Bears. pic.twitter.com/gjh71QN5sJ — Chris Emma (@ChrisEmma1) November 3, 2026 Luther Burden III comes up big with a 24-yard touchdown on 3rd and 17 CALEB WILLIAMS. LUTHER BURDEN III. TOUCHDOWN! title: Reviewing the Bears’ PFN grades from Week 8 vs. Seahawks
summary: The Bears made an impact in primetime on Monday night, decisively beating the Seahawks 34-17 to improve their record to 6-2 for the 2026-27 NFL season. It was a convincing win which saw Chicago excel on both sides of the ball, limiting the Seahawks’ offense and gashing apart what is generally seen as one of […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - NOVEMBER 02: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears celebrates a touchdown by teammate D'Andre Swift #4 of the Chicago Bears during the third quarter against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on November 02, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Bears made an impact in primetime on Monday night, decisively beating the Seahawks 34-17 to improve their record to 6-2 for the 2026-27 NFL season. It was a convincing win which saw Chicago excel on both sides of the ball, limiting the Seahawks’ offense and gashing apart what is generally seen as one of the best defenses in the NFL. There were a lot of positive takeaways out of the All-22, and the analytics reflect that. Each week, I’ll review how Chicago’s eligible performers graded by Pro Football Network’s Impact Scoring model. Now that the rest of the NFL has caught up, and the numbers have all been crunched, here’s how Week 8 looked. Offense Caleb Williams: 78.0 (10th of 28 QBs) D’Andre Swift: 81.4 (6th of 40 RBs) Luther Burden III: 78.1 (7th of 52 WRs) Rome Odunze: 76.7 (16th of 54 WRs) Colston Loveland: 75.7 (10th of 32 TEs) Theo Benedet: 76.7 (16th of 49 OTs) Joe Thuney: 82.4 (9th of 73 OGs) Garrett Bradbury: 72.5 (21st of 25 Cs) Jonah Jackson: 85.1 (2nd of 73 OGs) Darnell Wright: 79.1 (12th of 49 OTs) Caleb Williams was an above-average performer at quarterback across the board on Monday night, which is made more impressive considering the quality of the Seahawks’ defense. He graded in at least the top 12 in such categories as EPA per dropback, success rate, adjusted net yards per attempt, completion percentage, completion percentage over expected, and passing yards. It helped that he had three efficient weapons to throw to; though Luther Burden III led all Bears weapons in PFN Impact grading, it was Rome Odunze who had the highest EPA per target, ranking fourth in the metric at +1.07. Likewise, Chicago had two top-ten performances at guard for the week out of both Jonah Jackson and Joe Thuney. Defense Montez Sweat: 80.0 (14th of 97 EDGEs) Austin Booker: 75.4 (39th of 97 EDGEs) James Lynch: 75.2 (40th of 97 EDGEs) Daniel Hardy: 52.6 (91st of 97 EDGEs) Jeffery Simmons: 89.9 (3rd of 92 DTs) Grady Jarrett: 55.4 (85th of 92 DTs) Devin Bush: 82.6 (11th of 77 LBs) D’Marco Jackson: 76.7 (30th of 77 LBs) Noah Sewell: 66.7 (73rd of 77 LBs) Kyler Gordon: 77.7 (29th of 95 CBs) Jaylon Johnson: 75.4 (42nd of 95 CBs) Tyrique Stevenson: 67.1 (87th of 95 CBs) Cam Lewis: 80.0 (14th of 77 SAFs) Dillon Thieneman: 74.9 (45th of 77 SAFs) Jeffery Simmons made his Bears debut on Monday, and he absolutely shined on the big stage. His six tackles tied for the most on the team and tied for third among 92 qualified defensive tackles, and he also added a sack into the mix, despite facing a heavy double-team focus from Seattle’s offensive line. The two biggest benefactors from Simmons’ presence in Week 8 were Montez Sweat and Devin Bush, as both ended up with sacks, and the latter tied Simmons for the Bears’ lead in tackles for the night. The Seahawks picked on Tyrique Stevenson often, as he was targeted ten times and gave up a targeted passer rating of 124.2 for the game. However, strong auxiliary performances from Cam Lewis, Austin Booker, James Lynch, and D’Marco Jackson gave Chicago an all-around solid defensive outing. Special teams (for the sickos) Cairo Santos: 80.5 (8th of 24 Ks) Tory Taylor: 79.7 (11th of 28 Ps) Cairo Santos hit all of his field goal and extra point attempts, nailing his two field goal tries from 44 and 38 yards, respectively. His +0.4 field goals made over expected tied for the fourth best in the NFL in Week 8. On the other end of special teams, Tory Taylor finished above average with a 45.0-yard net punt average, including the lucky bounces he got on the one punt that got tipped.

full_text: Aug 1, 2026; Nashville, TN, USA; Tennessee Titans defensive end Earnest Brown IV (99) goes through drills during training camp at Vanderbilt Health Football Center. Mandatory Credit: Steve Roberts-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Chicago Bears have a 16-man practice squad, but the list will be fluid, and we’ll update it throughout the year. UPDATE (11/4): The Bears signed TE Stephen Carlson to the active roster and signed DE Earnest Brown IV to the practice squad. Caden Barnett, OG Christian Jones, OT Salvon Ahmed, RB Kaden Davis, WR J.P. Richardson, WR Scotty Miller, WR Qadir Ismail, TE Miller Moss, QB Wayne Matthews III, LB Buddy Johnson, LB Keidron Smith, S Elijah Jones, CB KC Eziomume, CB Josh Butler, CB Earnest Brown IV, DE Beau Gardner, LS Practice squad injured: Anthony Johnson Jr. (S) Here are the qualifications for practice squad eligibility and some rules to remember. A 17th player is permitted as long as he qualifies for the NFL’s International Pathway Program. Players with no accrued seasons (rookies) and those with fewer than nine regular-season games in their lone accrued season. A maximum of ten players are allowed who have earned no more than two accrued seasons. Up to six players with unlimited accrued seasons are permitted on the practice squad. However, the number of players in the last two categories cannot exceed 10 total players. Teams can elevate up to two practice squad players for each game, but they can still only have 48 players active on game day. After the game, the elevated player(s) will revert to the practice squad. A player can be elevated up to three times, but if he’s needed after that, the team would be required to sign him to the 53-man active roster. Players on practice squads are free agents who can be signed to another team’s active roster. A player’s current club can’t block him from leaving; they can only make a counteroffer to keep him. Ultimately, it’s the player’s decision. If a player is signed away, his new team must keep him on its 53-man roster for three weeks, but if he’s released, he’ll revert to his previous team. Players signed to another active roster are also guaranteed three weeks’ salary. A practice squad player can’t sign with his team’s upcoming opponent unless he does so six days before the upcoming game or ten days prior if his team is on its bye week.

title: NFL Trade Deadline Rumors: Bears checking on cornerbacks
summary: The Chicago Bears made the biggest splash ahead of the 2026 trade deadline when they acquired All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons from the Tennessee Titans, but they may not be done. In a recent ESPN article, Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano shared the latest intel and buzz around the trade deadline, and Graziano wrote that […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - SEPTEMBER 20: Mike Sainristil #0 of the Washington Commanders lines up before the snap during an NFL football game against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears made the biggest splash ahead of the 2026 trade deadline when they acquired All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons from the Tennessee Titans, but they may not be done. In a recent ESPN article , Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano shared the latest intel and buzz around the trade deadline, and Graziano wrote that the Bears and the Detroit Lions are “poking around on potentially available cornerbacks.” Fowler agreed that the Bears were looking for a corner, telling Graziano, “A few league evaluators told me what you heard — that cornerback is becoming more of a need.” “Washington’s Mike Sainristil is a name that has circulated this week, though I don’t get the sense the Commanders plan to trade him,” Fowler said. “An available corner such as the Eagles’ Riq Woolen for a Day 3 pick could make sense.” The Commanders are 2-4-1, third in the NFC East behind the 4-2-1 New York Giants, so they may be ready to sell. They host the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday, two days before the November 10 trade deadline. The Eagles are 2-6 and lost starting quarterback Jalen Hurts for the season, and are readying to start their third QB, Joe Milton, this Sunday at home against the Giants. In other quarterback news, the Baltimore Ravens are trading for Jacoby Brissett from the Arizona Cardinals, so you can disregard those Tyson Bagent rumors. Fowler also wrote that the Bears “have been linked to edge rushers such as Khalil Mack.” Yesterday, Ian Rapoport also mentioned Mack and the Bears, while adding, “The problem with that is Joe Hortiz, the general manager for the Chargers, has shown no indication that he wants to sell at all. They like how Khalil Mack has helped the young edges and helped the locker room. It’s bad there. They do not want to give up on the season.” The winless Los Angeles Chargers played Mack a season-low number of snaps last week, and this Sunday they host the Houston Texans. Rapoport also said former Bear cornerback Nahshon Wright, who has yet to play for the New York Jets, is a name to watch for the Bears.

title: 3 Reasons Why the Chicago Bears Won vs. the Seahawks
summary: In front of a national audience, once again, the Chicago Bears defeated a conference champion. This time in the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks. Considering the Bears are on the verge of a certain level of success the franchise hasn’t experienced in decades thanks to Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams, I am going to […]
full_text: Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images | Getty Images In front of a national audience, once again, the Chicago Bears defeated a conference champion. This time in the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks. Considering the Bears are on the verge of a certain level of success the franchise hasn’t experienced in decades thanks to Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams, I am going to leave them out of this piece from now on – as it is a given that both were instrumental to Chicago’s success. Instead, I will be highlighting 3 other factors that contributed to Chicago’s win or loss. So let’s get to it. 1. Jeffery Simmons Simply put: Simmons was a game-wrecker Monday night. The way he stepped in and made an immediate impact was reminiscent of Khalil Mack’s Bears Intro back in 2018. Except Chicago won in dominating fashion this time around. Simmons presence was felt and it was noticeable when he was off the field. By now, we have all seen the stats showing that the Seahawks averaged close to 3 years per play when he was on the field compared to 13+ when he was off it, but the way he changed how Dennis Allen called this game was what fascinated me the most. The Bears came into MNF averaging a 40% blitz rate. Against Seattle, they cut that down to 15%…and their pressure rate *went up.* Discussed the Jeffrey Simmons effect with @BenjaminSolak 👇 pic.twitter.com/hHizP5a6iF — Mina Kimes (@minakimes) November 3, 2026 Jeffery Simmons’ mere presence allowed Dennis Allen to keep more defenders in coverage while simultaneously occupying the attention of more offensive linemen. This allowed guys like Devin Bush, Montez Sweat and Austin Booker to really shine in ways we have not seen. Montez Sweat should have had 3 sacks were two of them not called back for some questionable penalties in the secondary. Austin Booker was able to get in the face of Sam Darnold multiple times and even block a kick. Jeffery Simmons has completely changed the complexion of this team and the defense has leveled up in the process. 2. Rome Odunze Man, you have to feel good for Rome Odunze. The former top 10 overall selection in the 2024 NFL draft has failed to live up to those lofty expectations on draft night but he most certainly has been flashing his unique skillset in recent weeks and had arguably his best game of the season on Monday night. Not only did the former Washington Husky not commit his weekly dropped pass in front of his family and friends, but he also made himself an extremely friendly target for Caleb Williams in some of the most critical moments – a characteristic of his play we have come to expect these days. Not only that, but he was catching the ball downfield and creating huge chunk gains for the offense, which was backbreaking for the Seattle defense. Another characteristic of his play this season! Wide receivers this season with 30+ targets and an explosive play rate of 20% or higher. pic.twitter.com/drPSASxspP — Matt Harmon (@MattHarmon_BYB) November 3, 2026 When Rome is playing the way he is, and we still have Luther Burden III and Colston Loveland available, this offense will be nearly impossible to stop. Especially when you have this next guy continuing to run hard. 3. D’Andre Swift Without his running mate once again, D’Andre Swift continued to carry the load in the run game and for the second consecutive week makes this list. Much like last week, it wasn’t pretty as evidences by his 69 rushing yards on 27 attempts for a 2.6 yard average with a long of just 7 yards. But Swift got it done and moved the chains when it mattered in addition to punching the ball in the endzone THREE times like he has continued to do all season. In fact, his 10 rushing TDs lead the entire NFL at this point, and his ability to turn drives into 7 points has become a critical component for a Chicago offense that can hurt you in multiple ways. While Caleb and Ben get most of the credit, the way that Swift and this offensive line have not missed a beat when Ben Johnson goes no-huddle, hurry-up, or Caleb calls an audible at the line of scrimmage has been amazing. The fact that we haven’t had more mishaps or pre-snap penalties is a tribute to the work being done by all week in and week out, and Swift has deserved every bit of the 3-year, $33.75 million extension he was awarded at the beginning of the season. Now, if Kyle Monangai would finally return, Swift can spend less time in the ice tub during the week resting his wounds. Hopefully Monangai is back after the BYE. What about you? Who, outside of Caleb and Ben, felt most important to the Bears’ upset over Seattle on Monday night?!

title: Bears Lose OT Braxton Jones for the Year
summary: The Chicago Bears received some unfortunate news on Wednesday, as offensive tackle Braxton Jones will miss the remainder of the 2026 NFL season. Jones underwent surgery on his right knee, officially ending any hopes of a return this season. Jones originally suffered the injury during Chicago’s Week 3 victory over the Philadelphia Eagles, exiting the […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 28: Braxton Jones #70 of the Chicago Bears sits on the field after sustaining an injury during an NFL football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Soldier Field on September 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears received some unfortunate news on Wednesday, as offensive tackle Braxton Jones will miss the remainder of the 2026 NFL season. Jones underwent surgery on his right knee, officially ending any hopes of a return this season. Jones originally suffered the injury during Chicago’s Week 3 victory over the Philadelphia Eagles, exiting the game in the third quarter. The Bears subsequently placed him on injured reserve on October 3, initially leaving the door open for a return after the mandatory four-game absence. Unfortunately, that return will no longer happen. From the Chicago Tribune’s Brad Biggs . Jones suffered a partially torn patellar tendon, and the plan was for him to rehabilitate the injury before determining if it was feasible for him to return this season and delay surgery. After a little more than a month, it was decided to have the injury repaired, an NFL source said Wednesday. The 27-year-old tackle entered the season having won the competition for the starting left tackle position after signing a one-year, 5 million dollar deal to remain in Chicago this past offseason. After starting the first three games, another injury has cut his season short, raising questions about his future with the organization. The 6-foot-5, 303-pound tackle is in his fifth NFL season, having spent his entire career in Chicago after being selected in the fifth round (168th overall) of the 2022 NFL Draft out of Southern Utah. Despite his relatively modest draft position, Jones has accumulated 47 starts in 49 career appearances, including starting all 17 games during his rookie campaign. For Jones, this is another frustrating setback in a career that has shown promise but has increasingly been interrupted by injuries. With his contract expiring after this season, it’s fair to wonder whether we’ve seen his final snap in a Bears uniform. Regardless of what happens next, here’s hoping Jones makes a full recovery.
