title: The hits keep coming for wild-card hopefuls chasing the Packers
summary: Heading into Week 9, the Green Bay Packers—and the rest of the NFC North—would make the NFL playoffs if the season ended now. Per the league’s website, the NFL projects the Packers make the playoffs about half the time in simulations, with the Minnesota Vikings (81 percent), Chicago Bears (82 percent), and Detroit Lions (80 […]
full_text: (Photo by Jane Gershovich/Getty Images) | Getty Images Heading into Week 9, the Green Bay Packers—and the rest of the NFC North—would make the NFL playoffs if the season ended now. Per the league’s website , the NFL projects the Packers make the playoffs about half the time in simulations, with the Minnesota Vikings (81 percent), Chicago Bears (82 percent), and Detroit Lions (80 percent) well ahead. Here’s the good news: The Packers have a full-game lead over the next two teams breathing down their neck for the final wild-card spot, the Seattle Seahawks and Los Angeles Rams. On paper, it’s a tight race between these teams, as the Seahawks are given a 47 percent chance of making the postseason, and the Rams are at 46 percent. With how the landscape is playing out right now, the three wildcard spots in the NFC will likely all come down to North or West teams, and the South and East will just get one playoff team apiece. That means that two of Minnesota, Chicago, Detroit, Green Bay, Seattle or Los Angeles will be on the outside looking in at the end of the year. Here’s another bit of fortunate (I’ll hesitate to call it good) news for the Packers, though: The Seahawks and Rams are banged up. Already, it’s been announced that Seattle quarterback Sam Darnold will miss next week’s game against the Arizona Cardinals with a quad injury and is considered week-to-week. Darnold’s backup, Drew Lock, is also dealing with an elbow injury. Per the NFL’s projections, the Seahawks’ chances of making the playoffs drop from 47 percent to 29 percent if they lose this weekend. On the Rams’ end of things, cornerback Jaylen Watson, their big $51 million free agent signing, will have shoulder surgery, as announced by head coach Sean McVay on Wednesday, and will not return this season. If, for whatever reason, they lose to the Washington Commanders, the Rams’ playoff chances will drop from 46 percent to 31 percent. Packers fans might not like it, but the team is firmly in the “already caring about the results of other teams’ games” portion of the season — and honestly has been for a couple of weeks now. The Seahawks and Rams are the only legit threats to push Green Bay out of the postseason, at least for now, and there hasn’t been a lot of positive news to come out about those clubs early on in Week 9.

(Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images We got one big early November Tuesday ordeal out of the way. Now the countdown is on for another one. The annual “will they/won’t they” dance that precedes the NFL trade deadline every year is in full swing, with various speculators wondering who the Packers should target and what, if anything, they should give up to get them. The Packers are still in the aftermath of their last big trade, of course, which affects what they could do at this year’s trade deadline. They seem unlikely to give up any serious assets in the 2027 NFL Draft considering they don’t have a first round pick. But a lower-level trade might still be possible, especially if Gutekunst can get someone to bite on an offer involving 2028 assets. Even so, as cap-strapped as the Packers are, it doesn’t seem super likely they’re going to be buyers at this year’s deadline. And there’s little the Packers could sell off, either. Keisean Nixon and Carrington Valentine are probably their two most notable assets on expiring (and thus very movable) contracts, and I don’t think the Packers are in a position to jettison either one, even if Valentine has fallen out of favor this year. The safest bet seems like banking on this year being a quiet trade deadline. You’ll probably hear something about the Packers making calls or being in conversations, as always, but the chances of them landing a difference maker at the deadline seem low. title: Value of Things: By the Numbers
summary: In this edition we usually take a look at the offense or defense as a whole. This time we will take a look at C.J. Stroud specifically. We are going to do this in three parts. The first way is to simply take the best per game statistics that we have (since he has had […]
full_text: Ohio State quarterback C.J. Stroud hugs his mother, Kim, after his workout on the Buckeyes' pro day. CJ Stroud | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co In this edition we usually take a look at the offense or defense as a whole. This time we will take a look at C.J. Stroud specifically. We are going to do this in three parts. The first way is to simply take the best per game statistics that we have (since he has had his bye week) and compare that to the other quarterbacks in the league. I should pause here for a moment to lay out some ground rules. The first ground rule is that they have to have qualified with minimal playing time so both Lamar Jackson and Baker Mayfield didn’t make the cut. Secondly, any placeholder quarterback wasn’t considered with the exception of Kirk Cousins. That left us with the 22 quarterbacks. We are looking at yards per game, net yards per attempt, touchdown percentage, interception percentage, completion percentage, and quarterback rating. We will take Stroud’s rankings in each of these categories and come up with a composite ranking. That will be the first part of the test. Stroud’s Numbers Yards per game: 266.7 (6th) Net yards per attempt: 6.8 (10th) Completion percentage: 64.8 (12th) Touchdown %: 4.5 (15th) Interception %: 0.4 (2nd) QB Rating: 100.7 (8th) Composite Ranking: 8.83 In other words, based on these rankings and these rankings alone, we could classify Stroud as a top ten quarterback. Naturally, there are all kinds of caveats we have to look at before making a declarative statement. First, none of these numbers include running numbers which obviously will tip the scales for the Josh Allens of the world. Secondly, there are those that would question the efficacy of such rankings because talent is not equally distributed and let’s just say that coaching know how is not equally distributed. However, ESPN published their report on the negotiations in the offseason and they would seem damning now that Stroud is almost half way into the season. So, we are looking at similarity scores through two different means. The first round is to simply take the two quarterbacks closest to Stroud in the composite rankings. I think everyone will find this one fascinating. Similarity Score One The two quarterbacks most similar to Stroud in composite ranking are Drake Maye and Caleb Williams. As luck should have it, those are the two quarterbacks most likely to get extensions this next offseason. So, it will be a race to the bank so to speak as the first contract is likely to inform the other two. The third quarterback on the list was Josh Allen, but since these numbers didn’t include his rushing statistics, that comparison would be pretty moot if we really tried to make it stick. Similarity Score Two The second way to do similarity scores is to look category by category and identify the three quarterbacks in each category that come closest to his score. Obviously, if we see the same names multiple times then we could also surmise that they are similar to Stroud. If we see Williams or Maye on the list then it strengthens the notion that those three quarterbacks are similar. Yards Per Game: Matthew Stafford, Kirk Cousins, Bryce Young Net Yards per attempt: Caleb Williams, Jordan Love, Matthew Stafford Completion percentage: Dak Prescott, Deshaun Watson, Kirk Cousins Touchdown percentage: Aaron Rodgers, Dak Prescott, Sam Darnold Interception percentage: Jaden Daniels, Jared Goff, Caleb Williams Quarterback rating: Patrick Mahomes, Kirk Cousins, Drake Maye I think the names are repeated enough to give us something to go on. Kirk Cousins appears three times, Matthew Stafford, Dak Prescott, and Caleb Williams all appear twice. The rest only appear once. So, one could credibly claim that Stroud is most similar statistically to Kirk Cousins. Since Williams is a holdover from the other list then we can add his name as an obvious second choice. Ramifications This is where context comes into play. The Las Vegas Raiders and Chicago Bears are two of the best offensive teams in the NFL with two gifted offensive head coaches. The fact that Stroud is in the same conversation as them is a testament to him and not necessarily meant as a shot. Certainly if one looks at the pedigree of Williams and the accomplishments (regular season) of Cousins then it is easy to see what could be possibly if Stroud were given that mythical long term contract. Of course, the other half of that is having an offensive line and coaching staff that can take full advantage of his talents. This is where quarterback ratings become part science and part art. Where would he rank if he were not addled with Nick Caley and this offensive line? Ninth seems low in that scenario. Maybe he brushes up against the top five. He probably settles in at somewhere around sixth or seventh if he had a Ben Johnson type at offensive coordinator. Is that worth 60 or 65 million dollars? That is obviously the 65 million dollar question. Ironically, while much has changed through his play this season, this point really hasn’t. If you are going to continue to play ball control and put training wheels on Stroud then he probably isn’t worth that money. It has nothing to do with him per se. If you were to put the same shackles on Patrick Mahomes then you’d probably reach the same conclusion. If they install an offense that takes full advantage of his abilities then he definitely is worth the money. That all comes down to DeMeco Ryans and whether he can fully admit that you aren’t a smash mouth football team. Time will tell if that ever happens.

title: Houston Texans NFL Power Rankings: Week 9
summary: The Houston Texans enjoyed a reprieve from the horrors last Sunday, as their bye week had arrived. This Sunday off came at a time when it felt like the moon was crashing down on the entire franchise, with cascading failures and injuries pushing the team, many Texans fans, and pretty much everyone on this website […]
full_text: The Houston Texans enjoyed a reprieve from the horrors last Sunday, as their bye week had arrived. This Sunday off came at a time when it felt like the moon was crashing down on the entire franchise, with cascading failures and injuries pushing the team, many Texans fans, and pretty much everyone on this website to a breaking point. Some are already declaring the season “lost,” some are wondering if the Texans should entertain the idea of tanking, and rumors had to be shut down at the possibility of the Texans dealing DE Jadeveon Clowney. Yet, despite all of the doom and gloom, the Texans are still getting a 24.9% chance of making the playoffs from ESPN’s Football Power Index, largely because of their extremely favorable remaining strength of schedule: Week 9: @ Los Angeles Chargers (0-7) Week 10: @ Cleveland Browns (5-3) Week 11: Vs. Indianapolis Colts (2-6) Week 12: Vs. Baltimore Ravens (4-4) Week 13: @ Pittsburgh Steelers (6-2) Week 14: @ Washington Commanders (2-4-1) Week 15: Vs. Jacksonville Jaguars (5-2) Week 16: @ Philadelphia Eagles (2-6) Week 17: @ Green Bay Packers (5-3) Week 18: Vs. Tennessee Titans (1-7) It’s not a very intimidating final half of the regular season, and ESPN is actually favoring Houston in eight of these final ten games! Although, Houston was favored to win in multiple contests they lost in the first half of this season, and with how this team has been playing recently, do you really expect them to look much better against the Chargers or the Browns? The road back to contention is clearly there for Houston, but it will require both their defense to shake off their rocky start to the season and their offense to find some consistency – even as the injury bug targets some of their best players. Second-year WR Jaylin Noel is now on IR thanks to a season-ending turf toe injury, meaning QB CJ Stroud will be relying on his connection with trade acquisitions Kayshon Boutte and Marvin Harrison Jr. to develop at a record pace…which will be another challenge for Houston’s quarterback to overcome this year. He’s overcome stalled contract negotiations, a complete collapse of his team’s defensive backfield, multiple WR and RB injuries, and the reality that scoring 30+ points can still not be enough to win. It’s been a whirlwind of a year for the Texans franchise in general, but for Stroud in particular, this season was a big bet on himself, and despite the win/loss record, he is succeeding. Texans OT Trent Brown is always insightful and one of my favorite players to chat with. We talked about the bye week, what this 2 and 5 Texans team needs to do moving forward and why he has such high praise for QB C.J. Stroud. Here’s our conversation. #Texans #CJStroud … pic.twitter.com/F6qi806at4 — Kim Y. Davis (@kimydavis) November 2, 2026 In fact, just yesterday, ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler and DJ Bien-Aime released a piece on Stroud’s stalled contract negotiations, shedding some light on what Stroud’s camp was asking for. It turns out that, at least according to Fowler and Bien-Aime’s reporting, Stroud’s team was not looking for record breaking money, and instead was looking for something, “…similar to the deal Trevor Lawrence signed with Jacksonville two years ago, placing Stroud in the second-tier [of highly-paid QBs] of around $55 million per year.” Stroud and his agent, David Mulugheta, made a counteroffer. They did not demand that Stroud be the league’s highest-paid quarterback, per a source. Stroud understands the business side of being an NFL player, from market pay for players at multiple positions, to team construction. He knows if he takes every penny possible, paying the players around him becomes harder. – Jeremy Fowler, DJ Bien-Aime, C.J. Stroud turned down a big contract. A bigger one awaits. Now, this admittedly paints a favorable picture of Stroud and his agent, David Mulugheta, as some kind of “good faith” negotiators in the process, and the truth is probably something more complicated than this. Mulugheta is also not a stranger to using his relationship with ESPN reporters to cast his clients in a favorable light, so everything said in this article should be taken with a grain of salt. However, I still highly recommend reading through the article in its entirety, as it gives us an idea of what to expect next offseason: A lot of cap-clearing moves, potentially a big trade or two to get some big contracts off the books, and maybe even a yearly salary north of $70 million for Stroud. But, all of this discussion can be spared for the offseason. We’re still in the thick of 2026, and the Texans aren’t dead yet, no matter who says so! Here’s where the Houston Texans are ranked following their bye week: NFL.COM : 19. title: Texans Sign DT Naquan Jones
summary: The Texans are making more midseason moves at defensive tackle. On Monday morning, the team announced that they are signing former Houston Texan DT Naquan Jones from the San Francisco 49ers’ practice squad: In a coinciding move, the Texans are also waiving DT Jaden Crumedy. Crumedy, 26, was signed by Texans off of the Green […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - JANUARY 04: Naquan Jones #91 of the Houston Texans jogs off the field against the Indianapolis Colts during an NFL football game at NRG Stadium on January 4, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Texans are making more midseason moves at defensive tackle. On Monday morning, the team announced that they are signing former Houston Texan DT Naquan Jones from the San Francisco 49ers’ practice squad: We have signed Naquan Jones and made other roster moves. pic.twitter.com/eyRuvODPrO — Houston Texans (@HoustonTexans) November 2, 2026 In a coinciding move, the Texans are also waiving DT Jaden Crumedy. Crumedy, 26, was signed by Texans off of the Green Bay Packers’ practice squad on September 11th, following rookie DT Kayden McDonald’s placement on IR to begin the season. Crumedy would appear in six games for the Texans, tallying six tackles, a QB hit, half a sack, and a 53.8 PFF Grade (51.4 RDEF, 71.4 TACK, 59.4 PRSH) in 87 snaps on defense. As of today, Crumedy has cleared waivers and is being signed to Houston’s practice squad. Naquan Jones, who is returning to the Texans after failing to make the initial 53-man roster, returns after a brief stint with the San Francisco 49ers, where he appeared in three games and tallied two tackles, one pressure, and a 29.5 PFF Grade (33.0 RDEF, 28.4 TACK, 52.5 PRSH) in 44 snaps on defense. He will replace Crumedy on the DT depth chart. The current lineup consists of: Sheldon Rankins Tommy Togiai Kayden McDonald Logan Hall Naquan Jones Mario Edwards Jr. (Season-Ending IR) Crumedy may not have been a complete disaster for the Texans, but he does not offer the veteran experience that Jones has, especially considering he played over 100 snaps in Houston’s final month of action in 2025. Naquan Jones should provide some much needed run stopping depth to the interior of the Texans dline. Here's some evidence of that from the end of last season. pic.twitter.com/Q0FR3Uwd2P — Houston Stressans (@TexansCommenter) November 2, 2026 Following Houston’s 27-21 overtime loss to the New York Giants, it was clear that improvements had to be made in stopping the run before every team starts copying the Giants’ playbook against the Texans. At 6’ 3” and 313 lbs., Jones should plug right into the LDT spot, next to Logan Hall, Sheldon Rankins, Tommy Togiai, or Kayden McDonald depending on the situation. Hopefully, he’ll pick up where he left off in Houston last year as a solid, if unspectacular interior defender that possesses enough strength and speed to be a handful for opposing offensive lineman. His experience in DeMeco Ryans/Matt Burke’s scheme should give him a chance to make an impact right away, which could be great news if he and McDonald are able to complement each other. In addition to the Naquan Jones signing, the Texans are also signing UDFA RB Joshua Pitsenberger to the practice squad and releasing RB Deuce Vaughn. They also claimed former Cowboys RB Emari Demercado off waivers last week . Lastly, the Texans also announced today that UDFA WR Daniel Sobkowicz is also joining the practice squad along with Jaden Crumedy, and they are releasing 2025 7th round pick DT Kyonte Hamilton and TE Zaire Mitchell-Paden. What do you think of these moves? Are the Texans a better team with Naquan Jones on the roster instead of Jaden Crumedy, or was this a mistake? Will Joshua Pitsenberger and/or Emari Demercado contribute on special teams or the offense this coming weekend, or will we all just be anxiously waiting for RB David Montgomery’s return from injury? Let us know your thoughts down in the comments below! Go Texans!

title: Texans front office face a must-win game against the Chargers
summary: The Houston Texans face the only winless team in the NFL this Sunday when they take on the Los Angeles Chargers. Both teams had bigger plans that to waste away at the bottom of the AFC leaderboard The Chargers season is toast. The Texans still have a glimmer of hope purely based on their history […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - OCTOBER 25: C.J. Stroud #7 of the Houston Texans runs out of the tunnel prior to an NFL football game against the New York Giants at Reliant Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Houston Texans face the only winless team in the NFL this Sunday when they take on the Los Angeles Chargers. Both teams had bigger plans that to waste away at the bottom of the AFC leaderboard The Chargers season is toast. The Texans still have a glimmer of hope purely based on their history of digging themselves out of holes in the past. Plus, the AFC South is as winnable a division as there is this season. The Texans lost their last three games by a combined 12 points. The Chargers have only scored above 20 points once this season, including scores of six, nine, and 14 twice. For Houston, a win not only rights the ship and re-opens the opportunity to make a last-ditch effort to save the season, but its a mandatory performance for this coaching staff and front office. For all intents and purposes, a loss to the 0-7 LA Chargers will end the Nick Caserio era. A 2-6 record with no early second round pick and a long list of undeveloped day two picks will be too much for this ownership group to look past. Houston has mortgaged their future without any near-term payout. They are $33.8M in the hole next year… before they even extend C.J. Stroud. Plus, they stand to lose Davis Mills, Tank Dell, Tommy Togiai, and Trent Brown. Houston is over-leveraged and is crashing like the ‘08 market. One person not in the spotlight is Frank Edgerly the Senior Director of Football Research and Game Management. He’s been with the team since 2023 and is a disciple of Caserio stemming back from their time in New England. The Texans defensive scheme was observed, analyzed, and addressed by the entire league this offseason. His role in not addressing these issues by self-scouting has been apparent. Not to mention the game management issues late into the fourth quarter where the team has been our maneuvered time and time again. The Chargers woes have stemmed from their horrific offensive line, inability to run the ball, and QB Justin Herbert’s regression. He’s thrown five touchdowns and 10 interceptions. When the Texans faced him in the 2024 AFC Wild Card Round, he had thrown just three interceptions all season. He’s been sacked 23 times on pace to pass his career high last year of 54. Houston desperately needs to add to both his interception and sack totals to win this do or die game against the Chargers. On defense, the Chargers have struggled to generate pass rush all season. DEs Tuli Tuipulotu and Khalil Mack lead the team with three sacks each. Like Houston, they lack an inside pass rusher who can disrupt the pocket. Thats ideal for Houston, whose achilles heel has been conceding pressure on the inside. With a good pocket, C.J. Stroud should be able to find his top targets on offense. Houston’s hot seat will remain hot even if Houston wins against the Chargers. They face next the Deshaun Watson-led Cleveland Browns, who are the darling of the 2026 season with a 5-3 record. Deshaun Watson’s trade, orchestrated by Nick Caserio in just his third month as General Manager. That trade netted Houston three first round picks, two fourth round pick, and a third. As it turns out, the compensation on the blockbuster trade has changed: Browns now are giving up six draft picks for Deshaun Watson; also instead of giving up a 2024 5th-round pick, it’s now a 2024 6th-round pick, per today’s wire. pic.twitter.com/Y98WFPmYeE — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) March 21, 2022 Without the overwhelming draft capital he was able to use to maneuver throughout drafts, he has struggled to make sound decisions early in the draft. He’s reached on players to fill needs, creating further issues at critical positions such as offensive line and defensive tackle. The 2025 and 2026 draft classes have been rife with under-performing draft picks at high value selections. Caserio will be directly graded against the outcome of both this Chargers game Sunday and the upcoming matchup against Cleveland. Both games are on the road. All that being said, if Houston can turn it around these next two weeks, things do look up for them. They play the actively taking Colts, a Lamar Jackson-less Ravens team, a winnable game against the Steelers, and a tossup against the Commanders. If Houston exits this six-game stretch at 7-6, they will be squarely in the hunt for another wild card spot in a crowded AFC. 5-1 is mandatory for Houston. Otherwise they need to close up shop on this season and multiple members of the front office.
author: Kenneth Levy

title: The Jets will have the last laugh on the Colts
summary: As this season continues to spiral, the effects are currently being felt. All of the losing has cost the Indianapolis Colts two of their franchise pillars. More could fall soon. The losing is taking its toll on fans and players alike. Sometimes there is a silver lining, though. The good thing is that it’s true […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: Sauce Gardner #1 of the Indianapolis Colts arrives prior to an NFL football game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images As this season continues to spiral, the effects are currently being felt. All of the losing has cost the Indianapolis Colts two of their franchise pillars. More could fall soon. The losing is taking its toll on fans and players alike. Sometimes there is a silver lining, though. The good thing is that it’s true in this case. The bad thing is that silver lining belongs to the New York Jets. Two first-round picks were surrendered for Sauce Gardner. Two. The first one was felt as the Colts dropped from Super Bowl contention and into the middle of the draft. That is pain most can live with. It’s this year’s lingering pain that has carried over and is making this dreadful season that much worse to watch. Instead of the Colts anticipating a potential top-ten pick in the first round of the draft, the Jets are sitting pretty at fourth overall. You can’t have a rainbow without the rain, and sometimes there is a pot of gold at the end of that rainbow. That isn’t the case for the Colts this year. Normally, pain is rewarded with a great opportunity to start fresh, gather new cornerstones to build your franchise out of the ashes. Yes, the Colts, with whatever horrific record they finish, will still have good positioning in subsequent rounds, but that lack of a first-round selection could haunt them. Let’s not even talk about the return. As good as Gardner can be, he has missed way too much time in his short stint with the Colts to be deemed worthy of the trade. Oh, and what did the Colts throw in at the end? Adonai Mitchell. He seems to be having a bit of a resurgence after getting into Shane Steichen’s doghouse and being a throw away piece. Seeing any success he has is also a tough watch. These are the stings that can stick with a franchise for a long time. If it all holds, not having the fourth overall pick is going to make some people sick. It has already cost some their jobs. That will only compound the issue. If the Jets select a Hall of Fame player with that selection, look out. This is the state of the Colts, and the Jets will be laughing all the way to the bank
author: Jon Spradley

title: The Daniel Jones Hate Is Just A Bit Out of Control
summary: Hear me out, because I know even the thought of this article is going to upset a lot of people. Daniel Jones has not played good football. I realize that. When you’re the quarterback of an NFL franchise, especially on a new contract, you’re paid to deliver. It’s November, and the only thing he’s delivered […]
full_text: Hear me out, because I know even the thought of this article is going to upset a lot of people. Daniel Jones has not played good football. I realize that. When you’re the quarterback of an NFL franchise, especially on a new contract, you’re paid to deliver. It’s November, and the only thing he’s delivered is a firesale. I’m not naive about how bad he’s been. He has 9 INTs and 2 wins, ranks 32nd in passer rating, has the second-worst TD-to-INT ratio and EPA/dropback in the league, and sits 25th in completion percentage. Do I have to keep going? But I truly believe quarterbacks get too much praise when things go well and too much blame when they don’t. I’m not absolving Jones of his play, but proper criticism requires proper context, and a lot of the criticism he’s getting has none. Let’s start with how the Colts built this roster in the first place. The idea behind Jones’ play last year was that he was in a better ecosystem than he had in New York. Then the Colts paid him and put him out there with ten other guys who now look a lot like what he had with the Giants. Why are we so surprised? Heading into the year, the Colts were essentially running it back on offense, swapping out Pittman and Braden Smith for Keenan Allen and Jalen Travis. Shouldn’t be too bad, right? Well, it has been. Without AD Mitchell, there was no depth on the roster, and the Alec Pierce injury proved devastating. Josh Downs was supposed to soften the blow by playing more in heavier personnel looks. Obviously, that hasn’t worked out. Not to make this about Downs, but when you give up on highly talented WRs, do a lackluster job replenishing the room, and bet on guys to take on expanded roles they probably were never suited for, this is what happens. IMO if you get Base to 11 as an offense, you need to take that personally It’s shown up for multiple weeks. The defense is saying “we don’t respect your WRs” I don’t understand how Chris Ballard was ok with this. pic.twitter.com/Q1Y0JlM9GJ — Colts Film Room (@ColtsFilmRoom) November 3, 2026 Base to 11 is a major part of what’s plaguing the Colts at the moment. What is Base to 11? When the Colts come out in three WR sets or 11 personnel, defenses are leaving their base defense on the field. The Colts have seen the 2nd most Base defense to 11 personnel in the NFL this year. They're averaging just 2.4 yards per play on those snaps, with only one play gaining more than 10 yards. — Colts Film Room (@ColtsFilmRoom) November 5, 2026 Why would they do that? They don’t respect the speed of the offense. Why bring out more corners if you know none of these WRs are going to run by you. We can just leave bigger bodies and sell out vs. the run, because if they pass, we’ll be just fine. The Colts are battling some very complex looks that the personnel deficiencies make it impossible to overcome. Every defenses is compressed. Safeties are playing top down and nailing down on anything underneath. In my opinion, this is the issue with the Colts right now. They cannot pass out of these looks. They don’t have enough speed on the field. Base-to-11 and aggressive coverage techniques are one thing, but they also are consistently shooting themselves in the foot. They are averaging 7.5 penalties a game in the last two weeks, back-to-back weeks of holding penalties negating large kickoffs and leading to backed up scenarios, missed field goals, dropped passes that turn into pick 6’s.. the list really goes on. Daniel Jones Pick 6 Only fair I post Tyler's bad plays too. This INT, in my opinion, is completely on Tyler Warren Not only does he drop it, but he runs what I believe is a very very poor (borderline lazy) jerk route that lets the LB undercut the ball and make the catch harder pic.twitter.com/UIhVsTNxAV — Colts Film Room (@ColtsFilmRoom) November 4, 2026 The Colts have a laundry list of problems and the biggest indictment on Daniel Jones is that he hasn’t been the solution. He is a guy who is fighting off an Achilles issue, playing behind an offense that can’t stretch a defense, and asked to carry a roster that has failed to support him at every turn. The Colts needed a quarterback who could elevate the entire roster, and I mean elevate it to a level most teams have reached in the last five years … the postseason. But has Daniel Jones ever been that kind QB? No. We just saw that in New York. So why did the Colts pay him just to ask him to elevate a bad WR room, while he’s coming off an achilles injury. It just doesn’t make sense. Not to mention the defense has been one of the worst in the league, if they were even league average the Daniel Jones discourse wouldn’t be as loud, because the Colts would likely have more than just 2 wins. Week after week we see defenses sell out to stop the run while Daniel Jones tries to pass his way behind the sticks in environments that aren’t optimized for a QB like him to be successful. So yes, Daniel Jones has not played good football. But if you’re going to hate him for the way he’s played, hate the front office first. Because I think Daniel Jones can play a lot better than he has, and maybe if he’s traded he’ll get a chance to show that again.

title: Colts’ Week 8 QB Analysis: Somehow, Even Worse
summary: Thanks to the nflFastR project, Pro Football Focus for the timely sources of data. For those of you new to this, I will publish key QB stats each week judging how well the Colts’ QB performed. Yes, O-Line, receivers, and play-calling impact these numbers but they are primarily QB measures. I will probably modify the charts throughout the season. […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - NOVEMBER 01: Quarterback Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts runs a quarterback sneak up the middle for a first down during the first half of the game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at EverBank Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Don Juan Moore/Getty Images) | Getty Images Thanks to the nflFastR project, Pro Football Focus for the timely sources of data. For those of you new to this, I will publish key QB stats each week judging how well the Colts’ QB performed. Yes, O-Line, receivers, and play-calling impact these numbers but they are primarily QB measures. I will probably modify the charts throughout the season. Commentary will be brief but feel free to let me know in the comments that stats aren’t everything. (click charts for larger view) Nothing sets the tone for a game quite like punt, punt, punt, fumble, punt, punt, pick-six, kneeldown. In case you were thinking that a competent passing game might be hidden in there, let me relieve you of that notion. In terms of EPA efficiency, Daniel Jones was NOT the worst QB this week, but he was close. Three other quarterbacks actually managed to do worse, but here’s what it took: You either had to be Baltimore’s third-string QB, Joe Fagnano, who probably expected to spend the afternoon holding a clipboard; throw 4 picks in an ugly, rain-soaked game like Michael Penix Jr.; or play in that same monsoon and fail to complete a single pass like Baker Mayfield. That’s right, those are the only guys Jones outperformed. So… hooray. HOW WELL? mouseover definitions: arsr , edp , sg% , oz% , pr% , tip , ttt , adot , ay/c , yac , yacoe , yd/c , ac% , cpoe , aypa , drp , scr% , ta% , sck% , aa% , ny/d , ny/p , 1st% , td% , to% , qbsr , epa/p , adj/p The Colts running game struggled somewhat while the offense leaned heavily on early down passing. ( 22nd ARSR; 7th EDP) Daniel Jones again faced heavy pressure, and was forced to get the ball out quickly ( 8th PR%; 24th TTT ) Those quick throws translated to short passes, which generated very little production after the catch. This left Jones with one of the lowest yards per completion totals in the league . . . AGAIN . ( 27th ADOT; 30th AY/C; 20th YAC; 27th YCOE; 31st YD/C ) Jones accuracy was OK, completing passes at a roughly average rate, even when adjusting for the short depth, but the lack of yardage on those completions left him near the bottom of the league in yards per attempt. ( 15th AC%; 18th CPOE; 30th AYPA ) Under pressure, Jones scrambled twice and threw the ball away once, but also took three sacks. Those abandoned passing plays accounted for a relatively large portion of his dropbacks. (15th DRP; 9th SCR%; 17th TA%; 13th SCK%; 12th AA% ) Between the limited passing production and the abandoned attempts, Jones unsurprisingly finished with poor overall yardage efficiency. ( 28th NY/D; 28th NY/P ) He struggled to generate first downs which obviously limits trips to the end zone. ( 25th 1ST%; 19th TD% , 3rd TO% ) It was bad enough that Jones struggled to generate successful plays, but the sacks and interceptions — particularly the pick-six — were so damaging that it’s no surprise his overall EPA efficiency was atrocious. (23rd QBSR; 29th EPA/P) mouseover definitions: ay< , dp% , ay/c , yac , yd/c , ac% , aypa , drp% , aypa , ta% , ypa , sck% , ny/a , scr% , ny/d , car% , ny/p , 1st% , any/p , td% , any/p , to% , any/p , epa/p , opd , adj/p Jones’ efficiency curve was a disaster from the start, with almost no deep passing production and very little yardage on his completions. A decent completion rate provided some relief, but the interceptions erased much of that improvement. The enormous negative impact of the pick-six dragged his final EPA per play down to the seventh-worst single-game performance by any quarterback this season. Jones produced almost no positive value in the first half, capped off by the disastrous pick-six. Things didn’t get much better in the third quarter, although he eventually put together a productive stretch that included a touchdown pass. Overall, Jones generated positive EPA on just 13 of 34 quarterback plays (38.2%), and his few productive plays were completely overwhelmed by the costly negatives, leaving him with a horrible -0.55 EPA per play. The long-term trends continue to head in the wrong direction, as Jones makes a serious run at being the least efficient quarterback in the league (look out Justin Herbert). HOW FAR? As previously mentioned, Jones’ accuracy wasn’t the problem, as he put together multiple stretches of completed passes. The issue was that many of those completions gained little meaningful yardage, and it wasn’t until late in the third quarter that he managed to string together enough first downs to move the ball downfield. Last week, he didn’t attempt a single pass beyond 20 yards, and this week, his only attempt beyond 20 yards fell incomplete. (I was so depressed after this game that I redesigned this chart.) After two weeks of unusually deep targets, Jones has now spent two consecutive weeks throwing some of the shortest passes in the league. This week, his average target depth dropped to just 4.6 yards, while his average completion depth fell even further to 3.1 yards, continuing an overall trend towards shorter passes. The Colts now throw the fifth-shortest passes in the league this season, without generating enough yards after the catch to make up for it. TO WHO? Keenan Allen led the Colts with a whopping 62 receiving yards. Meanwhile, Tyler Warren was targeted nine times but managed only three catches for 15 yards. Josh Downs and Keenan Allen lead the Colts in season-long receiving production, with Downs holding a slight edge in both total receiving yards and completed air yards. Passes targeting Tyler Warren were an absolute disaster, generating -19.6 EPA on nine targets (-2.18 per target), largely because both interceptions, including the pick-six, came on throws intended for him. On the positive side, Keenan Allen, Laquon Treadwell and Josh Downs all generated well-above-average value, albeit on relatively short passes for wide receivers. For the season, most receivers are generating above-average EPA per target, with Pierce and Burks doing so on considerably deeper passes. Despite being one of Jones’ most frequently targeted receivers, Warren is far below average production. HOW ACCURATE? Jones bounced back from last week’s poor completion performance, completing 19 of 28 passes and finishing with a 73% adjusted completion rate and +2% CPOE, a significant improvement over last week’s -11% CPOE. However, his season-long completion rates remain below league average at nearly every passing depth, with his biggest struggles coming on throws beyond 20 yards. HOW FAST? Jones averaged just 2.44 seconds to throw this week, his quickest since Week 4. I’d like to think that was by design, but given the pressure he’s faced and how short his passes have become, I have my doubts. For the season, his time to throw remains slightly quicker than expected for the depth of his targets, sitting just below the league trend line. TO WHERE? Jones threw nearly 61% of his passes to the left, where he averaged a miserable -0.46 EPA per attempt, with the pick-six doing much of the damage. He was even worse over the middle (-0.62), where his other interception occurred. Passes behind the line of scrimmage were also particularly ineffective (-0.60), while his only real bright spots came on isolated intermediate throws to either sideline. For the season, Jones has struggled across nearly every area of the field. Overall, Jones is generating essentially zero EPA per attempt, well below the league average of +0.20.
author: T. Troy Russell

title: Colts fans need to prepare for lots of new lows.
summary: I’m choosing not to write about Sunday’s loss. Allen good, Farmer serviceable, everything else bad. We will not be good this year, regardless of anything administration or coaches do. I can’t understand Shane’s stubbornness to play Jones and Lou’s to play ADG. Not playing them would not likely change the outcome of the coming games, […]
full_text: I’m choosing not to write about Sunday’s loss. Allen good, Farmer serviceable, everything else bad. We will not be good this year, regardless of anything administration or coaches do. I can’t understand Shane’s stubbornness to play Jones and Lou’s to play ADG. Not playing them would not likely change the outcome of the coming games, but it could become more palatable. I want to bring up a date that gives me chills. The Colts lease for Lucas Oil Stadium runs through 2038. However, the Colts can re-evaluate that lease as early as 2030. We simply can’t take a ton of time rebuilding. If it looks as bad in three years as it does right now, the Colts could be the ones going to London instead of the Jags. Sure, the Colts can turn it around, but as witnessed by our first 15 years in Indy, it is not a guarantee by any shot. There has been some venting that includes disowning their team, or giving up their season tickets from some Colts fans, but that would make it easier for the Colts to justify a sale or a relocation, or both. I was there renewing each year from 85 to 2011, so I saw the worst and best that the Colts had to offer, in that order. It wasn’t easy plopping down the price of two season tickets each year, but I was always afraid that if I gave them up, I’d never be able to get them back, once we finally turned the corner. I had the newness factor on my side as well. I mean, it was NFL football, just an hour up the road! I was also young enough that I could be as happy with the tailgating before and the bar hopping afterwards, as I was with the results of the game. Make no mistake, aside from a couple of playoff trips, we were really bad. I actually had money on the other team at times. I didn’t mind losing my bet if we happened to win, but there was no reason not to recoup the price of the ticket, if we lost? We don’t have the same newness factor in our favor this time around. Many seem to think that our ten years on the Ballard Merry-go-round, somehow were as bad or worse than the 15 pre Peyton years. Just from one person’s perspective, I can’t make much sense of that. If you were not around yet for the Dolt years, just look up the record each year and look at where we picked in the draft. We had multiple high picks that did not pan out until we finally made the right call in the Manning/Leaf sweepstakes. The Manning/Leaf decision changed our stars, but it took the signing of Polian to facilitate that correct decision. It wasn’t as cut and dry as you might think. So, that is what has to happen first. We have to find a GM, or whatever title the person prefers, to make the decisions. That person has to find our head coach and our players. That head coach has to find the right position coaches that spend as much time developing players as they do getting them in the right place on the field. The players have to want to win, above any quality that they possess. I’m not trying to be a Debbie Downer, but given the lease situation, I don’t think the Colts have near as much time to turn this around as they did upon the Mayflower’s arrival. I’m not sure that we survive, unless the next hire is as good and fast as Polian. How is that ray of sunshine from your resident optimist?

title: Stampede Blue Reacts Survey (Week 9): Should the Colts trade Jonathan Taylor?
summary: With the November 10 NFL trade deadline rapidly approaching, the Indianapolis Colts are facing one of their most difficult decisions in recent memory: whether to trade superstar running back Jonathan Taylor. Following the departures of Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner last week, Indianapolis appears to be embracing a rebuilding approach, and Taylor could be the […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - NOVEMBER 01: Quarterback Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts hands off the ball to runningback Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts during the second half of the game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at EverBank Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Don Juan Moore/Getty Images) | Getty Images With the November 10 NFL trade deadline rapidly approaching, the Indianapolis Colts are facing one of their most difficult decisions in recent memory: whether to trade superstar running back Jonathan Taylor. Following the departures of Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner last week, Indianapolis appears to be embracing a rebuilding approach, and Taylor could be the next major name on his way out. Multiple teams have reportedly expressed interest in acquiring the 27-year-old, including the Denver Broncos, Minnesota Vikings, Seattle Seahawks and New York Giants, with the Colts reportedly seeking compensation equivalent to a first-round pick. While Taylor remains one of the NFL’s premier running backs, the question is whether his remaining prime years align with Indianapolis’ timeline for returning to contention. He is under contract through 2028 and has publicly expressed his desire to remain with the franchise, but with the Colts sitting at 2-6 and already without their 2027 first-round selection, acquiring additional premium draft capital could prove extremely valuable. On the other hand, trading Taylor would leave an already struggling offense without its most dependable playmaker, potentially making life even more difficult for whoever eventually takes over at quarterback. With the deadline just days away, should Indianapolis capitalize on Taylor’s trade value or retain him as a cornerstone of its future? Should Jonathan Taylor be traded? Are you confident in the Colts? Any optimism surrounding the Colts following Chris Ballard’s dismissal appears to be fading quickly, particularly after Sunday’s humiliating 42-7 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars. Indianapolis was thoroughly outplayed on both sides of the football, trailing 28-0 at halftime before eventually suffering its fourth consecutive defeat. The offense managed just seven points, while the defense surrendered 42 in a performance that raised further questions about the team’s immediate future under Shane Steichen. What was already shaping up to be a disappointing season has now turned into a potential organizational reset, with several established veterans either traded or reportedly drawing interest from contenders. Last week’s Reacts survey showed that only 31 percent of Colts fans believed the franchise was headed in the right direction, a significant decline from the previous week’s 47 percent. That drop came after the trades of Nelson and Buckner, and the latest defeat is unlikely to have improved the mood surrounding the team. However, with the organization finally beginning to make significant changes and potentially accumulating additional draft capital, some fans may view the current struggles as a necessary step toward building a more competitive roster. Whether that long-term optimism outweighs the frustration of watching another lost season remains to be seen. title: George Karlaftis can relate to R Mason Thomas’ rookie progress
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs made a splash in April’s draft by selecting former Oklahoma pass rusher R Mason Thomas in the second round. Thomas made his presence felt immediately in his NFL debut by registering a sack against Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix in Week 1. While he has had promising moments since — and […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs made a splash in April’s draft by selecting former Oklahoma pass rusher R Mason Thomas in the second round. Thomas made his presence felt immediately in his NFL debut by registering a sack against Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix in Week 1. While he has had promising moments since — and has nine quarterback pressures on the year — Thomas has yet to get home again on an opposing quarterback. Kansas City’s entire pass rush has had a woefully slow start to 2026 with only nine total sacks on the year. Speaking before Wednesday’s practice, defensive end George Karlaftis recalled his own slow start to his career in 2022. He knows what Thomas — as well as first-round defensive tackle Peter Woods — are going through as the stat sheet continues to elude them. “I had this conversation before this season,” Karlaftis explained, “and we’re having conversations from time to time in season. ‘Look guys, I was a first round pick. Whatever success I’ve had, I was a first-round pick, and I didn’t have a full sack until after Thanksgiving. ‘” Adjusting to the NFL can be daunting. Ultimately, Karlaftis tallied 5.5 sacks over the last seven games of his rookie season and finished with 21 pressures. “There’s ebbs and flows,” continued Karlaftis. “You doubt yourself. You see yourself do something good on the tape, and it makes a man of you to be honest. You’ve just got to produce at the end of the day. With those guys, always keep at it. It’s like in Finding Nemo when Dorie says, ‘Just keep swimming.’ “ The veteran believes the advice from the animated feature will eventually come through for the rookies. “Those guys love football,” he said of Woods and Thomas. “When they just keep at it, keep chopping wood, keep improving, keep finding those little details in you game to where maybe that pressure becomes a sack. Or maybe that missed tackle becomes a TFL. It’s really about just finding the little things. I can remember myself vividly going through hours after games or after a bad practice of just figuring it out because it’s a long process and it takes everything out of you.” In Karlaftis’ rookie season, a Week 8 bye week after facing the San Francisco 49ers provided a chance to work on his game. “For me, personally,” he recalled, “I feel like it started clicking after the bye week. We played San Fran, and I felt like during the fourth quarter I missed two or three sacks. I was so ticked off. I was pissed at myself. I remember calling Joe Cullen maybe 20 times that week. ‘I’ve got to get it right. Coach, can you help me out?‘ “We kind of laid together a play of how I could be successful or how I could help this team more. I felt like it clicked. Whenever you have time off as a rookie — or as a vet t00 — you get a chance to reflect and review and ultimately improve on everything. For me, it was during that time. I really took a step back and I was like, ‘What am I doing well? What can I improve on?’ That’s really for me what it was.“

title: Harrison Butker is still the Chiefs’ kicker heading into Week 9
summary: Last week, the Kansas City Chiefs brought in former All-Pro kicker Justin Tucker to the practice squad after Harrison Butker’s shaky start to the season. Tucker impressed the Chiefs and special teams coordinator Dave Toub in his tryout, but will stay with the reserves for at least another week as the team continues to trust […]
full_text: (Photo by Matthew Stockman/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last week, the Kansas City Chiefs brought in former All-Pro kicker Justin Tucker to the practice squad after Harrison Butker’s shaky start to the season. Tucker impressed the Chiefs and special teams coordinator Dave Toub in his tryout, but will stay with the reserves for at least another week as the team continues to trust their guy. When Pete Sweeney of The Kansas City Star asked about the placekicking situation before Wednesday’s practice, head coach Andy Reid said there would be no change. “Harrison will be in, yeah,” Reid confirmed. The question comes after Butker missed a 54-yard field goal in the rainy fourth quarter of the close loss to the Denver Broncos ; he made a 45-yard field goal and converted on all three of his point-after attempts. He is 12-for-18 on field goals this year, tied for the lowest rate in the NFL among qualified kickers currently on an active roster; former Los Angeles Rams kicker Harrison Mevis (56%) is the only one with a lower rate. Butker has attempted the third-most 50-or-more-yard kicks in the league this year (7) but has made only two. Five of his six misses have come from long range, but he has also missed a 45-yard field goal and a point-after attempt through seven games. On offense, Reid shared that there is also “a good chance” that starting left guard Kingsley Suamataia will be in after being benched (for an unclear reason) in the Week 8 loss to Denver. He played five snaps on special teams, a notable difference from his benching in Week 4 against the Las Vegas Raiders , another divisional road game. Veteran backup Mike Caliendo filled in for Suamataia in both games. In his most recent game, Caliendo allowed five pressures — including a sack and two quarterback hits — over 68 snaps at left guard, according to Pro Football Focus . It was also a woeful performance against a Broncos defense that Kansas City ran all over in the season-opening matchup. With a strong indication that Suamataia will be back in the lineup, it feels like the team knows he is the better player. So why has a coach’s decision kept him off the field in two crucial games this season? It feels like we’ll never get that answer.
