title: Washington Commander vs. Rams in Week 9: Inside the Matchup
summary: Back in June and early July, HH veteran writer Bill-in-Bangkok, offered a week-by-week preview via the 5 O’Clock Club of the Washington Commanders regular season schedule for 2026. As we roll into the actual games during the regular season, Hogs Haven will revisit each of these previews with John Portis adding additional thoughts and updates […]
full_text: Back in June and early July, HH veteran writer Bill-in-Bangkok, offered a week-by-week preview via the 5 O’Clock Club of the Washington Commanders regular season schedule for 2026. As we roll into the actual games during the regular season, Hogs Haven will revisit each of these previews with John Portis adding additional thoughts and updates as we go inside the matchup to get you ready for every opponent the Commanders face in 2026. From John Portis: The 2-4-1 Washington Commanders head into Week 9 coming off their second win of the season and the first for Jayden Daniels as a starter since October of 2025. While the team showed improvement in their victory over the Eagles, plenty of questions remain around the team’s ability to repeat the performance against a tougher opponent. The Los Angeles Rams may fit the bill after recovering from a shaky start, squaring their record at 4-4 following a victory over the winless Chargers on Sunday. L.A.’s offseason additions of cornerback Trent McDuffie and EDGE Myles Garrett made the Rams a popular preseason pick to make the Super Bowl even before All-Pro defensive tackle Aaron Donald un-retired to re-join the team. Unfortunately for head coach Sean McVay and the Rams, things have not gone according to plan. After a rough opening-week loss in Melbourne, Australia, to the 49ers, the Rams moved Garrett to injured reserve; wide receiver Davante Adams subsequently ruptured his hamstring late last month. Los Angeles has missed both players this season, losing close matchups to the Broncos, Bills and Cardinals by four points or less . Even so, the Rams’ wins have been been against a modest lineup of opponents. The Giants, Eagles, Raiders and Chargers have a combined record of 10-19-1, with only the Giants above .500. The team did open Garrett’s 21-day practice window this week but his status for Sunday is uncertain, as is that of tight end Colby Parkinson. Cornerback Jaylen Watson was surprisingly ruled out for the season Wednesday with a shoulder injury while Trent McDuffie sat out with a back injury of his own. The Rams’ offensive line is a different animal than the one the Commanders faced last week and is rated as one of the best in the NFL, allowing the least pressures in the league so far this season. As Bill mentioned in his preview (which you can see below), McVay retained the services of Matthew Stafford and Puka Nacua with the luxury of two talented running backs in Kyren Williams and Blake Corum. The two rushers combined for 192 rushing yards against the Raiders and another 129 versus the Chargers. It is no surprise, considering McVay’s presence, that the Rams have one of the top offenses in the NFL. What is surprising is their lack of explosiveness, especially in the passing game, as the Rams’ explosive play rate of 5.8% ranks 27th in the league. Despite missing Adams and tight end Terrance Ferguson, McVay and offensive coordinator Nate Scheelhaase continue to run plenty of heavy 13 personnel ( 35% rate), throwing out of the formation frequently. The Rams have the second-best success rate on designed runs this season (48.3%). Yet they continue to not run the ball (37.7% designed run rate coming into today ranks 21st). pic.twitter.com/agGI0O2jJN — SūmerSports (@SumerSports) November 1, 2026 Commanders linebacker Sonny Styles should help match up against those looks, but Washington placed defensive tackles Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw on injured reserve on Wednesday. While the Commanders are hopeful they will get defensive tackle Johnny Newton back for Sunday’s game, expect Los Angeles to test Washington’s replacements inside early. If Charles Omenihu, Tim Settle and Shy Tuttle can hold up against the Rams’ offensive front, the defense should have a good chance of limiting their offense. Daronte Jones and the defensive secondary should also continue to focus on generating takeaways. Los Angeles has now given the ball away 12 times in 8 games . That works out to 1.5 turnovers per game, with most being charged to Matthew Stafford, who has thrown eight interceptions in eight contests. That’s as many as he gave up in a full 17-game season in 2025. The Rams have compiled a .500 record despite those turnovers with a defense that is also very good. In fact, Chris Shula’s defense is ranked in the Top 5, with cornerback Trent McDuffie and safety Quentin Lake playing at elite levels. Chris Shula's defense: 21 PPG allowed (12th) 301.1 YPG allowed (5th) -0.12 EPA/play (6th) 41.3% success rate allowed (8th) 6.23 yards per pass attempt (5th) 8 turnovers forced (17th) 11.1% missed tackles (9th) …. all without Myles Garrett. — Sosa Kremenjas (@QBsMVP) November 2, 2026 Is Trent McDuffie making a case as the BEST CB in football? – Lowest passer rating allowed: 34.7 – T-2nd in PFF coverage grade – ZERO touchdowns allowed Rams got an absolute steal this offseason… pic.twitter.com/s0OwzLYSCl — LAFB Network (@LAFBNetwork) October 30, 2026 Among safeties through Week 8, Quentin Lake ranks: 🔵1st in passes defended (8) 🔵1st in incompletions as primary defender (17) 🔵T-2nd in INTs (3) 🔵2nd in hurries (5) 🔵T-11th in tackles (50) (TruMedia) pic.twitter.com/jm4FQ0nipi — Los Angeles Rams PR (@TheLARamsPR) November 3, 2026 In a case of mirrored situations, the Commanders offense should test the interior of the Rams defense, as they’re missing defensive tackles Poona Ford and Kobie Turner. In their victories over the Rams, the Bills and Cardinals totaled 230 and 120 rushing yards, respectively. Obviously, a team with a top offense and defense doesn’t secure a 4-4 record without having some flaws. This holds true for McVay’s team, as they have 61 accepted penalties (24th) against them so far this season. For reference, the Commanders have 55 accepted penalties this year. Special teams have also been an Achilles’ heel for the Rams, and they have already changed kickers twice this season, swapping Harrison Mevis for Blake Grupe and then Grupe for Brandon McManus while adding second kicker Joshua Karty exclusively for kickoffs. Special teams coordinator Larry Ott’s group has not stood out this season but did show up last week , and the Commanders’ special teams could give Washington an advantage on Sunday. Special Teams EPA through Week 8 pic.twitter.com/jkmVWblN8Z — SFdata9ers🏈📊 (@sfdata9ers) November 3, 2026 Dan Quinn and the Washington Commanders will need to take advantage of every opportunity they can find to get ahead of Sean McVay and the Rams in what should be an interesting matchup in Landover. Betting Lines Point Spread : Rams -5.5 Game Total (Over/Under) : 47.5 points Opening odds for the Commanders have them as 5.5-point home underdogs against the Los Angeles Rams. The Over/Under opens at 47.5 in a game expected to be higher scoring than last week’s game against the Eagles. Original article from Bill-in-Bangkok published July 7 Week 9 Preview: LA Rams at Washington Commanders Date: November 8, 2026, 1:00 p.m. ET Location: Northwest Stadium in Landover Maryland The Rams are led by quarterback Matthew Stafford, who has had a career renaissance in Los Angeles. With the championship window possibly closing as Stafford reaches his 18 th season at age 38, the front office acquired edge rusher Myles Garrett through a trade and signed cornerbacks Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson to bolster the defense. With respect to the coaching staff, Sean McVay promoted Nate Scheelhaase to offensive coordinator to maintain playbook continuity after Mike LaFleur’s departure to the Cardinals. The team also hired former Commanders OC Kliff Kingsbury as assistant head coach, and Bubba Ventrone from Cleveland to lead the special teams unit. All in all, analysts see this as a winning combination. The Commanders will need to be at their best against a Rams team that will come to Landover in Week 9 fresh off of three west coast games against the Cardinals, Raiders and Chargers, ranked 29 th , 28 th , and 7 th , respectively, in ESPN’s 2026 Power Index .…

full_text: The Washington Commanders are back at practice after a win, and unfortunately that’s only the second time I’ve been able to write that sentence that season and it’s Week 9. In most other seasons that would mean the mock drafts/coaching searches were weekly features instead of playoff scenarios. This is not most other seasons, and an unexpectedly weak NFC East has kept hope alive for the Commanders season. They host the 4-4 Los Angeles Rams on Sunday, and the results of that game will play a big factor in how the rest of the season is managed, including next week’s trade deadline. Head coach Dan Quinn spoke to the media before the team hit the practice fields in Ashburn, VA. The team placed three players on injured reserve this week, including starting DTs Javon Kinlaw (knee) and Daron Payne (foot) who both had likely season-ending surgeries. Kinlaw was injured in Week 6, but more testing was done with the hope that he could still play later in the season. That changed with surgery this week, and getting shut down for the season. The Commanders also announced two DT moves before Quinn stepped up to the podium. Ricky Barber was signed from the practice squad, and Daniel Ekuale took his spot there. Washington chose to elevate veteran Byron Cowart for last week’s game against the Eagles, and they still have that option two more times this season. Jer’Zhan Newton’s 21-day practice window was opened last week, but he wasn’t activated for the Eagles game. Quinn said he’s in great shape, but the team wants to see him stack another week of practice and get his technique ready to go. Quinn praised the play of Shy Tuttle who had to step up, along with Charles Omenihu, due to injuries. Quinn was asked about third-round rookie WR Antonio Williams who led the team in snaps vs the Eagles with Terry McLaurin now on injured reserve. He said the moments were never too big for Williams, and first-round rookie LB Sonny Styles. Three more players likely done for the season: Dan Quinn at the podium. full_text: The Daily Slop – 4 November 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Bullock’s Film Room Commanders Film Review: Pass Rush vs Eagles Coming off the bye, they were hoping to turn things around and against the Eagles they certainly did. They delivered five sacks and multiple other pressures. According to NextGenStats, the Commanders had a season-high pressure rate at 46.5%. When they blitzed, they had a pressure rate of 83.3%, the second highest pressure rate on blitzes by any team in the NFL this season. So how did the Commanders do it? During the bye week, I wrote about some schemes that worked which they could use more frequently, and we definitely saw them come up against the Eagles on Sunday night. Things like read blitzes, disguised overloads and B gap stabs were all effective against the Eagles. The Commanders pass rush was under the microscope over the bye week, but against the Eagles they generated 5 sacks and a ton of pressure. Is this sustainable success? I took a closer look: https://t.co/7k6fTzlSnl pic.twitter.com/5QKuOo7s0u — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) November 4, 2026 This rush is Chaisson at his absolute best. He’s so quick off the snap and his speed is a real threat to any tackle when he gets it right. Mailata is one of the best left tackles in football and very few rushers beat him for speed, but Chaisson does exactly that here. Chaisson times the snap perfectly and by his second step, he’s already hip level with Mailata. He gets Mailata panicked and forces the tackle to completely turn around to try and stay with him. Mailata gets his outside hand on Chaisson’s shoulder, but Chaisson shows nice bend and dip as he gets under Mailata and turns the corner. Mailata makes one last effort to save the block by shoving Chaisson, trying to push him beyond the depth of the quarterback, but the quarterback fails to feel the pressure and step up in the pocket. That allows Chaisson to use that shove as momentum to close even quicker. Chaisson lands a big hit on the quarterback, who just about manages to get a throw away before Chaisson brings him down. That throw looked like it might have been intercepted by Nick Cross, but Shy Tuttle got his hand up at the line of scrimmage to knock it down. Towards the end of the game, Odafe Oweh got in on the action too. Oweh spent most of the game working against Mailata, the Eagles best lineman, so he wasn’t as effective overall as the other rushers. But by getting to work against the same man constantly, he was able to figure out ways to beat him. By the end of the game, Oweh got the better of him. Overall, the Commanders will of course be happy with the uptick from their pass rush unit in this game. They generated much more consistent pressure and of course finished those plays, putting up five sacks. However, this felt to me much more like the Eagles offensive line being bad than the Commanders pass rush being exceptionally good. Don’t get me wrong, you can only play against whoever the opponent puts out there each week, so I’m not trying to discredit this performance. But I do wonder how sustainable it is. The Commanders blitzed at a significantly lower rate than they have done all season. Much of these pressures and sacks came on four-man rushes. We’ve seen through the first six games of the season that this pass rush isn’t good enough to consistently win with four, and that Daronte Jones has had to blitz a lot and dial up various pressure packages in order to generate consistent pressure. This game doesn’t line up with that theme so far this season, which speaks to an issue with the Eagles offensive line rather than some big adjustment the Commanders made over the bye week. Individually, everyone played well up front. Chaisson had perhaps his best game in a Commanders uniform. Omenihu was a menace to whoever had to try and block him on the inside. Armstrong got the better of Bell frequently. Oweh had a solid game against one of the best tackles in the league. While Oweh and Chaisson had some very good reps against Mailata, they’ve had some very good reps individually in lots of games this season and the overall rush unit hasn’t looked this good. So I’m reluctant to say that this group has turned the corner. I definitely believe in their talent and I like the unit overall, but I’m eager to see if they can stack up performances like that against a Rams team with a much stronger offensive line. Commanders.com Final thoughts | Updates on McNichols, pass-rush is more in sync — Both Trey Amos and Nick Cross, who missed extended portions of the season with various injuries, are getting more comfortable by the week. Quinn thought Cross operated well as the nickel defensive back, while Amos had a pair of key pass breakups. It also feels like their presence has helped stabilize the secondary, which needed reinforcements. “I really felt his communication in this game, the urgency of what we’re looking for from that,” Quinn said of Cross. “So, I thought that was a good step forward as well.” — One of the biggest storylines from Sunday’s game was how quarterback Jayden Daniels brought the offense together after going down 10-0 to rally the unit. It apparently worked, because the Commanders went on to score 27 unanswered points after that. Quinn said he loved the Daniels took charge. “There comes a point when it’s enough is enough and this is not a game plan specific one that can be all the way tricked out that’s hard to do. And so, for he and for his teammates to look one another in the eye and say, ‘Okay, let’s get this part of our football in order and do this now.’ It’s usually more effective that way. So the fact that it didn’t have to be me as the one doing that, I thought was good. Obviously, frustration and all that builds in, so I like it when that happens.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE ESPN 2026 NFL trade deadline: Players to watch, buzz and goals for all 32 teams Washington Commanders (2-4-1) Chance to make playoffs: 11.6% Projected first-round draft slot: No. 9 What is the deadline goal? Get better. It’s an obvious goal for any team, but it’s also how Washington views the situation and why the Commanders wouldn’t consider themselves too active in looking to acquire or trade players based on their record. Even if, say, they lost to the Rams on Sunday and started to trade veterans on one-year deals for draft picks, they could still look to add talent, too — not for this season alone but for the long hall. A player such as Jaguars receiver Brian Thomas Jr. would make sense. He has a high ceiling at a position they will need help at in 2027. Washington could also use more help at running back and offensive line. The Commanders have seven draft picks in 2027, the first time since 2024 that they have all of their selections. — John Keim Who could be on the move? Offensive tackle Andrew Wylie. Wylie is an swing-tackle type on an inexpensive contract who could be of interest in a market in which every team is looking for offensive line help and there’s rarely any available. — Graziano Who should they target? Chargers RB Kimani Vidal. One spot at which Washington could use an upgrade is running back. Commanders running backs have amassed minus-69 rush yards over expected, per NFL Next Gen Stats. Vidal has minus-2 RYOE this season as part of a three-man backfield in Los Angeles, but he flashed promise with 58 RYOE last season. — Walder To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Download the SB Nation app Commanders fans, take command of game day! summary: The Commanders injured list has grown longer, and at the worst possible time. Defensive lineman Javon Kinlaw has had season-ending surgery to repair his MCL.   ESPN reporter Adam Schefter broke that news on Wednesday morning.   This comes on the heels of Daron Payne being lost for the year with a fracture in his […]
full_text: The Commanders injured list has grown longer, and at the worst possible time. Defensive lineman Javon Kinlaw has had season-ending surgery to repair his MCL. ESPN reporter Adam Schefter broke that news on Wednesday morning. Injury update: Commanders DL Javon Kinlaw underwent season-ending surgery Tuesday on his MCL. Now Commanders defensive linemen Kinlaw and Daron Payne both have suffered season-ending injuries in recent weeks. pic.twitter.com/hHqlyexYdx — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) November 4, 2026 This comes on the heels of Daron Payne being lost for the year with a fracture in his foot, leaving the Commanders defensive line in a tough spot. Head coach Dan Quinn had talked about Kinlaw in softer tones and alluded to the fact he may be out for a while, but not in a way that suggested he was done for the year. The fact that he is out for the foreseeable future is a real blow, especially after his quality start to the season. He has one year left on his contract, which is worth $16.9 million in 2027 . Cutting him results in a $9.9 million dead cap hit. That puts Charles Omenihu in the spotlight, with Washington needing him to step up and fill a massive void. He was up to that task in a win over the Eagles, where he had four tackles, a sack and a fumble recover y.

title: NFL trade deadline: A deep dive into potential Commanders targets
summary: Once again, Washington finds itself at a familiar crossroads as the NFL trade deadline approaches, trapped in the classic dilemma of whether to buy or sell. However, the internal and external landscape has shifted dramatically. The team’s presumed primary trade target, left guard Quenton Nelson was shipped off to Seattle, while their most valuable trade […]
full_text: Once again, Washington finds itself at a familiar crossroads as the NFL trade deadline approaches, trapped in the classic dilemma of whether to buy or sell. However, the internal and external landscape has shifted dramatically. The team’s presumed primary trade target, left guard Quenton Nelson was shipped off to Seattle , while their most valuable trade asset , Daron Payne, was lost for the season after suffering a Jones fracture in his foot. While most front offices in this precarious position would choose to stand pat and do nothing, Washington’s circumstances are uniquely complicated. The NFC East remains wide open. Philadelphia is officially tanking, Dallas is imploding and the Giants are an incredibly flawed unit. Because no one else seems to want the division, a playoff berth remains a long, but realistic shot. On the flip side, Washington has glaring roster holes, and the coaching staff hasn’t inspired enough confidence to make a true postseason push feel believable. Ultimately, Sunday’s matchup against the Rams will likely act as the pendulum that swings the front office in one direction or the other. In the meantime, a comprehensive blueprint outlines the names to consider selling — and the pieces to look at bringing in. Selling EDGE Dorrance Armstrong Dorance Armstrong finally got himself on the sack scoreboard against Philly, but he increasingly looks like the odd man out in this rotation. He is still working his way back into form after an ACL tear derailed a highly impressive start to his campaign last year. While his current market value might not trigger a bidding war, his status on an expiring contract makes him a prime candidate to move. Getting any draft capital in return is better than letting him walk for nothing. Potential Buyers: Dallas Cowboys, Green Bay Packers, Chicago Bears, Detroit Lions, Cincinnati Bengals EDGE K’Lavon Chaisson I’m really against trading K’Lavon Chaisson, as he has arguably been the team’s most effective pure pass rusher and fits Daronte Jones’ defensive scheme to a tee. However, he is also on an one-year deal , which automatically makes him Washington’s most valuable healthy trade asset. Contending teams are always desperate for EDGE help down the stretch, meaning Chaisson would command a robust market and bring back the highest return if the front office decides to pivot toward the future. Potential Buyers: San Francisco 49ers, Green Bay Packers, Chicago Bears, Detroit Lions, Cincinnati Bengals. OL Andrew Wylie While casual observers might scoff at Wylie’s trade value; experienced, plug-and-play veteran offensive linemen are incredibly difficult to find midseason. Wylie has built a steady reputation across the league as a stable, high-floor, yet unspectacular right tackle who can also play inside. For a contender dealing with a sudden injury along the front five, Wylie represents an affordable insurance policy who won’t derail an offense. Potential Buyers: Teams requiring immediate, veteran tackle depth or frontline protection stability. QB Marcus Mariota Put the pitchforks down for just a second and hear this out. Everyone knows how vital a high-level backup quarterback is in today’s NFL, especially with Jayden Daniels playing a physical brand of football where a single bad hit puts the season in Mariota’s hands. However, multiple teams are desperate for immediate quarterback stability and are willing to overpay. If Mariota genuinely wants another shot to start, Washington could leverage that desire into significant draft capital. While a trade remains highly unlikely given his value as a locker room mentor and insurance policy, every player has a price tag if the right offer rolls in. Potential Buyers: Baltimore Ravens, Minnesota Vikings DBs Mikey Sainristil & Quan Martin These two young defensive backs belong in the same conversation because they present nearly identical dilemmas. If a buyer emerges for either player, it will be a team looking to gamble on their raw traits, hoping a change of scenery can salvage their development and unlock their potential in a different system. At this stage, if a front office offers even an ounce of real draft value for either defender, management should take the deal immediately and run. Potential Buyers: Buffalo Bills, Pittsburgh Steelers, Chicago Bears, Detroit Lions . Buyers Running Backs Jonathan Taylor The potential pairing of Jayden Daniels and Jonathan Taylor in the same backfield is nothing short of electrifying. One could easily argue that Taylor represents the most talented, game-changing trade piece currently available on the market. However, that elite pedigree comes with a massive price tag, which might ultimately cause Washington’s front office to hesitate. At 27 years old, Taylor carries a heavy career workload on his body. Trading premium assets for a running back with significant mileage always raises red flags. Yet, if he can maintain his current high level of production, he would instantly become the most dominant skill-position player Daniels has ever shared a huddle with in Washington, completely redefining the team’s offensive identity. Value: Low Day 1 or High Day 2 (plus) pick Tony Pollard It seems someone tipped Pollard off about the deadline rumors because he has put on an absolute clinic over the past two weeks. Pollard remains a highly underappreciated player who provides efficiency both as an interior rusher, and a reliable outlet in the passing game. While he may not be a game changer who completely tilts defensive game plans, he is the exact type of high-floor contributor who helps you win tight football games down the stretch. Hitting the age 30 threshold means his price tag is suppressed, but that exact same age factor might sway front offices away from making a move entirely. Projected Value: Mid-to-low Day 3 pick Breece Hall Despite recently signing an extension with the Jets , history shows that long-term contracts don’t make a player untradeable, look no further than how New York handled Sauce Gardner last year. While Hall is currently sidelined with an injury, his upside remains undeniable. When fully healthy, he is an elite, dynamic weapon out of the backfield, the exact type of premier playmaker that a young quarterback like Jayden Daniels has yet to work with in the NFL. Bringing in an explosive dual-threat like Hall would completely transform the offense’s ceiling. Value: High-to-Mid Day 2 Pick Keaton Mitchell/Omarion Hampton/Kimani Vidal Sitting at a disappointing 0-7, the Chargers are in complete disarray, and their lackluster running game has left a lot to be desired. Ironically, the backfield remains arguably the deepest room on the roster, making it prime real estate for draft capital. Los Angeles needs to accumulate as many assets as possible to jumpstart this rebuild and identify core players who can actually help turn the franchise around. • Omarion Hampton: As the prize of the group, Hampton possesses the true three-down skillset that will likely command a premium. • Projected Value: Day 2 Pick • Keaton Mitchell & Kimani Vidal: Both serve as highly intriguing change-of-pace options who could immediately boost a contender’s depth chart for a much lower entry cost. • Projected Value: High-to-Mid Day 3 Pick Receiver Josh Downs I wasn’t going to write anything about Downs until I saw some reports about him being tied to the team. Downs has been a solid and reliable WR for the Colts given his size he would be a slot WR wherever he goes and at 25, you’re getting a really sound player . I do worry about his next contract. Indy first-hand saw how outrageous the free agent market for WRs can get with the Alec Pierce deal. Investing a ton of money into him while sending out draft capital will the be real question for teams here. summary: Here's a look at what each NFL team is wearing in Week 9, led by throwbacks from the Eagles.
full_text:
While Week 8 meant the debut of two "Rivalries" jerseys, another alternate look returns to the field in Week 9, and a popular throwback comes back. 

 

 The Los Angeles Chargers are wearing their "Super Chargers" all-navy threads against the Houston Texans . Unveiled in 2025, the Chargers deemed the navy uniforms "a true modern throwback." It's a nod to threads worn in the 1990s and early 2000s, which coincided with a Super Bowl XXIX appearance and four AFC West titles. The navy jersey includes white modern numbers with an old-school outline and gold trim. The navy pants boast a bolt on the side, while a bolt also runs on the shoulders and helmet. "Super Chargers" is stitched in white on the neckline. 

 In a trend that's becoming more common around the league, the New York Giants and Philadelphia Eagles offer a matchup of throwback uniforms. The Eagles are rocking their "Kelly Green" threads, while it's a "Vintage White" look for the Giants. "Thursday Night Football" between the Denver Broncos and Seattle Seahawks in Week 6 also brought a throwback threads matchup. Philadelphia brought back the iconic Kelly Green combination in 2023, while New York's look returned in 2025 after a one-year hiatus. 

 Alternates are still represented well throughout the week, though.

 The Baltimore Ravens are wearing their "Purple Rising" combination on "Thursday Night Football" against the Jacksonville Jaguars . Baltimore unveiled the look in the offseason as part of their wardrobe overhaul. It includes a new "Purple Rising" helmet, first introduced in 2024 with the alternate purple jersey. The primary logo appears on the metallic purple lid instead of the front-facing Ravens one. Different from the previous all-purple combination is a new "midnight purple" color, which is meant to emulate the iridescence of a raven's feather, and "Purple Rising" running on the inside collar.

 The New Orleans Saints are going gold against the Cleveland Browns . And it's another navy look for the Dallas Cowboys against the Indianapolis Colts , who are doing a rare home white out.

title: What has gone right -- and wrong -- for 10 new NFL head coaches in 2026 season
summary: There are 10 new head coaches in the NFL this season, which ties the most ever. How are things going for each of them after eight weeks?
full_text:
The  2026 NFL offseason featured 10 head coaching changes, which tied with 1978, 1997, 2006 and 2022 for the most ever in an offseason, per ESPN Research.

 The Raiders hired Klint Kubiak after his Super Bowl win  as the Seahawks' offensive coordinator. Three AFC North teams -- the Browns (Todd Monken), Steelers (Mike McCarthy) and Ravens (Jesse Minter) -- also changed coaches. Elsewhere in the AFC, the Bills promoted offensive coordinator Joe Brady to head coach, the Dolphins hired former Packers DC Jeff Hafley, and the Titans brought in Robert Saleh. In the NFC, Mike LaFleur, Kevin Stefanski and John Harbaugh were hired by the Cardinals, Falcons and Giants, respectively.

 How have these new coaches fared at their new destinations? We called on our NFL Nation reporters to evaluate both the positive and concerning signs from each team so far. Then, we provided a key stat on each team's start.

 The 10 teams with new coaches are listed below by ESPN Football Power Index 's playoff odds. We'll start in Western New York.

 

 
 Jump to a team: 
 ARI | ATL | BAL  |  BUF | CLE 
 LV | MIA  |  NYG | PIT | TEN 

 
 

 

 Joe Brady, Buffalo Bills 
 Record: 6-1 
 FPI chance to make playoffs:  99.4%

 What has gone right this season:  Brady's offense, and his partnership with quarterback  Josh Allen , is working. The Bills lead the NFL in points per game (33.3) and rank second in both yards per game and yards per play. The  trade for wide receiver  DJ Moore in the spring has made the Bills' offense more vertical, with Allen leading the NFL in yards per pass attempt (8.7). And their red zone rushing attack, led by Allen and RB  James Cook III , has them converting red zone trips into touchdowns at a 70% clip.

 What has gone wrong this season:  The pass defense has been a mess. The Bills have already moved on from safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson and benched cornerback Maxwell Hairston . Nickelback  Dee Alford has been in and out of the lineup with injuries . Now, the Bills are relying on a rookie and a couple of players who started the season on the practice squad to take significant snaps for a unit that ranks 30th in yards allowed per game. -- Nick Suss, Bills reporter 

 Key stat to know:  This is the second time in the past 30 seasons that Buffalo has started 6-1 or better. The last such start was in 2022, when it finished 13-3 and lost to the Bengals in the divisional round of the playoffs.  -- ESPN Research 

 

 
 

 Mike McCarthy, Pittsburgh Steelers 
 Record: 6-2 
 FPI chance to make playoffs:  81.0%

 What has gone right this season:  A Pittsburgh native, McCarthy took the job with a special understanding of the core identity of the team. Halfway through his first season, he has upheld that in a big way. Led by running back Jaylen Warren and a young core of offensive linemen, the Steelers' offense is a physical unit capable of creating explosive plays in the run game. Defensively, McCarthy brought in coordinator Patrick Graham to reinforce those classic principles with his 3-4 front. The Steelers have held opponents to a league-best 51.3 rushing yards per game in the past three games.

 

 What has gone wrong this season:  While McCarthy was brought in to maximize quarterback Aaron Rodgers , the passing game still lacks consistency. The Steelers rank 20th in passing yards per game (210.5) and 21st in air yards per attempt (6.5). And it's not all on Rodgers. Top receiver DK Metcalf has been plagued by drops, including one this past Sunday that resulted in an interception. The strong run game has carried the offense in the open field, but the Steelers are scoring touchdowns on only 50% of their red zone trips (tied for 26th in the NFL). Part of the problem is the playcalling. In the past four games, the Steelers utilized designed runs on just 31% of plays in goal-to-go situations. -- Brooke Pryor, Steelers reporter 

 Key stat to know:  The Steelers have a 4-0 record at home in 2026, which is their first such start since going 6-0 at home in 2020. And McCarthy's offense has shown up at Acrisure Stadium, averaging 27.8 points per game in Pittsburgh versus 17.3 on the road. -- ESPN Research 

 

 
 

 John Harbaugh, New York Giants 
 Record: 4-2-1 
 FPI chance to make playoffs:  47.0%

 What has gone right this season:  A lot. The Giants have already matched their win total from 2025. They're clearly a more buttoned-up and fundamentally sound team after repping situational football endlessly in training camp. And they're 3-1-1 in one-score games after finishing 1-7 last season. The biggest gains have been made by their special teams (ranked eighth in EPA) and defense (ninth overall). Hiring defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson has worked out, as Wilson has done a solid job with a group that isn't loaded with talent and lost its best player in edge rusher  Brian Burns  ( torn ACL ). They're allowing 46.5 fewer yards per game than last season.

 What has gone wrong this season:  Injuries have hit the Giants hard. They lost Burns and starting quarterback Jaxson Dart  ( left knee injury ), arguably the two most important players on each side of the ball, for the season. New York spent the spring and summer creating an offense that prioritizes the quarterback's legs and had to pivot. Offensive coordinator Matt Nagy has made it work relatively well with Dart, Jameis Winston and now J.J. McCarthy . But the injuries still have the Giants working with limitations. Their quarterbacks are averaging 13.2 yards rushing per game since Dart's injury.  -- Jordan Raanan, Giants reporter 

 Key stat to know: After their Week 7 win  over the Texans, the Giants became the favorites to win the NFC East (-150 on DraftKings), the first time since 2016 that has happened at any point during a season. That year, they finished 11-5 and lost in the wild-card round  to the Packers.

 

 
 

 Todd Monken, Cleveland Browns 
 Record: 5-3 
 FPI chance to make playoffs:  16.8%

 What has gone right this season:  The Browns are the second-youngest team in the NFL but have taken on a gritty, resilient persona behind Monken to help them dominate late-game situations. All five of Cleveland's wins have been courtesy of game-winning drives. "Coach Monk has put us in these situations in practice time after time ... so whenever we get into the game and whenever we get into these situations, we already have the confidence to go down there and set up a game-winning drive," rookie wide receiver KC Concepcion said.

 

 What has gone wrong this season:  The offense -- Monken's area of expertise -- remains a work in progress. Quarterback Deshaun Watson has raised his level of play this season but still ranks 28th out of 30 qualifying players in QBR, and he could miss Week 9 after being put in concussion protocol . Inconsistent play from a new-look offensive line has also contributed to an offense that ranks 29th in points per game (17.4). "It's been a little bit of an up-and-down challenge," Monken said. "But that's part of the NFL, right? That's part of when you play the best in the world as you're trying to find your way, your footing, your players, coaches, schematically, to be consistent." -- Daniel Oyefusi, Browns reporter 

 Key stat to know: Monken's team has already surpassed the Browns' win total from 2024 (three) and is one win away from beating Cleveland's 2025 total. Before Sunday's loss to the Steelers, Cleveland's four straight wins in division games (dating back to last season) were its longest streak since 1987. -- ESPN Research 

 

 
 

 Klint Kubiak, Las Vegas Raiders 
 Record: 4-4 
 FPI chance to make playoffs:  10.7%

 What has gone right this season:  Despite the Raiders having an insufficient run game and weak WR room, they rank sixth in points per game (27.6) and 12th in total yards (342.4). That's because the dynamic between Kubiak and veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins has orchestrated one of the league's best passing games. Kubiak has been a good play designer, while Cousins'…

title: NFL Week 9 latest intel, buzz questions, fantasy tips and trade deadline news
summary: What now for the Ravens without Lamar Jackson? What are people around the NFL saying about Justin Herbert's struggles? And what's the latest on the looming trade deadline?
full_text:
It's Week 9 of the  2026 NFL season , which means two things. First, we're about to hit midseason. Second, the trade deadline is right around the corner. And insiders Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano have been calling sources around the league for the latest news and notable buzz.

 The Ravens are in a tough spot, dropping to 4-4 and losing not only QB1 Lamar Jackson but also QB2 Tyler Huntley to injuries. What's next for Baltimore? Will the Ravens focus their attention on 2027 or still try to turn things around this season in a tight AFC North? Out west, what's going on with Justin Herbert ? The Chargers obviously have big problems at 0-7, and Herbert hasn't played well. What are we hearing on his struggles?

 And what about trade buzz? What's the latest around the league? Which teams could be active, and which players could be on the move before the Tuesday deadline? It's all here, as Jeremy and Dan answer big questions, hand out useful fantasy football nuggets and empty their reporting notebooks heading into Week 9.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Next steps for the Ravens 
 Buzz on Herbert's struggles 
 Deadline intel | Fantasy advice 
 More notes and nuggets 

 
 

 What's your sense on where the Ravens go from here? 
 Graziano: Baltimore isn't a throw-in-the-towel type of organization. My sense is that the Ravens will work to solve the problem and will be open to a number of ideas at quarterback with Lamar Jackson  ( thumb ) and Tyler Huntley  (toe) out. Undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano has been announced as their starter  for  Thursday night  against Jacksonville, but if, for example, the Cardinals are done with Jacoby Brissett , Baltimore would be a team I'd expect to at least look into bringing in Brissett for Week 10 on. (Update: The Ravens are trading for Brissett , per ESPN's Adam Schefter.)

 

 Fowler: In the short term, there are several players with lower-cost contracts if the Ravens choose to pursue them. Brissett was with Ravens quarterbacks coach Isaiah Woolfork last season in Arizona. Bears backup Tyson Bagent has familiarity with Ravens offensive coordinator Declan Doyle. And some conversations I had early this week made me think the Colts' Daniel Jones is at least on the radar. Baltimore could essentially sign him without spending a lot because of his struggles. Jones' $5.5 million base salary is tradable, and his 2027 guarantees don't trigger until the offseason. He's roughly 11 months post-Achilles tear , so perhaps his play improves.

 Graziano: My bigger question is a long-term one involving Jackson's future with the franchise . I believed going into this season that the most important big-picture goal the Ravens had was to get to next offseason with Jackson feeling good about signing an extension that keeps him in Baltimore for years to come. Now that it is apparent that the season isn't going the way he or they hoped, my focus is trying to figure out what comes next for the Ravens and Jackson.

 Fowler: Assuming Jackson is done for the season, his $84 million cap hit in 2027 is an albatross for Baltimore, which could give Baltimore justifiable hesitance about giving him a top-of-the-market extension because of durability concerns. Thursday will mark Jackson's fourth missed game this season -- the fourth time in six seasons he has missed four or more games.

 I'm pumping the brakes on the "Lamar played his last down in Baltimore" talk for now. He's under contract in 2027. But the Ravens must at least now consider life without him. They had a chance to extend him last offseason, and it didn't happen -- either because he didn't want to sign or they didn't make him an irresistible offer. Both sides eventually need to figure out what they want out of their immediate future together.

 Graziano: Yeah, if they get to next spring and still can't get a deal done, they are simply going to have to consider trading him. The no-franchise tag clause in his contract gives him incredible leverage and means he has no reason to sign an extension with Baltimore that he doesn't absolutely love. If nothing happens before March 2028, Jackson would be an unrestricted free agent with at least two MVP awards on his résumé. And the no-trade clause means he could decide his team.

 Jackson didn't get the fully guaranteed deal he was looking for the last time he was up for an extension, but he got an awful lot  of money. And the reason he got those clauses in his contract is because he wants to have control over where he finishes his career.

 Fowler: The no-franchise tag and no-trade clauses make for a fascinating dynamic. He entered the season with considerable leverage, which he mostly still has. But the sheen is wearing off slightly. He'll be 30 in January, which isn't a big deal for quarterbacks but is at least a consideration in terms of his rushing ability.

 

 But if Baltimore were to listen, his trade market should look more robust than it did a few years ago when he was on the franchise tag and whispers of collusion persisted . Whether Baltimore entertains a deal is still a big "if." But come March, Jackson will be 12 months from the chance to enter true free agency, so the clock is ticking.

 

 
 What's the buzz around the league on Justin Herbert 's struggles? 
 Fowler: League evaluators typically support Herbert more than the media does, but it has been harder to defend him this season. He looks hesitant and is seeing the field poorly. "He doesn't seem comfortable in the offense," an AFC exec said. "I don't know that it's a great schematic fit for his talents. He's throwing a lot of picks where he simply isn't seeing defenders. I don't know how it gets better."

 Coaches are more inclined to give him grace. "The entire team has been devastated around him," said an NFL defensive coach who recently prepared for him. "The O-line is a mess, the running game is bad, and the skill guys aren't very good. It's nearly impossible to have success with that setup."

 Herbert has proof of concept -- six seasons of quality quarterback play, some of it at quite a high level -- but is in the kind of funk that makes you wonder whether this type of downturn was inevitable, no matter how much Jim Harbaugh tried to motivate him publicly or privately.

 Graziano: I have heard similar things about him being an awkward fit for what Mike McDaniel wants his quarterback to do, specifically diagnosing the defense at the line of scrimmage and adjusting accordingly. Oddly, McDaniel's success in Miami came because of his ability to scheme around Tua Tagovailoa 's deficiencies, but one thing Tagovailoa could do was make the right decisions when he got to the line. If that's not something that comes as easily to Herbert, that might be showing up.

 The question is whether this becomes a completely lost season or if there's some way for Herbert to get to the end of it feeling better about what lies ahead. Considering the Chargers' 0-7 record, the former feels more likely.

 

 Fowler: What's amazing is the Chargers could have used the Week 7 bye to improve their offense. But Harbaugh made zero changes . It's almost as if the Chargers felt that they could roll the ball out and magically turn things around. They probably should have received more heat for not tweaking much of anything.

 McDaniel did tweak Herbert's mechanics in the offseason, having him use a weighted, bright green ball to promote a quicker release. Part of me wonders whether the changes affected his confidence. Or maybe he simply never recovered from that ugly playoff loss to New England last season, when he was sacked six times and Los Angeles scored three points. He has taken 248 sacks in six-plus years. Those hits add up.

 Graziano: No doubt. I've been asking teams if they have a sense of what the Chargers are going to do ahead of the trade deadline, and a couple told me over the weekend that they don't get the sense that Los Angeles is eager to enter teardown mode. At least entering Sunday, I wasn't getting the…

title: Millennial minds: How Doyle, Udinski leapt to head of the OC class
summary: There are nine NFL offensive coordinators 35 or younger. How did these millennials land gigs so early in their careers?
full_text:
At age 22, when Declan Doyle arrived in New Orleans in 2019 shortly after getting hired for his first NFL job as an offensive assistant, he wrote down some of his goals and aspirations on sticky notes that he bunched around a mirror.

 One of the messages read: "Youngest NFL coordinator in history, February 2024."

 When Doyle was hired to become the Chicago Bears ' offensive coordinator in 2025, he remembered that note and thought to himself, "Oh, I was a year late."

 Doyle's obsessive determination is why he is leading the charge with the new generation of offensive coordinators, which is a storyline for Thursday's game between the Baltimore Ravens and Jacksonville Jaguars (8:15 p.m. ET, Prime Video). Doyle, who is in his first season as the playcaller for the Ravens at age 30, and the Jaguars' Grant Udinski (also 30) are among nine NFL offensive coordinators who are 35 years old or younger.

 These members of Generation Y represent a young wave in the NFL that has nearly doubled in size in a year. With five offensive coordinators 35 or younger in 2025, that number has grown in 2026 to include Doyle, Udinski, Denver's Davis Webb , Washington's David Blough , Cleveland's Travis Switzer, Philadelphia's Sean Mannion , Atlanta's Tommy Rees, Carolina's Brad Idzik and Los Angeles Rams ' Nate Scheelhaase.

 Their experiences this season range widely: guiding high-scoring offenses, getting stripped of playcalling duties, going from being celebrated to criticized and dealing with multiple quarterback changes. But all of these millennial minds born in the 1990s have proven to be young and relentless, rising rapidly to the role of offensive architects because of their connections, creativity and sacrifice.

 As a student football assistant at the University of Iowa, Doyle worked 100 hours a week while taking a full course load, which meant he drew up scout cards for the football team during his own classes. As a graduate assistant at Baylor University, Udinski had so little money that he lived in his car in a Walmart parking lot.

 Now, Doyle is tasked with keeping the Ravens' offense afloat with undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano , who will start Thursday night, and Jacoby Brissett , a veteran journeyman who is expected to be acquired in a trade this weekend . Udinski is the right-hand man of Jaguars coach Liam Coen, helping Jacksonville produce the fifth-most points per game (28.0) this season.

 "This is going to be my 11th year coaching, and I've pretty much been younger than every guy in the room I've been in," Doyle said. "I've always been too young for every job I've ever had. And what I've noticed is that it really doesn't matter. Knowledge is power."

 Here are the stories of the NFL's nine millennial offensive coordinators:

 

 
 Offensive Coordinators 35 and under: 
 Doyle | Udinski | Webb 
 Blough | Switzer | Mannion 
 Rees | Idzik | Scheelhaase 

 

 

 

 Declan Doyle, 30, Baltimore Ravens 

 Inside Doyle's offensive meeting room is a sign that reads: "Nobody adjusts better than us." His first few months as Baltimore's offensive coordinator have tested that mantra.

 Jackson has played only 14 full quarters this season because of ankle and hand injuries. He will have surgery on his right thumb and be placed on injured reserve with "potentially" a season-ending injury, according to coach Jesse Minter.

 Backup quarterback Tyler "Snoop" Huntley also suffered a season-ending turf toe injury, which would lead to a rare occurrence: Fagnano will become the second undrafted rookie to start at quarterback in Ravens history.

 Plus, the Ravens' top three centers have all suffered season-ending injuries, which has led to six different starting offensive line combinations. 

 As a result, the Ravens have been held to 14 or fewer points in three straight games. That hasn't happened in Baltimore in 21 years.

 "I've said it to the group, but it's all about just fixing this week's problems," Doyle said earlier this season. "So, you figure out what the problems are this week, how do we minimize those things [and] how do we take advantage of giving our guys that are up and that are playing, the best chance to go win the game and to be able to execute at a high level?"

 At 30, Doyle is the NFL's youngest playcaller. Others inside the Ravens' facility have different names for him.

 Jackson, who is 10 months younger than Doyle, calls him "a wizard." Flowers refers to him as "a genius." And defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver described him as a "human computer" for the rolodex of offensive plays in his head.

 One of Doyle's finest trick plays came in Week 6 in Cleveland when tight end Josh Cuevas lined up between the center and left guard. Cuevas positioned himself a step behind the line of scrimmage, which kept him as an eligible receiver.

 This unusual formation confused the Cleveland defense and allowed Cuevas to slip into the open field for a 29-yard catch.

 

 "He's somebody that knows where he's going in life," Ravens tight end Mark Andrews said. "He's not like copycatting guys. He's making his plays, and I feel like he's a trendsetter in the league. He's going to be like that for a long time just because he's so smart."

 Some players believe Doyle is too cold-blooded. In the season opener, Flowers scored on a spectacular 54-yard touchdown. When the TV camera panned to Doyle, he sat there stonefaced.

 "You are trying to eliminate anything that would cloud your judgment or what is going to happen next," Doyle said when asked about not showing any emotion. "If he gets tackled, [and] we are at the 8-yard line, I have to have a play as fast as I possibly can to get into [ Lamar Jackson ]. You do not smile until it hits zeroes." -- Jamison Hensley 

 

 

 

 Grant Udinski, 30, Jacksonville Jaguars 
 In Jacksonville, Udinski's journey from his first coaching job to offensive coordinator for the Jaguars began in a Walmart parking lot.

 When Udinski arrived at Baylor in 2019 to be a graduate assistant under then-coach Matt Rhule he had little money and no place to stay. He also knew nobody in Waco, Texas, so his solution was to hunker down in his car in a store's lot near campus.

 That lasted about a week until Baylor's assistant defensive coordinator Phil Snow found out and convinced Udinski to move in with him. A year later Udinski was a coaching assistant under Rhule with the Carolina Panthers lasting two seasons, followed by three seasons with the Minnesota Vikings . Then Jaguars head coach Liam Coen called in January 2025.

 Udinski's path from several uncomfortable nights sleeping in his car to the Jaguars' offensive coordinator at only 29 years old took just six years. It's a journey that Udinski acknowledges has been surprisingly quick but also one that wouldn't have happened without help from a lot of people -- and he's grateful for all of it.

 "Those are the things that you look back and you almost think the amount of stars to align seems impossible for things like that to work out the way that they did," Udinski said. "Those type of things, you pinch yourself and on the long days and long nights, you remind yourself where you came from."

 Udinski doesn't call plays for the Jaguars but his impact on the offense throughout the week and on game day is significant. Coen, who is Jacksonville's playcaller, likes that Udinski is level-headed, which balances out his own ups and downs.

 "If something doesn't look good on a Wednesday, I'm typically going to be the one to say, 'Let's throw it out. Why waste our time on that? We have a million other plays,'" Coen said. "Whereas he can then communicate to me, 'Hey, no, no, no. Let's try it again tomorrow.'"

 Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence , 27, called Udinski one of the best coaches he has ever had.

 "Sometimes I think Grant's double my age, honestly. Not three years older," Lawrence joked. "Just the way he's about his business.

title: 2026 NFL trade deadline: Players to watch, buzz and goals for all 32 teams
summary: We outlined deadline plans for all 32 teams, including who could be dealt before 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday. Here's what you need to know.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL trade deadline is Tuesday at 4 p.m. ET. We have already had a fair share of trades made this season , but could more be on the horizon? Will the Colts continue to trade players away -- such as  Jonathan Taylor -- and build draft capital for the future? Will the Chiefs finally find a trade for a dependable wide receiver for QB  Patrick Mahomes ? How will the Eagles and Ravens approach things without their QB1s? Let's take a 32-team look at what to expect over the next week.

 First, we checked where each team stands through Week 8 using ESPN's Football Power Index projections. Then, we asked our NFL Nation reporters to name each team's trade deadline goal. Who is staying put, and who is open for business? Next, NFL insiders Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano leaned on their reporting to predict which players on every team could be on the move. Finally, analysts Aaron Schatz and Seth Walder picked one player each team should try to acquire.

 Here's everything you need to know heading into the deadline.

 
 Jump to: 
 ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN 
 CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND 
 JAX | KC | LAC | LAR | LV | MIA | MIN 
 NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF 
 SEA | TB | TEN | WSH 

 
 

 

 

 Arizona Cardinals (3-5) 
 Chance to make playoffs: 1.1% 
 Projected first-round draft slot: No. 8

 What is the deadline goal?  Keep building for the future. That seems to be the M.O. of another M.O. -- Cardinals general manager Monti Ossenfort. He's in Year 4 of a three-year rebuild that hasn't blossomed yet. Moving players who are unhappy or veterans for draft capital is not out of the question after trading Marvin Harrison Jr . to the Texans last month. The Cardinals want to build toward the future, especially for next season when they will likely have to address the quarterback position again.  -- Josh Weinfuss 

 

 Who could be on the move? Edge  Josh Sweat . The Cardinals have received trade interest on Sweat, who would be a natural fit in Dallas. Word is he wants a new deal, which could be a hurdle. Safety Budda Baker and quarterback Jacoby Brissett  are also names to watch. (Update: Brissett was traded to the Ravens on Wednesday.)  -- Fowler 

 Who should they target? Vikings WR Tai Felton . Felton has only six receptions in a season and a half in the NFL, but the Cardinals could try to find the skills that made him a third-round pick in 2025. They need young receiving talent behind Michael Wilson . -- Schatz 

 
 

 

 Atlanta Falcons (3-5) 
 Chance to make playoffs: 7.9% 
 Projected first-round draft slot: No. 10

 What is the deadline goal? Don't give up valuable future assets. New Falcons general manager Ian Cunningham hated that the team had only five draft picks in 2026. He vowed that the franchise would never have that few again. Cunningham wants to build the Falcons through the draft. So, do not expect him to gamble away picks unless there's a no-brainer offer out there. The Falcons are unlikely to be active with their 3-5 record, because they still believe they can win the NFC South. They just won't give up important draft capital to do it. -- Marc Raimondi 

 Who could be on the move? Safety  Jessie Bates III . To be clear ... I do not believe the Falcons are trying to trade Bates, and I would be surprised if they did. But he's an excellent player in the final year of his contract, and there are teams out there that would like to know whether they can get him. I believe it would take a huge offer. -- Graziano 

 Who should they target? Texans WR Kayshon Boutte . This would be the second time Boutte has been traded this season, after the Patriots dealt him to Houston in August. But that was before the Texans traded for Marvin Harrison Jr . (and before the Texans got out to a 2-5 start). The Falcons are 3-5 but not out of the race in the NFC South, so adding a cheap player who could help is not out of the question, and Boutte is exactly that. -- Walder 

 
 

 

 Baltimore Ravens (4-4) 
 Chance to make playoffs: 7.2% 
 Projected first-round draft slot: No. 11

 What is the deadline goal? Trade for a QB or listen to offers. With injured QB Lamar Jackson (right thumb) out for at least four games and perhaps the season, the Ravens have to decide whether they want to add a quarterback to try to keep the season afloat or trade their own players for capital. Running back Derrick Henry could be a target for a championship contender. But it wouldn't be surprising if the Ravens stand pat. -- Jamison Hensley 

 Who could be on the move?  Wide receiver  Rashod Bateman . Several teams are looking for receiver help, and Bateman would have value, should Baltimore entertain it. He's not a focal point in the offense and would probably welcome the chance to be more of one elsewhere. -- Fowler 

 

 Who should they target? Cardinals QB Jacoby Brissett . The injury to Jackson completely changes the Ravens' needs. They're still in the playoff race and need a quarterback with more experience than undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano . Brissett might have lost his job to  Gardner Minshew II  on Sunday, but he still ranks 24th among qualified quarterbacks with a 48.9 QBR. That's not good, but that's not undrafted rookie level, either. (Update: Brissett was indeed traded to the Ravens on Wednesday.)  -- Schatz 

 
 

 

 Buffalo Bills (6-1) 
 Chance to make playoffs: 99.1% 
 Projected first-round draft slot: No. 31

 What is the deadline goal? Be aggressive with secondary options. With the way the Bills' offense is playing, a league-average defense should be enough to make them serious contenders. Now, the salary cap situation complicates things. With the roster as is, the Bills have a little less than $4 million to spend. But they should be in the market for an extra safety or nickel corner to fortify a weakness and alleviate some of the concerns caused by injuries and early-season mistakes. -- Nick Suss 

 Who could be on the move? Wide receiver  Keon Coleman . Coleman has played well enough to stay in Buffalo's short-term and maybe long-term plans. But I'm not sure this team will trade anyone . So consider this pure speculation that Coleman could be attractive enough to a receiver-needy team to bring back the defensive help Buffalo seeks. -- Graziano 

 Who should they target? Buccaneers edge Yaya Diaby . He would provide a jolt of pass rush to a defense that badly needs it. Buffalo ranks 26th in pass rush win rate, but Diaby's win rate at edge is in the 97th percentile this season, and he has 3.0 sacks. The Bills are in a tight cap situation, but Diaby is a pending free agent. -- Walder 

 
 

 

 Carolina Panthers (3-4) 
 Chance to make playoffs: 23.6% 
 Projected first-round draft slot: No. 13

 What is the deadline goal?  Find cost-effective help, if possible. The Panthers are in an awkward spot after losing two consecutive games and firing defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero last week. But while they are under .500, they're still leading the NFC South entering Week 9. Carolina needs help at cornerback and on the offensive line. Coach Dave Canales said they're open to improving the roster with a trade, but they'll need to use some salary cap gymnastics (they have less than $1 million in cap space) to make that happen. -- Mike Kaye 

 

 Who could be on the move? Tight end  Ja'Tavion Sanders . Sanders has fallen out of favor in Carolina and was a healthy scratch last Thursday night in Green Bay. Sanders doesn't hold significant value, but perhaps a Day 3 pick swap gets this done. -- Fowler 

 Who should they target? Jets S  Andre Cisco . New York can send a veteran free safety to the contending Panthers in exchange for youth at the position. This would also allow sixth-round rookie Zakee Wheatley more time to develop and improve the Panthers' pass defense, which ranks 21st in DVOA against deep passes. -- Schatz
