title: What 18 contenders should do at the NFL trade deadline: Who could get aggressive?
summary: Should the Giants keep adding? Could the Bills go all-in? Would the Steelers stay conservative? Here's how 18 teams at or above .500 should approach the deadline.
full_text:
Should your favorite team be going all-in at the NFL trade deadline , which hits at 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday? Should it be realistic about its strengths and weaknesses and stay put over the next week? Or is the best plan something in between?

 Today, I'm going to answer those questions for the 18 teams that reached Week 9 at .500 or better. Given their roster and play so far this season, I believe that four teams should stand down at the deadline and avoid sacrificing serious draft capital for any moves. Nobody is going to turn down a steal of a deal if one is available, but those four franchises shouldn't be prioritizing major additions.

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 But as for the rest, I've split the other 14 teams into several tiers, ranging from organizations that should be extremely active at the deadline to ones that should be very selective and careful about making the right move for a very particular sort of player. I'll lay out each team's needs and current situation.

 I'll also name two possible trade candidates for each team. One will be a luxury trade addition, where the team would be adding a starter or even a borderline star to the roster and paying accordingly for the privilege. The other is a bargain deal, where the team would instead be looking for a rotational player or depth for the back of its roster. (Teams are listed alphabetically within each tier.)

 

 
 Jump to: 
 BAL | BUF | CHI | CIN | CLE | DEN 
 DET | GB | JAX | KC | LV | LAR 
 MIN | NE | NYG | PIT | SF | SEA 

 
 

 Should be aggressively adding 
 Let's start with the teams that should be most aggressive in seeking out talent before the deadline and work our way down to the ones that should put their phone on airplane mode.

 

 Buffalo Bills  (6-1) 
 Positions of need: OL, LB, S

 Was Buffalo's 36-10 victory over the Ravens a sign that defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard was able to find the right mix of players and pressures during the bye week or a product of the Ravens being stuck playing Joe Fagnano at quarterback for most of the game? I'd lean more toward the latter than the former, but I also wouldn't be shocked if Leonhard's defense took a step forward after having a week to rest and reflect on what went wrong early in the season. Playing an early-season schedule that included the Lions, Patriots and Rams also didn't help matters for Buffalo, who will now get the Vikings, Jets and Dolphins over the next three weeks.

 

 That self-scouting might determine how aggressive general manager Brandon Beane wants to be at the deadline. The Bills believe in linebackers  Dorian Williams and Terrel Bernard , but adding a cover linebacker to rotate in wouldn't hurt. The Bills also just cut C.J. Gardner-Johnson , who started six games for them earlier this season, so landing a safety who can hold up in coverage would be a helpful move.

 Luxury target: I loved the idea of the Bills going after guard  Quenton Nelson , which would have given them a difference-maker at their weakest spot up front, but that's no longer an option. Would the Cardinals ever be willing to trade safety  Budda Baker , who has made eight Pro Bowls and continues to make an impact as a disruptive force in centerfield and along the line of scrimmage in his age-30 season? Baker is due more than $8 million over the remainder of this season and $17.8 million in 2027, which is the final year of his existing deal.

 Bargain target: If the Chargers are unloading, the Bills might call about cornerback Elijah Molden , who is due $3.3 million over the remainder of the season. The Colts could also be interested in moving 28-year-old Cam Bynum , a move that would save Indy nearly $6 million in cash. Buffalo doesn't have a ton of cap space, but it could restructure  Greg Rousseau 's contract or ask the Cardinals or Colts to retain some money by sending a better pick as part of either deal.

 

 
 

 Detroit Lions  (5-2) 
 Positions of need: DL, LB, CB

 The Lions have seen their rivals in Chicago make a huge move in trading two first-round picks for Jeffery Simmons , and the Packers are also going to get Micah Parsons back from a torn ACL . Yes, the Lions have welcomed Brian Branch back into the lineup and will hope to get Kerby Joseph on the field in the weeks to come, but even with those two safeties in the lineup, the Lions have real questions about their defense.

 Those issues were sadly exacerbated by the neck injury suffered by star linebacker Jack Campbell in the win over the Vikings on Sunday. Campbell's health is more important than any football situation, and it seems callous to talk about replacing him in the lineup. But as one of the better linebackers in the league, the Lions will have to adjust without one of their best players on the field.

 Detroit is fielding the league's fourth-best offense by points allowed per possession, so anything general manager Brad Holmes can do to help the defense would go a long way to getting the Lions to the top of the NFC North. The good news is virtually anything would be of use. A rotational edge rusher to work in with  DJ Wonnum  across from Aidan Hutchinson ? A cover linebacker to help fill in for Campbell? A cornerback -- or even two -- to push Roger McCreary , Rock Ya-Sin  and  Ennis Rakestraw Jr ., none of whom have looked like they are ready to start for a playoff team this season? The Lions don't want to mortgage their future, but finding the right trade would go a long way toward topping their rivals in the division.

 Luxury target: In my column suggesting trades a few weeks ago, I argued for the Lions to swoop for  Khalil Mack and  Donte Jackson in a deal with the Chargers to address both edge and cornerback. That would cost Detroit nearly $8 million over the remainder of the season, a not insignificant amount for any team to take on in the middle of the season. The Lions could trade more draft capital to get the Chargers to pay that total down, but the picks should be more important to Holmes than the cash at the moment.

 Bargain target: Veteran cornerback Mike Hughes was with a very different version of this Lions team in 2022 before leaving for the Falcons in free agency. He has started most of his time there, but after A.J. Terrell Jr . returned from injured reserve, Hughes has been in a reserve role, including a season-low eight defensive snaps during last week's loss to the Buccaneers . He wouldn't be an obvious upgrade on any of the options in Detroit, but the 29-year-old has been a reliable low-end starter at corner for most of his time in Atlanta.

 

 

 
 

 Jacksonville Jaguars  (5-2) 
 Positions of need:  OT, DT, CB, S

 The Jaguars could be one of the few competitive teams to deal away players at the deadline if they decide to move on from wide receiver  Brian Thomas Jr . But most of their calls should be about adding talent to the roster. A swing tackle would be helpful with Anton Harrison expected to miss the remainder of the season and Patrick Mekari  -- who can play either guard or tackle -- on injured reserve after undergoing back surgery before the season.

 General manager James Gladstone might also have to address the defense, which lost defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton and safety Eric Murray to season-ending injuries last week against the Colts . Cornerback might also be a concern, given that Travis Hunter 's offensive role has expanded, which could lead to some series off on defense.  Montaric Brown was having a rough season before suffering a hamstring injury, too. The Jags don't need to add a star on defense, but another solid contributor or two would be big as they enjoy a three-game lead atop the AFC South.

 Luxury target: Eagles defensive tackle Moro Ojomo could be set to follow Milton Williams ' path toward a big contract in free agency. Ojomo's path to the starting lineup in Philadelphia has been buried by the presence of Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis , both of whom are on long-term contracts for significant…

title: Ravens look to stabilize crumbling season with QB Jacoby Brissett
summary: Given the veteran QB's recent track record, it remains to be seen whether Baltimore can truly salvage its season.
full_text:
OWINGS MILLS, Md. -- The Baltimore Ravens have dropped three straight games, lost star quarterback Lamar Jackson indefinitely and watched their playoff hopes quickly crumble. 
 
 Still, Baltimore is not throwing in the towel at the midway point of a 2026 NFL season that's spiraling downward. 
 
 The Ravens are finalizing a trade for Arizona Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett , sources told ESPN's Adam Schefter and NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, which shows they're not giving up on the season. But, given Brissett's track record, the Ravens have a better chance of stabilizing the season than saving it. 
 
 Baltimore (4-4), which is in last place in the AFC North, has a 6.4% chance of making the playoffs and an 0.5% chance of winning the division, according to ESPN Analytics. With such dismal odds and the uncertainty surrounding Jackson, Ravens general manager Eric DeCosta could have considered punting on the final nine games of the season by trading some starters and acquiring more picks for what is supposed to be a loaded 2027 draft . 
 
 Instead, the Ravens are trying to salvage a season that has been devastated by injuries at quarterback. Jackson is expected to go on IR with a right thumb injury he suffered in Sunday's 36-10 loss at the Buffalo Bills and is potentially out for the rest of the season. To make matters worse, Tyler "Snoop" Huntley , Baltimore's top backup, is out for the season with turf toe, according to Schefter and Rapoport. 
 
 The trade is a move that can curb a free fall in Jesse Minter's first year as a head coach and Declan Doyle's first as an offensive playcaller. The veteran Brissett offers hope of fielding a competitive offense. 
 
 
 
 The Ravens are so desperate at quarterback that they're starting undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano , who practiced with a brace on his injured right ankle, for Thursday night's game against the Jacksonville Jaguars . Baltimore's other two active quarterbacks on Thursday are Kedon Slovis and Austin Reed , both of whom were signed within the past three days. This means that the Ravens' three quarterbacks -- Fagnano, Slovis and Reed -- have combined for no previous starts, 23 pass attempts and no touchdown throws. 
 
 Brissett, 33, provides much-needed experience at quarterback but not a winning track record. He's never had a winning record in any of his 11 NFL seasons, losing 16 of his past 19 starts. 
 
 His career record of 23-50 (.315) is the second worst in the NFL among quarterbacks with at least 50 starts over the past decade. The only quarterback with a worse record over that span is Justin Fields (16-37, .302). 
 
 The reason Brissett is available is that he was benched by the Cardinals (3-5) and dropped to No. 3 on the depth chart. Baltimore has familiarity with him because Ravens quarterbacks coach Israel Woolfork was Brissett's quarterbacks coach in Arizona last season.   
 
 Brissett has thrown 86 career touchdowns, which gives Baltimore a chance to get the offense out of its rut. The Ravens have been held to 14 points or less in three straight games, which hadn't happened in Baltimore in 21 years. 
 
 Even though Baltimore has been without Jackson for a majority of the season, the Ravens still have playmakers on offense in running back Derrick Henry and wide receiver Zay Flowers . But over the past three weeks, Baltimore has been among the worst offenses in the league with off-target throws, poor offensive line play and penalties. Since Week 6, the Ravens have totaled more false starts (eight) than touchdowns (three). 
 
 It has been a startling turn of events for the Ravens, who entered the season as one of the Super Bowl favorites and started 4-1. Baltimore's season unraveled after that when Jackson hurt an ankle and hand. 
 
 With half the season left, there are several 30-or-older Ravens who aren't in a position to resign themselves to a lost season, from Henry to defensive end Calais Campbell to offensive tackle Ronnie Stanley . It'll just be a difficult challenge if Jackson doesn't return this season. Baltimore is 7-14 (.333) since 2019 when Jackson hasn't been its starting quarterback. 
 
 The addition of Brissett gives the Ravens a better option at quarterback than they had. But it remains to be seen whether Brissett improves their chances at turning the season around.

title: Could the Panthers make a trade deadline move? 5 potential targets
summary: Let's dive into which players could make sense for a trade for the NFC South-leading team with limited cap space.
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers remain an intriguing team just a few days before the NFL trade deadline on Tuesday at 4 p.m. ET.

 Even at 3-4, the Panthers will be in the mix for a second consecutive NFC South division title, regardless of the results of Week 9's home game against the Denver Broncos (6-2) on Sunday ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ). That's life in the NFC South, where no team is above .500, and the Panthers, despite their up-and-down start to the season, remain at the top entering the midway point of the campaign.

 

 A plausible case can be made for the Panthers to add reinforcements at the deadline. There's also a reasonable case to trade away an expensive and/or underperforming player, especially if a contender offers a quality draft pick in return. General manager Dan Morgan could also, as he did last year, simply stay put with his roster and hope history repeats itself with the Panthers on top of a forgettable divisional scrum in January.

 The Panthers have limited salary cap space ($684,323, as of Wednesday, according to the NFLPA salary cap report). But they have the flexibility -- like all NFL teams -- to maneuver their cap situation with contract restructures that would open up space while pushing current cap charges into the future. Still, it's more likely the Panthers look for a bargain (particularly players on rookie deals) than a big name on the trade market.

 Here's a look at three players who could make sense to add before the deadline and two internal players who might garner trade interest with an advantageous exit:

 

 Three players the Panthers could add: 

 Jackson Powers-Johnson , G/C, Las Vegas Raiders 
 

 Age: 23 | Stats: Seven games (four starts) in 2026; 30 games (25 starts) in three seasons.

 Why Powers-Johnson makes sense for Panthers: Powers-Johnson, a 2024 second-round pick, probably needs a change of scenery after being benched in Las Vegas. He has guard/center versatility, and while the Panthers just activated Brady Christensen's 21-day practice window on injured reserve, Powers-Johnson is cost-effectively signed through 2027 ($1.6 million base salary in 2026 and just under $2 million next year). The former Oregon standout doesn't have to start immediately to be valuable, but he'd be a clear upgrade as the swing interior backup if Christensen or Sam Hecht gets the call to replace center Luke Fortner .

 Why Panthers would pass on Powers-Johnson: The O-lineman hasn't played particularly well under new Raiders coach Klint Kubiak. He is probably a better fit for center, but with Tyler Linderbaum on the roster, he wasn't going to get much of a chance. Powers-Johnson is a better pass blocker than run blocker, and so there might be similar issues with him in Carolina as there have been with Fortner in Brad Idzik's offense. Given their immediate need on the line, the Panthers might not want to give up value for a player who is still finding his place in the NFL.

 

 Will McDonald IV , DE, New York Jets 
 

 Age: 27 | Stats: 14 tackles and three sacks in eight games (two starts); 86 tackles and 24.5 sacks in 55 games (31 starts) in four seasons.

 Why McDonald makes sense for the Panthers: The previous regime -- which Morgan was a part of -- was quite fond of McDonald as a prospect in 2023, multiple sources with knowledge of that year's Panthers draft plans told ESPN. Before the Jets selected McDonald with the No. 15 overall pick, the then-Panthers' brass had "heavily discussed" him as a potential trade-up target later in the draft, one of the sources said. Four years into his New York tenure, McDonald has been an effective situational pass rusher and not much more. Still, the Panthers could use some help in that regard with a 29th-ranked (4.56%) sack rate.

 Why Panthers would pass on McDonald: The Panthers have been terrible against the run for years, and that aspect of their defense is a priority for coach Dave Canales and company down the final stretch of 10 games. McDonald won't offer a whole lot in that regard, and it could be argued he is somewhat redundant with Princely Umanmielen already on the roster. McDonald, while he would come cheap this year ($1.66 million base salary), is set to play on a guaranteed $13.7 million fifth-year option in 2027. And because of McDonald's cost-effectiveness, as well as his pass-rushing success, the Jets aren't likely to part ways with him without a substantial return.

 

 

 Kimani Vidal , RB, Los Angeles Chargers 
 

 Age: 25 | Stats: 29 carries for 132 yards (4.6 YPC) and a touchdown and nine catches for 50 yards and a touchdown in seven games (one start) in 2026; 227 carries for 930 yards (4.1 YPC) and four touchdowns and 30 catches for 248 yards and three touchdowns in 30 games (11 starts) in three seasons.

 Why Vidal makes sense for the Panthers: Chuba Hubbard has taken on a ton of work in the first seven games and already has more rushing yards (540) and total touchdowns (7) than he did in 15 appearances in 2025. The Panthers have playoff aspirations but  Jonathon Brooks  and Trevor Etienne  have yet to prove they can be reliable cogs. Vidal has experience as a starter and a rotational player -- who can be effective as a runner and receiver -- and he would be coming from a Mike McDaniel offense that has influenced Idzik's playcalling.

 Why Panthers would pass on Vidal: A late-round pick swap for a running back on an expiring contract might not interest Morgan, who has invested notable draft capital in Brooks and Etienne. The Panthers plan to have Brooks back in the lineup (he's on IR for a core muscle/groin injury) eventually, and after dedicating a lot of development time to him and Etienne, the Panthers will probably want to see that through this season. Carolina might just want to be patient in the backfield despite the optics of an underwhelming rotation (with a 22nd-ranked rushing attack).

 

 Two players the Panthers could trade away: 

 Robert Hunt , RG, Panthers 
 

 Age: 30 | Stats: Seven games (seven starts) in 2026; 86 games (80 starts) in seven seasons. Voted to Pro Bowl in 2024.

 Why trading Hunt makes sense for the Panthers: Hunt has struggled this season between Fortner and rookie right tackle Monroe Freeling . With Christensen on the mend, perhaps the Panthers could make Hunt available for a notable return.

 

 Christensen had the best stretch of his career at right guard, while filling in for Hunt, in the middle of last season, and with the interior line trade market fielding high demands -- Cam Jurgens and Quenton Nelson both warranted historic hauls in midseason swaps -- it might make sense to at least consider moving on from the 2024 Pro Bowl lineman. Trading Hunt would open up $19 million in cap space next year, per Over The Cap.

 Why Panthers would pass on Hunt trade: The Panthers' offensive line depth is a mess right now. The starting lineup has had its lumps, so it's fair to wonder what Hunt would bring in return, especially as the front office isn't likely to just give him away. While opening up cap space and getting something for Hunt sounds appealing on paper, a team with playoff aspirations probably shouldn't risk moving on from a proven talent in the middle of a postseason push.

 

 Ja'Tavion Sanders , TE, Panthers 
 

 Age: 23 | Stats: Healthy inactive for all seven games this season; 62 catches for 532 yards yards and two touchdowns in 29 games (13 starts) in his career.

 Why trading Sanders makes sense for the Panthers: The tight end hasn't played all season. Earlier this week, ESPN NFL analyst Benjamin Solak mused about Sanders being sent to the Chicago Bears for a sixth-round pick. Given Sanders' lack of a role, a deal like that might appeal to the Panthers, who have effectively used a rotation of Tommy Tremble , Darren Waller and Mitchell Evans at the position, plus Feleipe Franks on special teams. Sanders, a 2024 fourth-round pick, clearly needs a change of scenery, and his draft pedigree and long-term cost effectiveness (signed on…

title: NFL survivor power rankings: Why this is the week to use Seahawks, Chiefs
summary: ESPN NFL survivor pool strategy, predictions and ranking the top seven options for Week 9.
full_text:
Only 1.9% of total entries remain entering Week 9 on ESPN Survivor, though it was nearly much less. The Cincinnati Bengals needed a late fourth-quarter comeback to hold off the Tennessee Titans in overtime, saving 27% of the remaining ESPN Survivor entries. It would have been the third straight week with a double-digit upset.

 Only three favorites ended up losing last week, but the Dallas Cowboys knocked out another 13% of entries, blowing a 14-point 4th-quarter lead at home against the Arizona Cardinals . It was the third time this season the Cardinals have won as at least a seven-point underdog, all on the road.

 

 This week, the Cardinals are once again big road underdogs as they visit the Seattle Seahawks . The Seahawks are the biggest favorites of the week, but surprisingly, they are only 17% selected as of Wednesday morning on ESPN. If that number is accurate, Seattle is the obvious pick.

 The Seahawks are coming off a double-digit loss in prime-time, while the Cardinals are coming off another huge upset last week. That combination could scare some players off Seattle, though I expect them to be the chalk pick in higher stakes contests.

 Instead, the Detroit Lions are getting the most selection at 31%. If that number is close to accurate, they are a pretty easy fade with several other big favorites out there including the Kansas City Chiefs , San Francisco 49ers and Jacksonville Jaguars . None of those three teams are widely available, but if you have them, this is a good week to use them at lower rates.

 If you're looking to burn a lower-quality team, the Dallas Cowboys make sense on the road in Indianapolis, but the Cowboys host the Tennessee Titans and Philadelphia Eagles in Weeks 11 and 12. The Chicago Bears (vs. Tampa Bay Buccaneers ), Houston Texans (at Los Angeles Chargers ), Los Angeles Rams (at Washington Commanders ) and New York Giants (at Philadelphia Eagles) are the other teams with any viability this week.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings and subject to change. Future value based on Mike Clay's cheat sheet .  

 1. Seattle Seahawks (vs. Arizona Cardinals ) 
 

 The biggest question regarding the Seahawks is what you think their selection rate will be. At 17%, they are an easy choice. If they cross the 30% mark, which I think is very possible in sharp contests, then there's much more of a debate. The Seahawks still have several usable games left, including a three-week stretch against the Cowboys (home), Giants (home) and Eagles (road) in Weeks 13-15, but this is by far their easiest spot. Seattle is on a short week, but Arizona is playing its third road game in four weeks. While the Cardinals have been friskier than expected, two of those upset wins have come against the Chargers and Cowboys, who are a combined 3-12 this season, so the Seahawks should prove to be a tougher test.

 
 Chance to win: 82% (ESPN Analytics), 87% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Seahawks -12.5 (-700 moneyline) 
 Future value: Seventh 
 Availability: 81% 
 ESPN Selection: 17% 
 
 Editor's Note: This article was published prior to Seattle announcing Drew Locke will start instead of Sam Darnold (quad) and will be updated. 

 2. Kansas City Chiefs (vs New York Jets ) 
 

 If you still have the Chiefs, this is a great week to spend them, and they are my top choice in sharper contests where you expect Seattle to be more heavily picked. They are just 28% available on ESPN, but they do not have many usable spots coming up. Week 11 at home against the Cardinals looks great, but it looks like that week will have plenty of other similarly strong options. After that, they probably aren't usable again until Weeks 17 and 18 (at Chargers, vs Raiders). The Chiefs won't take the Jets lightly coming off back-to-back losses, and while New York's offense has improved of late, their defense has regressed significantly.

 
 Chance to win: 80% (ESPN Analytics), 79% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Chiefs -9.5 (-575 moneyline) 
 Future value: 15th 
 Availability: 28% 
 ESPN Selection: 12% 
 

 3. San Francisco 49ers (vs. Las Vegas Raiders ) 

 Normally a double-digit favorite at 4% selection would be an easy call, but taking the Chiefs gives you a little more flexibility down the road than the 49ers. The 49ers' top matchups after this week will be Week 17 (vs. Eagles), Week 15 (at Chargers) and Week 13 (at Giants).

 
 Chance to win: 84% (ESPN Analytics), 85% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: 49ers -10 (-535 moneyline) 
 Future value: Fifth 
 Availability: 29% 
 ESPN Selection: 4% 
 

 4. Jacksonville Jaguars (at Baltimore Ravens ) 
 

 The Jaguars are a similar case to the 49ers, but they have more future value. They still have two games left against the Titans and several more relatively easy matchups down the stretch. As a result, I probably would save them again and opt for one of the favorites above them, but they are clearly a plus-EV pick this week, so I can't blame you if you take them. Remember, this game is Thursday night, so make your pick early.

 
 Chance to win: 81% (ESPN Analytics), 92% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Jaguars -10 (-535 moneyline) 
 Future value: First 
 Availability: 47% 
 ESPN Selection: 7% 
 

 5. Chicago Bears (vs. Tampa Bay Buccaneers ) 

 

 The biggest question with taking the Bears now is how you want to handle Week 14 when they visit the Dolphins. They will likely be the heavy chalk that week, so if you use the Bears now at lower selection, it helps you get off that pick later, especially if you can save the Lions or Seahawks. I would be less willing to use them in contests that have multi-pick weeks, as the Bears will have several other games they are smaller favorites in. But in single-pick pools, they aren't a bad contrarian choice.

 
 Chance to win: 63% (ESPN Analytics), 75% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Bears -6 (-290 moneyline) 
 Future value: Fourth 
 Availability: 80% 
 ESPN Selection: 8% 
 

 6. Dallas Cowboys (at Indianapolis Colts ) 

 This would purely be an selection play, as the Cowboys are unlikely to be popular this week. While they do have two more really strong weeks in Weeks 11 and 12 (vs. Titans, vs. Eagles), that might be it for them in terms of future value. And Week 11 should have plenty of other options. The Cowboys have already lost twice this season as even bigger favorites, but the Colts are quickly joining the NFL's bottom tier, so being able to fade them at low ownership is an appealing contrarian option.

 
 Chance to win: 61% (ESPN Analytics), 71% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Cowboys -6 (-285 moneyline) 
 Future value: 10th 
 Availability: 85% 
 ESPN Selection: 5% 
 

 7. Detroit Lions (at Miami Dolphins ) 

 

 The Lions are likely to be higher selected than their win probability would suggest. That's especially true on ESPN when they are currently 31% selected. While I think the number will be lower in a lot of pools, it's hard to justify a popular -355 favorite over a number of slightly smaller favorites at significantly lower selection rates. Their schedule is tough after this, but they still host the Titans in Week 14, the Buccaneers in Week 11 and the Giants in Week 16, so there is merit in saving them.

 
 Chance to win: 78% (ESPN Analytics), 70% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Lions -7 (-355 moneyline) 
 Future value: Ninth 
 Availability: 56% 
 ESPN Selection: 31%

title: Wetzel: $17 billion Cowboys have a penny-pinching owner in Jerry Jones
summary: The owner of the most valuable sports franchise insists there's no correlation between coaching salaries and winning. Let's pause for the skepticism.
full_text:
Jerry Jones has spent more than three decades claiming the Dallas Cowboys are one great decision away from getting back to a Super Bowl.

 On Tuesday, the Cowboys' owner and general manager offered a new explanation for why that hasn't happened: He doesn't believe paying for great decision-makers is particularly important.

 Jones was asked on 105.3 the Fan in Dallas about the perception he doesn't spend top dollar when hiring head coaches. Jones responded by saying he was too smart for that.

 "In the NFL, this is after years of looking at all the teams and all the coaches, there is zero correlation between how much you pay a coach or how many coaches you have as to winning," he told the radio station. "There is no correlation. And that's a random sample of years and all 32 teams involved. So put that in your hopper and smoke it."

 That's quite a bit to put in the hopper, particularly from the owner of a franchise that hasn't appeared in even an NFC Championship Game since the 1995 season.

 

 It's particularly stunning considering the Cowboys are the most valuable sports franchise in not just the NFL or the United States, but the entire world. How is Dallas, of all places, playing some version of small-market, resource-limited Moneyball?

 The immediate issue is coach Brian Schottenheimer , whose Cowboys are 3-5 after blowing a 14-point lead and losing to the  Arizona Cardinals  in overtime on Sunday.

 Schottenheimer went 7-9-1 in his first season and is now 10-14-1 as an NFL head coach. He is reportedly making somewhere between $5 million and $8 million annually, making him one of the league's lowest-paid head coaches .

 That would be an interesting arrangement for almost any franchise. For Dallas, it is patently ridiculous.

 Forbes estimates the Cowboys are worth $17 billion , a whopping 25% more than the NFL's second-most-valuable franchise, the Los Angeles Rams , which the publication valued at $13.5 billion. In 2025, Dallas delivered $677 million in operating income on $1.28 billion in revenue.

 This isn't an owner trying to scrape together enough money to keep the lights on. Jerry Jones can afford any coach he wants, but apparently he has decided that the market's going rate is an unnecessary expense.

 Or, as a coaching agent told NFL Network's Jane Slater when asked how aggressive Jones had been in looking for a veteran coach after the 2024 season: "Jerry won't pay $13M and up, and that's the starting point."

 Instead, Dallas promoted Schottenheimer, its own offensive coordinator and a longtime assistant. The Cowboys were the only team to interview him that year. Schottenheimer might prove to be a good coach despite his 10-14-1 start, but should the most valuable team on the planet be led by a guy who has to grow into the job?

 The NFL does all it can to level the competitive playing field and limit any advantage a legacy, big-market franchise or extremely wealthy owner might have. There is a hard salary cap, a college draft that favors losing teams and a weighted regular-season schedule. Any Given Sunday is the motto.

 What it doesn't restrict is spending on everything else -- from head coaches and full staffs that might better train and prepare teams to personnel departments that might better identify and acquire talent.

 

 Yet, given the chance to use the franchise's considerable resources on such things, Jones has chosen to not just punt, but dismiss the concept. He, himself, famously doubles as the team's general manager, despite the Cowboys' repeated stumbles and the fact the job has become increasingly complex.

 Jones' insistence that there is no correlation between coaching salaries and winning deserves skepticism. Recent Super Bowl-winning coaches, including Andy Reid, Sean McVay and Bill Belichick, have been highly compensated by league standards.

 Jones could also look up in the NFC East standings where the first-place New York Giants are experiencing an immediate return on investment from hiring John Harbaugh, at the sum of $20 million per year, according to ESPN's Adam Schefter .

 Writing a blank check does not automatically produce a Vince Lombardi Trophy. The players matter the most. Coaching is complicated.

 But the absence of a guarantee is not evidence that an investment has no value. In the meantime, the Cowboys' actual value keeps going up even as the title drought continues.

 At some point, the question isn't whether Jerry Jones can find the right formula to deliver a winner.

 It's why the richest team in football thinks it's actually smart to not bother investing in one of the few places where the franchise's wealth might actually be an asset.

title: How Gary Kubiak paved the way for his sons, Klint, Klay and Klein, in the NFL
summary: Klint, Klay and Klein Kubiak are all on their respective NFL journeys. But their father, Gary, helped each along the way.
full_text:
LEVI'S STADIUM HAS provided special memories for Gary Kubiak and his family. It was the place where he won Super Bowl 50 as the  Denver Broncos ' head coach. Ten years later, his eldest son, Klint, as an offensive coordinator also won in the same stadium, helping the Seattle Seahawks earn the Super Bowl LX title.

 And during the Las Vegas Raiders ' Week 9 game against the San Francisco 49ers , another family memory will be created in Santa Clara, California, on Sunday ( 4:25 p.m. ET, Fox ). On one sideline, Klint, 39, will be leading the Raiders as a first-time head coach. Across the field, his brother Klay, 38, will help 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan as the offensive coordinator. Meanwhile, the youngest of the three brothers, Klein, 35, will sit in the press box doing advanced scouting ahead of the  Dallas Cowboys ' Week 10 matchup against San Francisco.

 "It's weird how the world works," Klein, a national scout/special projects for Dallas since 2022, told ESPN.

 

 Gary, 65, never imagined his three sons would follow his path of working in the NFL. But they were destined to.

 As Gary served as the offensive coordinator in Denver from 1995 to 2005, working for Kyle's father and former head coach, Mike, his kids were around football almost 24/7, forging their passion for the sport.

 Gary, who was quarterback John Elway's backup in Denver from 1983 to 1991, is also known for his four Super Bowl victories (three as an assistant and one as a head coach in 2016) with the Broncos and recording 63 wins as the  Houston Texans ' coach from 2006 to 2013. But his greatest accomplishment could very well be the football legacy he created with his kids.

 Klint, one of the league's most respected offensive minds, is the second head coach in his family and a key figure in the Raiders' rebuild. Klay, in the midst of his sixth season with the 49ers and second as the team's offensive coordinator, is on track to follow in his brother's footsteps as the next head coach in the Kubiak household. And Klein is building on a respectable career as a scout.

 Each brother's journey is unique. The commonality is Gary's impact and how they have embodied their father's ideologies along the way.

 "I knew if [Gary's kids] wanted to get into coaching, they'd be great because of everything that their dad did," former Broncos coach Mike Shanahan, a two-time Super Bowl champion, told ESPN. "[Gary] took as much pride as any football coach would take, knowing that when he got his opportunity, he didn't want to let anybody down. I think his kids take right after him.

 "It's pretty obvious why the Kubiaks have had so much success as a family."

 
 

 KLINT DIDN'T THINK he wanted to be a football coach. But when he sat in on the Texans' draft meetings in 2009, listening to his father and other coaches talk about defensive ends, he began to have a change of heart.

 "I think they were maybe studying [defensive end Jason] Pierre-Paul that day," Klint, a Texas native, said. "... I just saw this big room full of guys just talking football, and then when the meetings were over, I was in the coach's locker room, and it was my dad and all the coaches, and they were just sitting there and shooting the bull.

 "I just remember thinking at that moment, like, 'Man, this isn't such a bad job.'"

 Klint played wide receiver and defensive back at Colorado State from 2005 to 2009. After his playing days were over, Klint received a taste of the family business. He was an offensive quality control coach (2010-11) and a graduate assistant at Texas A&M (2012), working with wide receivers such as Mike Evans (new to the 49ers this season).

 Initially, Klint wanted to work on defense, given his playing background as a DB. Two weeks into the job, then-Texas A&M coach Mike Sherman, who also spent five seasons as the Green Bay Packers coach and was on Gary's staff in Houston, told Klint that he wanted someone else to take his job. And so Klint had to be an offensive graduate assistant.

 "I was really upset about it. ... Then it ended up being the best thing that ever happened to me," Klint said.

 David Beaty, the Aggies' wide receivers coach in 2012, said Klint wasn't your "normal graduate assistant." He said Klint was a self-starter, always going the extra mile, and incorporated his own ideas to make plays easier for the players.

 

 "[Klint] could've been the full-time wide receiver coach," Beaty told ESPN. "This guy's work ethic was second to none [to anyone] I've ever been around."

 Beaty called Klint a "football junkie." No one could beat Klint into the building in the morning, and no one knew if he ever went home. When the team returned to campus from road games, Klint went straight to the office to grade wide receivers while everyone else went home.

 Beaty added that Klint spent an enormous amount of time breaking down video of opponents' defensive fronts, coverages and blitzes, providing an accurate report for him and Kliff Kingsbury, the Aggies offensive coordinator at the time, to use.

 Even though Klint wasn't sure he wanted to be a head coach, Beaty saw the signs.

 "He was the best nurse that a doctor could have," Beaty said. "When you came in, all you had to do was grab the scalpel and go to work."

 Evans, who was a freshman at the time, said Klint instilled confidence in him by watching film and critiquing his game.

 "Klint is the man. I love that guy," Evans said. "When you're 17, 18 years old, you ain't thinking about, 'Oh, this guy's going to be a great head coach one day.' I'm just like, 'Man, he definitely knows what he's talking about. I should listen to him."

 But being a graduate assistant didn't pay enough. Klint was married to his wife, Tessa, and even though none of his four children were born yet, Klint felt like he was letting his family down and wanted to try something new. So he left Texas A&M and worked at an oil field in Texas. Two weeks into his new job, Klint realized he missed being a part of a team. Klint appreciated his time at the oil field, but he belonged in football.

 A few months later, in 2013, Kubiak became an offensive quality control coach for the Minnesota Vikings before transitioning back to the college level.

 

 In December 2014, Beaty became the coach at Kansas, and as he was filling out his staff, he reached out to Kubiak about becoming the Jayhawks' wide receivers coach.

 Kubiak's first full-time coaching job didn't feature any team success. The Jayhawks finished 0-12 -- one of three times in program history they compiled a winless record.

 While in Kansas, Klint was itching to return to the NFL, where he didn't have to worry about recruiting -- only football. To his benefit, an opportunity to work for Gary in Denver opened. Brian Callahan left his offensive assistant position for the Broncos to become the  Detroit Lions ' quarterbacks coach, leaving an opening on Gary's staff.

 Previously, Klint never wanted to work for his father. He was aware of the stigma attached to being a coach's kid. In Klint's words, he didn't want to feel like the son who automatically landed on third base because of his parent.

 Klint softened on the idea, viewing it as a chance to spend more time with his dad, but also learn from him. But if he took the Broncos' job, Klint was determined to be the hardest-working person in the building.

 "That's always been something really important to me," Klint said. "Like if I got a chance to work for my dad, I want to make sure I did it the right way."

 Beaty thought so highly of Klint that he was prepared to offer the offensive coordinator job to convince him to stay.

 However, Klint's heart was made up.

 Klint spent three years as the Broncos' offensive assistant. He went back to Minnesota, where he served as a quarterbacks coach (2019-20) and offensive coordinator (2021). Minnesota was 12th in points (25 per game) and 14th in total yards (362.8) in Klint's lone season as the offensive playcaller. Since then,…

title: Chiefs' floundering pass rush starts with Chris Jones: 'I always can be better'
summary: Jones, 32, is off to another slow start, recording only 0.5 sacks through seven games. But he's not worried.
full_text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- Last week, Kansas City Chiefs defensive lineman Chris Jones admitted the obvious: Like in each of the past two years, he's off to a slow start.

 But even by Jones' usual high standards, his production this season -- or lack of it -- has been more than just slow. It's been snail-like.

 Through seven games, Jones, a six-time All-Pro, has generated 13 tackles (tied for 421st among all defenders), three quarterback hits (tied for 134th), two pass deflections (tied for 156th), a fumble recovery (tied for ninth) and half of a sack (tied for 261st).

 

 "I always can be better," Jones said last week. "I'm my biggest critic."

 Although Jones is still quick once the ball is snapped, he has been unable to make the splashy, highlight-worthy plays that typically define his game. Too often, the opposing quarterback has been able to evade Jones to either complete a pass or scramble for a positive gain.

 Over the past two games -- losses to the Seattle Seahawks and the Denver Broncos -- Jones has failed to record a tackle, a pass deflection or a quarterback hit in his 87 combined snaps.

 Jones' play is reflected in the advanced metrics, too. Entering Sunday's game against the New York Jets (1 p.m. ET, CBS), he has produced 14 pressures (tied for 25th) and has a pass rush win rate of 13.1% (ranked 35th) when playing from the interior, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. Through seven games last season, Jones had 20 pressures (tied for 11th) and a pass rush win rate of 18.6% when playing from the interior (fifth).

 As the Chiefs' oldest and longest-tenured defender, Jones, 32, refused to use his age as a reason for his decline.

 "I feel pretty good," he said. "It's all about perspective, again, how you look at it. I've played a lot of games, fortunately. I've been very, very blessed to be successful in this league for a long time. I've seen a lot. I don't think my age right now is playing a factor. We've just got to take advantage of those opportunities when they present themselves."

 One issue is the number of double-teams Jones has faced. Against the Seahawks and Broncos, Jones, who has seen the eighth-most double-teams in the league, was regularly double-teamed.

 

 "I mean, that's part of the game," Jones said. "It's expected. For me, it's capitalizing on moments I don't get double-teamed. We can't fight the respect level of being double-teamed. I have to take advantage of those opportunities when they present themselves."

 He had limited such opportunities against Denver on Sunday. One came in the first quarter: Jones, who had a one-on-one with right guard Quinn Meinerz , won the battle quickly and forced quarterback Bo Nix into an incompletion on a third-and-2 snap that led to a punt. The matchup between the two occurred again early in the second quarter. This time, Nix negated Jones' beating Meinerz by climbing the pocket and connecting with receiver Jaylen Waddle for a 35-yard gain.

 For much of the rest of the game, the Broncos either doubled Jones or had Nix pass from designed rollouts away from wherever Jones lined up.

 "Chris is giving it his all," coach Andy Reid said Monday. "He's doing everything he can do. He gets doubled from various angles. He's going to draw a lot of attention. That's an advantage to the other guy to have a chance to get themselves home. As much emphasis is put on Chris, let's take advantage of that and get ourselves on the quarterback. Just not to the quarterback, but on the quarterback."

 Compounding the issue is the Chiefs' other pass rushers not named Jones or George Karlaftis -- such as defensive ends Felix Anudike-Uzomah , Ashton Gillotte and rookie R Mason Thomas -- haven't consistently won the one-on-one matchups Jones' presence has been creating for them. On Sunday, the Chiefs pressured Nix on only two of his 34 dropbacks (6%), marking the lowest pressure rate by any team in a game this season.

 

 Jones voiced his frustration after Sunday's game.

 "It's only one thing: Rush the passer, get the quarterback down," Jones said. "We blocked a couple of balls, but I don't think we got [Nix] down. I put that on the D-line. We've got to win our one-on-ones. We've got to take advantage of that. We get a one-on-one, we've got to win it."

 The Chiefs have collected nine sacks all season, which is tied with the New York Giants and the Miami Dolphins for the fewest in the league. Before the season began, the team was optimistic they had improved their pass rush after recording the fifth-fewest sacks (35) in the league (the D-line recorded 21.5).

 There's plenty of season left to play, however, and defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo is hopeful Jones particularly will have a pass-rushing revival, starting with Sunday's game against the Jets.

 "We're just going to rely on him to find a way to win," Spagnuolo said of Jones. "Hopefully, at some point, it all falls together."

 Last season, Jones played his best in the Chiefs' final 10 games. During that stretch, he recorded five sacks and had a pass rush win rate of 20.5%, the fifth-highest mark in the league. That performance also included successful rushes that led to 16 incompletions, according to NFL Next Gen Stats.

 That's why Jones believes he can have another memorable second half in 2026, one that helps the Chiefs return to the postseason.

 "I watch a lot of Kobe Bryant, and he [talked] about adversity and how you'll face storms," Jones said last week. "You've got to be ready when a storm passes. Eventually, it's going to pass. I don't waver my faith or my belief in myself or my work ethic that I put in."

title: Return of 'Kirko Chainz' and In-N-Out runs: Kirk Cousins brings joy to Raiders
summary: From reviving 'Kirko Chainz' to treating teammates to In-N-Out, Cousins is encouraging the Raiders to find joy.
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev. --- It took eight weeks into Kirk Cousins ' tenure with the Las Vegas Raiders for the veteran quarterback to unlock his alter ego, "Kirko Chainz."

 

 The Raiders defeated the New York Jets 38-33 in comeback fashion on the road Sunday, snapping a four-game losing streak and improving to 4-4 -- the first time the team has been .500 or better through eight games since 2021. The accomplishment caused much-needed celebration, so on the long flight back to Las Vegas, Cousins took off his shirt and let his teammates place several expensive chains around his neck and watches on his wrist.

 "It's been a while. The longer the flight, the more likely the chains," said Cousins, who recorded four total touchdowns in the win.

 

 "Kirko Chainz" originated in 2022 when he started for the Minnesota Vikings . Cousins helped complete a comeback win over the Washington Commanders to improve to 7-1. On the return trip, Cousins went viral when a video of him swaying to Florida rapper Real Boston Richey's song, "Bullseye 2," while wearing his teammates' jewelry, circulated across the internet.

 Raiders running back Dylan Laube was on the New Hampshire Wildcats when Cousins first channeled his alternate personality. Laube said it was cool to see at the time, but seeing Kirko Chainz in person was "funny."

 "I mean, he loves the attention," said Laube, who was named AFC Special Teams Player of the Week. "... He's just an unreal person."

 Raiders starting cornerback Eric Stokes said he "threw a little something" on Cousins' wrist. The large Millennium Ring necklace, which is from the iconic Japanese anime television series "Yu-Gi-Oh," came from defensive tackle Adam Butler .

 All-Pro defensive end Maxx Crosby said he contributed in a big way, giving Cousins multiple watches and chains.

 "Kirk is the man. ... One of the funnier dudes you'll ever meet," Crosby said. "He probably [has] the most dad vibe energy on the planet."

 The return of Kirko Chainz is one of the ways Cousins has brought joy to the Raiders this season. He generated smiles and laughter in the locker room with his "wellness" celebration after he snuck into the end zone for a touchdown in the third quarter against New York.

 

 Postgame, Cousins said his touchdown dance was a nod to the team's training staff. On Wednesday, he admitted Laube created the dance.

 "I don't get my own jokes, I steal them from other people, and then I'm just a better megaphone," Cousins said. "Dylan came up with it, and then I was like, 'I'm going to use that.'"

 Cousins has also led trips to In-N-Out Burger after every win. He invited more players each time, but the trips halted for a month during the team's losing skid. As the weeks grew and the losses mounted, Cousins said In-N-Out started sounding better.

 He promised his teammates a visit to In-N-Out near the team's training facility if they won. On Sunday night, Cousins treated No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza , left tackle Kolton Miller , tight end Brock Bowers , Laube and others to a postgame meal.

 "In-N-Out's not that expensive," Cousins said. "You put your card down; it doesn't go too far, which is nice."

 Before the Raiders win over New York, head coach Klint Kubiak asked Cousins to speak to the team about playing with joy. Cousins told his teammates that comparison is a thief of joy. And don't allow the league, which consists of making a ton of comparisons, to strip away their joy for the game.

 "He brings that joy every single day," Laube said. "This guy is 38, and he's still bringing that same energy as if he was a kid."

title: Is DeForest Buckner's 'nostalgic' trade return the final piece for the 49ers?
summary: After being traded from the 49ers in 2020, Buckner is back in the Bay Area. The goal for him and his teammates is the same as it was before: Super Bowl or bust.
full_text:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- For the better part of the past month, defensive tackle DeForest Buckner patiently waited for his phone to ring.

 With the Indianapolis Colts struggling and a rebuild underway , Buckner wanted to be traded somewhere he could play meaningful November and December games and pursue Super Bowl championships again. There was only one place he envisioned doing that: San Francisco, the place he began his NFL career.

 "I didn't want to go anywhere else," Buckner said. "This is where I wanted to be."

 

 When the San Francisco 49ers and Colts consummated the trade Oct. 27, with the Niners  sending a 2027 fourth-round pick to Indianapolis in exchange for Buckner, that call finally came.

 Upon getting word from new Colts general manager Ed Dodds that he was, indeed, going back to the team that drafted him No. 7 in 2016, Buckner said he dropped to his knees and began praying.

 "It's just crazy the way everything happened," Buckner said. "God, he'll open doors you thought were closed and he was able to open this one back up for me. I'm just trying to make the most of this opportunity."

 Buckner's return to the Bay Area isn't just some sentimental reunion. Sure, he joins receiver  Deebo Samuel Sr . and linebacker Dre Greenlaw as former 49ers to return in 2026, but there is no hiding from what they hope to get from Buckner -- and what he hopes to get from them -- this time around.

 When Buckner last played in a Niners uniform, he was trudging off the field following a devastating loss to the Kansas City Chiefs in Super Bowl LIV . Although that was in February 2020, the 49ers have seven players still on their roster from that game, now including Buckner.

 The rest of the list is made up of Greenlaw, Samuel, fullback  Kyle Juszczyk , tight end  George Kittle , defensive end  Nick Bosa and linebacker  Fred Warner . It's no coincidence that as Buckner's name picked up steam in trade rumors, that group spearheaded the efforts to bring him back.

 Bosa mentioned the idea of trading for Buckner to coach Kyle Shanahan a couple of months ago. Kittle and Juszczyk discussed it with other teammates and personnel types, remaining in contact with Buckner while he was in Indy. Buckner also heard directly from Greenlaw and Samuel at various points. That group holds a bond that Buckner said will "never be broken" from their previous time together.

 A common theme in the conversations that group has had over the years? Their shared unfinished business, not just from the Super Bowl loss but in the time that has elapsed since. In some ways, it would make getting over the hump and claiming the franchise's sixth Lombardi Trophy this season even sweeter.

 "It would make a good documentary if we did it," Bosa joked. "Obviously having him back ... we want to do it this year."

 

 To be sure, the Niners wouldn't have prioritized bringing Buckner back if they didn't think he could be more than a temporary energy boost. The need for help on the defensive line already existed in the preseason with questions at tackle, and that has only grown after injuries to  Alfred Collins ( patellar tendon ) and C.J. West ( knee ). Rookie Gracen Halton has emerged as part of the DT rotation, but Buckner's presence should set an example for young players such as Halton and lighten their workload so they can have more success on the field.

 Since entering the NFL in 2016, Buckner is one of four players with at least 75 sacks and 25 batted passes, joining Pittsburgh's  T.J. Watt , New Orleans'  Cameron Jordan and Kansas City's  Chris Jones . At 32, Buckner has 4.0 sacks this season, which would already put him atop the 49ers' list.

 The team hopes Buckner's addition and the eventual return of Bosa, who is aiming to play Sunday against the Raiders after missing five games because of a calf injury , should generate a more consistent pass rush without having to blitz. Through seven games, the Niners are getting pressure on just 23% of opponent dropbacks when they rush four, the second-lowest mark in the NFL. And though Buckner is more of a classic 3-technique, similar to Osa Odighizuwa and Halton, he still commands -- and beats -- double-teams on a regular basis. That should allow Buckner to play next to Odighizuwa on the interior.

 "You start in a spot, but you have to be interchangeable," Shanahan said. "I see it as you've got two inside guys."

 

 At kickoff against the Raiders, Buckner will be in his familiar spot, wearing his usual No. 99 after West offered it up without asking for anything in return -- though Buckner said he will take care of West for the gesture.

 Sunday will mark 2,471 days since Buckner last played for the Niners. In some ways, after six-plus seasons in Indianapolis, it will have felt like an eternity. In others, flanked once more by Greenlaw, Bosa and Warner, it will feel like he never left at all.

 But for Buckner, it will be the first step toward finishing what he and other foundational 49ers started almost a decade ago.

 "Me coming back, it's great," Buckner said. "It's a little nostalgic, but there's still a job to do.

 "It's Super Bowl or bust, and you don't want to be anywhere else. And that's why you play the game to form a legacy and to bring the organization back to the top. That's why I came."
